# Quick Start



**PerturbGen** is a foundation model that predicts how genetic perturbations reshape cellular state trajectories in scRNA-seq data. This page takes you from a fresh clone to your first in-silico perturbation in four stages: **install → tokenize → train (two stages) → perturb**. Everything you need to run the shipped pretrained encoder and tokenizer dictionaries comes bundled with the repository — only your own AnnData and, for training, a CUDA GPU are required.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L13), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L1-L30), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L5)

## PerturbGen at a Glance

The system follows a fixed data-to-prediction pipeline. A preprocessed AnnData (raw counts in `.X`, Ensembl gene IDs as the `var` index) is converted into a **tokenized dataset** on CPU; a frozen pretrained **scMASKGIT encoder** is then fine-tuned as a masking model, which in turn feeds a **count decoder** trained with a ZINB loss; finally the trained model performs in-silico gene perturbations (e.g., a knockout of *IL1B* at 6 h predicting the 10 h state). The diagram below shows the full data flow — read it left to right, and note that only the tokenizer step runs without a GPU.
Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L1-L30), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L697-L713)

![PerturbGen architecture overview](https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen/blob/main/docs/architecture.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L7-L9)

The same pipeline is exposed through **two surfaces**: an installable `perturbgen` CLI (four commands) and a scvi-tools-style Python API (`import perturbgen as pg`) that runs everything in-process — the API is the recommended entry point for beginners because it requires no shell argument lists and returns paths/checkpoints directly.
Sources: [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L1-L30), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L12-L14), [installation.rst](/docs/installation.rst#L44-L72)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Preprocessed AnnData\n(raw counts, Ensembl IDs)"] -->|"pg.tokenize / tokenise\n(CPU only)"| B["Tokenized dataset\nT_perturb/tokenized_data/"]
    B -->|"train_masking() / train-mask"| C["Stage 1: Masking model\n(frozen scMASKGIT encoder)"]
    B -->|"train_count() / train-decoder"| D["Stage 2: Count decoder\n(ZINB loss)"]
    C -->|"masking checkpoint"| D
    C -->|"get_embeddings() / extract-embedding"| F["Cell & gene embeddings"]
    D -->|"perturb(genes, mode)"| E["In-silico perturbation\n+ predicted target states"]
```

Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L697-L713)

## Step 0 — Install the Environment

Clone the repository, install [Poetry](https://python-poetry.org) once, then build the pinned Python 3.11 environment. Poetry resolves every dependency exactly (the lock file pins NumPy 2.2.0, PyTorch Lightning, `datasets`, and ~200 more packages), so avoid mixing in `pip install` upgrades until you know what you need.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L14-L31), [installation.rst](/docs/installation.rst#L5-L25), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L7-L80)

```shell
git clone https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen.git
cd Perturbgen
curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -   # one-time Poetry install
poetry env use python3.11
poetry install
source "$(poetry env info -p)/bin/activate"
pip install -e .    # registers the `perturbgen` CLI entry point
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L14-L31), [installation.rst](/docs/installation.rst#L14-L33), [installation.rst](/docs/installation.rst#L44-L55), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L12-L14)

**Hardware requirements** differ sharply by stage: tokenization and inference notebooks run on CPU (≥32 GB RAM recommended for larger datasets), while training requires CUDA. At the tutorial default `batch_size=64`, a full epoch peaks at **13.8 GB** (masking stage) and **15.8 GB** (count-decoder stage) of GPU memory — comfortable on 24 GB cards such as the RTX 3090/4090, tight on 16 GB.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L32-L48)

| Setup component | Requirement / Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11 (fixed via Poetry) | `poetry env use python3.11` |
| Tokenization | CPU, ≥32 GB RAM | No GPU, no encoder checkpoint needed |
| Training (masking) | CUDA GPU, ~13.8 GB peak @ batch 64 | 24 GB GPUs recommended |
| Training (count decoder) | CUDA GPU, ~15.8 GB peak @ batch 64 | Lower `batch_size` on 16 GB GPUs |
| Multi-GPU | Automatic (`devices=-1`) | DDP default; DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 via `--parallel_distribution deepspeed` |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L32-L48), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L64-L68), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L662-L670)

Training and inference log to **Weights & Biases**, which is **offline by default** — runs are saved locally (re-upload later with `wandb sync`) and never hang on authentication, which matters on machines without internet. To log live, either `export WANDB_MODE=online` or pass `--wandb_mode online`; point runs at your own account with `--wandb_entity <your-team>`.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L50-L68), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L190-L201)

> [!TIP]
> Trainings use `batch_size=64` by default to reproduce paper numbers, and `torch.compile` is enabled for the masking model on the CLI. Inside Jupyter, the Python API automatically disables compilation and uses a notebook-safe single-GPU strategy (`single_device=True`) because multi-process DDP cannot launch in an interactive kernel — so prefer the CLI or batch scripts for multi-GPU runs. Sources: [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L145-L158)

## The Four-Stage Workflow

Every path through PerturbGen — CLI, API, or notebook — traverses the same four stages. Stage 1 (tokenization) is CPU-only and idempotent; stages 2–3 form the **two-stage training** where the masking checkpoint feeds the count decoder; stage 4 consumes both checkpoints for perturbation or embedding extraction.
Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L697-L720)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["Step 0: Install\npoetry install + pip install -e ."] --> S1
    S1{"1. Tokenize\nCPU"} --> S2{"2. Train masking model\nGPU"}
    S2 -->|returns masking_ckpt| S3{"3. Train count decoder\nGPU"}
    S3 -->|returns count_ckpt| S4{"4. Perturb / embed\nGPU"}
    S4 --> OUT["Predicted target states,\nembeddings, gene programs"]
```

Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44)

| Stage | What happens | Hardware | Primary output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Tokenize | Tokenize + pair cells (source → later time points), select HVGs, write `.dataset` files | CPU | `T_perturb/tokenized_data/<dataset>/` |
| 2. Train masking | Fine-tune the frozen pretrained encoder for masked-gene prediction | GPU (13.8 GB) | `masking_ckpt` path |
| 3. Train count decoder | Train the count decoder with ZINB loss, seeded by the masking checkpoint | GPU (15.8 GB) | `count_ckpt` path |
| 4. Perturb / embed | Knock out / overexpress genes; extract cell & gene embeddings | GPU | Predicted states, embedding matrices |

Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L697-L720), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L69-L130)

## Path A — Quick Start via the Python API (recommended)

The `train_and_perturb.ipynb` tutorial is the fastest end-to-end route: it trains on the in-vivo LPS challenge (source state `6h_LPS`, target `10h_LPS`), then knocks out *IL1B* (`ENSG00000125538`) and predicts how the 10 h state changes. The complete logic is about a dozen calls: Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44)

```python
import perturbgen as pg

# 1) TOKENIZE your preprocessed AnnData (CPU; no encoder needed)
model_input = pg.tokenize(
    adata_path, dataset='lps_6h_perturb',
    reference_time='6h_LPS',                 # source state
    time_point_order=['6h_LPS', '10h_LPS'],  # pairs run source -> later points
    time_obs='Time_point', var_list=[...], main_pairing_obs='cell_pairing_index',
    gene_median_path=..., token_dict_path=..., gene_mapping_path=...,
)

# 2) BUILD THE MODEL — the pretrained scmaskgit encoder ships with the repo and
#    is used by default from pretraining_cohort/
model = pg.PerturbGen(model_input, source='6h_LPS', pred_tps=[1])

# 3) TRAIN in two steps so you choose which masking checkpoint feeds the decoder
masking_ckpt = model.train_masking(output_dir='model')
count_ckpt   = model.train_count(output_dir='model', masking_ckpt=masking_ckpt)

# 4) SAVE / EMBED / PERTURB (checkpoints are reused; load() restores them)
model.save('model')                                   # pg.PerturbGen.load('model')
emb  = model.get_embeddings(masking_ckpt=masking_ckpt)
pred = model.perturb(genes=['ENSG00000125538'],       # IL1B knockout
                     count_ckpt=count_ckpt, pred_tps=[1])
```

Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44)

Three API behaviors make re-running notebooks painless: `pg.tokenize()` is **idempotent** (if the output directory exists it returns immediately; pass `overwrite=True` to force a rebuild); `pg.PerturbGen.save()`/`load()` persist and restore both checkpoints so a kernel restart skips retraining; and perturbation modes are plain string aliases — `mode="knockout"` (also accepted: `overexpress`, `delete`, `pad`) and `where="source"` or `where="target"` control where the edit is applied in the sequence.
Sources: [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L69-L96), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L59-L66), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L13-L44)

The tutorial data for this example is the LPS challenge AnnData, downloadable without credentials from the project S3 bucket, and the tokenizer reference dictionaries (`gene_median`, `token_dict`, `gene_mapping`) are shipped inside `perturbgen/pp/` — you never need to generate them yourself.
Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L63-L100), [configs/paths.py](/perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L7-L11), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L46-L62)

> [!TIP]
> The pretrained encoder checkpoint is stored via Git LFS, and `git lfs pull` may fail with a 403 bandwidth error. Download it from Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/lotfollahi-lab/PerturbGen) instead and save the `.ckpt` into `pretraining_cohort/` keeping its filename — training then finds it automatically with no `--encoder_path` argument. Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L93-L99), [configs/paths.py](/perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L13-L17)

## Path B — Quick Start via the CLI

After `pip install -e .`, the `perturbgen` command exposes the same pipeline. Each CLI command delegates to a Python module, so any flag valid for that module (e.g., `--batch_size`, `--epochs`) works directly: Sources: [installation.rst](/docs/installation.rst#L44-L55), [\_\_main\_\_.py](/perturbgen/__main__.py#L60-L97)

| CLI command | Purpose | Delegates to |
|---|---|---|
| `perturbgen tokenise` | Data preprocessing & tokenization (CPU) | `perturbgen.pp.GF_tokenisation.main` |
| `perturbgen train-mask` | Train the masking model (stage 1) | `perturbgen.train.main` (`--train_mode masking`) |
| `perturbgen train-decoder` | Train the count decoder (stage 2) | `perturbgen.train.main` (`--train_mode count`) |
| `perturbgen extract-embedding` | Load a checkpoint and extract embeddings | `perturbgen.val.main` |

Sources: [\_\_main\_\_.py](/perturbgen/__main__.py#L60-L97), [\_\_main\_\_.py](/perturbgen/__main__.py#L72-L88), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L57-L62)

CLI invocations are argument-driven; the most common knobs for a first run are batch size, epochs, and the dataset paths. For example, training the masking model on tokenized data looks like: Sources: [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L83-L105), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L186-L189)

```shell
perturbgen train-mask \
  --src_dataset T_perturb/tokenized_data/<dataset>/dataset_hvg_src/<source>.dataset \
  --tgt_dataset_folder T_perturb/tokenized_data/<dataset>/dataset_hvg_tgt \
  --batch_size 64 --epochs 5
```

Sources: [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L83-L105)

Tokenization via CLI accepts the dataset name, gene-filtering mode (`hvg` by default; `hvg_flavor='seurat_v3'` matches the released recipe), and the observation keys used for pairing and time encoding. The Python API's `pg.tokenize()` forwards exactly these arguments internally, so both paths produce identical `.dataset` outputs.
Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](/perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L35-L100), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L69-L130)

## Where Your Files Live

PerturbGen creates a conventional workspace around itself the first time you run anything, so you do not need to configure directories manually. `ROOT` is the parent directory containing the repository; `data/`, `T_perturb/res/`, and `T_perturb/tokenized_data/` are auto-created at import. Note the repository ships its tokenizer dictionaries and the pretrained checkpoint under `perturbgen/pp/` and `pretraining_cohort/` — these are defaults, not files you generate.
Sources: [configs/paths.py](/perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L1-L35)

```
<ROOT>/                        # parent dir containing the repo (auto-detected)
├── Perturbgen/                # this repository
│   ├── perturbgen/
│   │   ├── pp/                # shipped tokenizer dicts (gene_median, token_dict, ensembl mapping)
│   │   ├── configs/paths.py   # path resolution + auto-mkdir
│   │   ├── model.py           # Python API (pg.tokenize, pg.PerturbGen)
│   │   ├── train.py           # training entry point (masking + count)
│   │   └── val.py             # embeddings / generation entry point
│   ├── docs/examples/         # 6 tutorial notebooks
│   └── pretraining_cohort/    # default location of the pretrained encoder .ckpt
├── data/                      # place your raw .h5ad here (auto-created)
└── T_perturb/                 # workspace (auto-created)
    ├── tokenized_data/        # output of stage 1
    └── res/                   # results
```

Sources: [configs/paths.py](/perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L1-L35), [README.md](/README.md#L77-L86)

| Path constant | Resolves to | Role in quick start |
|---|---|---|
| `GENE_MEDIAN_PATH` / `TOKEN_DICT_PATH` / `GENE_MAPPING_PATH` | `perturbgen/pp/*.pkl` | Tokenizer references passed to `pg.tokenize()` |
| `ENCODER_CKPT_PATH` | `pretraining_cohort/20250709_...ckpt` | Default frozen encoder, no flag needed |
| `DATA_DIR` | `<ROOT>/data/` | Where you put raw `.h5ad` inputs |
| `TOKENIZED_DIR` | `<ROOT>/T_perturb/tokenized_data/` | Output of `pg.tokenize()` / `tokenise` |

Sources: [configs/paths.py](/perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L7-L17), [configs/paths.py](/perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L22-L35)

## Troubleshooting First Runs

The four issues beginners hit most often all have one-line fixes documented in the code and README. Keep this table handy for your first training session: Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L32-L48), [README.md](/README.md#L50-L68), [README.md](/README.md#L93-L99)

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA out-of-memory during count-decoder training | 16 GB GPU vs 15.8 GB peak | Lower `batch_size` (or `batch_size=` in the API); use DeepSpeed (`--parallel_distribution deepspeed`) to cut per-GPU memory |
| Wandb run hangs at startup | Authentication blocks on offline machines | Offline is default; force with `--wandb_mode disabled` or log online via `export WANDB_MODE=online` |
| `git lfs pull` fails with HTTP 403 | Git LFS bandwidth limit on the checkpoint | Download the `.ckpt` from Hugging Face into `pretraining_cohort/` unchanged |
| Tokenization reruns from scratch each time | `overwrite` semantics | `pg.tokenize()` skips if output exists; only pass `overwrite=True` when data changed |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L32-L48), [train.py](/perturbgen/train.py#L190-L201), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L85-L96)

The tutorial notebooks are version-controlled as `_nb.py` scripts converted from Jupyter; regenerate runnable `.ipynb` files with `jupytext --to ipynb --execute <your_file>_nb.py` if you prefer the notebook interface.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L70-L76), [installation.rst](/docs/installation.rst#L35-L42)

## Where to Go Next

Once your first masking → count → perturb cycle completes, continue in this order: for deeper GPU sizing, Poetry alternatives, and multi-GPU guidance see [Installation and Hardware Requirements](3-installation-and-hardware-requirements); for guided notebook-by-notebook coverage of preprocessing, embeddings, and post-perturbation analyses see [Tutorial Notebooks Walkthrough](4-tutorial-notebooks-walkthrough); and to understand *why* the two-stage masking/decoder design works, read [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L77-L86), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L1-L30)

# Installation and Hardware Requirements



This page covers everything needed to get a working PerturbGen environment on your machine: the supported installation paths (Poetry, pip, and Docker), the exact dependency stack that gets installed, and the hardware you need for each workload — from CPU-only preprocessing to multi-GPU training. PerturbGen is distributed as the installable Python package `PerturbGen` ("Cell state and temporal prediction of scRNA-seq data") with a `perturbgen` command-line entry point, so a correct installation gives you both the library and the CLI in one step.

![PerturbGen architecture overview](https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen/blob/main/docs/architecture.png?raw=true)

## System Prerequisites at a Glance

Before running any installer, confirm your machine meets these requirements. The single hard constraint is **Python 3.11 or newer** — the project declares `requires-python = ">=3.11"` for the package and `python = ">=3.11,<4.0"` for the Poetry environment, and the Docker image is built on the official `python:3.11` base. Python dependencies resolve cross-platform (the locked requirements contain platform markers for macOS and Windows), but **GPU training effectively requires Linux with a CUDA 12.x driver**, because the PyPI PyTorch wheels ship CUDA 12.4 runtime libraries.

| Requirement | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python | ≥ 3.11 | `<4.0` upper bound in the Poetry environment |
| OS (training) | Linux + CUDA 12.x driver | PyPI wheels bundle CUDA 12.4 runtime (cuDNN 9.1, NCCL 2.21.5) |
| OS (preprocessing/inference) | macOS / Linux / Windows | Platform markers exist for Darwin and win32 |
| System package (Docker) | `libopenmpi-dev` | Required to build `mpi4py` inside the container |
| RAM (CPU workflows) | ≥ 32 GB recommended | For the larger preprocessing datasets |
| GPU (training) | ≥ 24 GB VRAM comfortable | See measured figures below |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L9-L20), [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L2), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L14-L28), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L159-L170), [README.md](README.md#L45-L46)

The files that govern installation live at the repository root and in the package directory. This is the terrain you are about to work with:

```
Perturbgen/
├── pyproject.toml         # Python ≥3.11, full dependency set, `perturbgen` CLI entry point
├── poetry.toml            # Poetry behaviour: virtualenvs.create = true
├── poetry.lock            # exact locked versions for reproducible installs
├── requirements.txt       # pip fallback, generated from poetry.lock
├── setup.py               # legacy setuptools stub (package name T_perturb)
├── Dockerfile             # linux/amd64 · python:3.11 · libopenmpi-dev · ENTRYPOINT perturbgen
└── perturbgen/
    ├── requirements.txt   # ⚠ legacy internal pins (cu118 dev wheels) — not the supported path
    ├── __main__.py        # CLI: tokenise · train-mask · train-decoder · extract-embedding
    ├── run_test.sh        # reference CPU test job (1 core, 10 GB RAM)
    └── run_sweep.sh       # reference GPU sweep job (4 exclusive GPUs, 8 cores, 50 GB RAM)
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L13), [poetry.toml](poetry.toml#L1-L3), [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L1-L14)

## Installing with Poetry (Recommended)

Poetry is the supported installation path: it creates an isolated virtualenv and installs the exact versions locked in `poetry.lock`. First install Poetry itself — either via the official installer or, alternatively, with `pipx`:

```shell
curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -
# or: pipx install poetry
```

Then clone the repository, pin the environment to Python 3.11, and install:

```shell
git clone https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen.git
cd Perturbgen
poetry env use python3.11
poetry install
```

Because `poetry.toml` sets `virtualenvs.create = true`, Poetry builds a dedicated virtualenv automatically; activate it with `source "$(poetry env info -p)/bin/activate"`. The build backend is `poetry-core>=2.0.0`, which is why Poetry (rather than raw setuptools) drives the whole process.

The following flowchart shows the complete path from zero to a verified installation, including the fork between CPU-only work and GPU training:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Install Poetry"] --> B["git clone Perturbgen"]
    B --> C["poetry env use python3.11"]
    C --> D["poetry install"]
    D --> E["Activate virtualenv"]
    E --> F{"NVIDIA GPU with CUDA 12.x?"}
    F -->|"Yes"| G["Training + inference + preprocessing"]
    F -->|"No"| H["Preprocessing, tokenisation, embedding extraction on CPU"]
    G --> I["Verify: perturbgen --help"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["Optional: download pretrained checkpoint from Hugging Face"]
```

Sources: [installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L4-L38), [README.md](README.md#L12-L41), [poetry.toml](poetry.toml#L1-L3), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L15-L17)

One detail to be aware of: the tutorial notebooks in this repository are stored as `_nb.py` script files rather than `.ipynb`, and are converted back (and executed) with `jupytext` — `jupytext --to ipynb --execute <your_file>_nb.py`. The `jupytext`-compatible Jupyter stack (`ipykernel`, `ipython`, `jupyter-client`) is part of the locked dependencies, so no extra install is needed for this.

Sources: [installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L40-L48), [README.md](README.md#L83-L88)

## Alternative: pip Installation

If your workflow mandates pip instead of Poetry, the repository ships a root-level `requirements.txt` that was **generated from `poetry.lock`** and therefore contains the same exact locked versions. The file header documents the intended invocation — install the locked dependencies first, then install the package itself without re-resolving dependencies:

```shell
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e . --no-deps
```

The editable install (`pip install -e .`) is also referenced in the official installation docs and is what wires the `perturbgen` command into your `PATH`. Poetry and pip are not interchangeable in *resolution behaviour* — pip with this file reproduces the lock exactly rather than re-resolving from `pyproject.toml`.

| Install path | Command | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Poetry (supported) | `poetry env use python3.11 && poetry install` | Day-to-day development; exact reproducibility |
| pip fallback | `pip install -r requirements.txt && pip install -e . --no-deps` | Constrained environments, Dockerfiles, CI |
| Docker | `docker build` (see below) | Fully isolated linux/amd64 environments |

Sources: [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L3), [installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L50-L53)

> [!TIP]
> Do **not** install from `perturbgen/requirements.txt`. That file is a legacy internal artifact: it pins a pre-release `torch==2.3.0.dev20240312+cu118`, CUDA **11** libraries (`nvidia-*-cu11`), older `lightning==2.2.1`/`scanpy==1.9.8`, and even a private `git+ssh` dependency on `amirvhd/T_perturb` — none of which match the current supported stack. The root `requirements.txt` is the only pip-sanctioned file.

Sources: [perturbgen/requirements.txt](perturbgen/requirements.txt#L43-L55), [perturbgen/requirements.txt](perturbgen/requirements.txt#L87-L94), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L3)

## Container-Based Installation (Docker)

The `Dockerfile` packages the entire environment into a reproducible image. It is pinned to the **`linux/amd64` platform** on the official `python:3.11` base, uses BuildKit cache mounts to speed up `apt` and `pip` layers, and — critically — installs the system package `libopenmpi-dev`, which is the native MPI library that the pinned `mpi4py==4.0.1` builds against. The image then performs an editable pip install of the repository and sets `perturbgen` as the container entrypoint, so `docker run <image> train-mask ...` maps directly onto CLI usage.

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 python:3.11
RUN ... apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libopenmpi-dev
COPY . /app
RUN ... pip install -e .
ENTRYPOINT ["perturbgen"]
```

For training inside a container you additionally need the NVIDIA Container Toolkit so the container can reach the host GPU; the image itself carries the CUDA 12.4 runtime libraries via the Python wheel dependencies, not a `nvidia/cuda` base image.

Sources: [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L2-L14), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L159-L170)

## Core Dependency Stack

A successful `poetry install` pulls a large locked set (~300 packages). Understanding the stack in layers makes the hardware requirements in the next section legible — each layer maps onto a specific workload. The versions below are the exact pins enforced by Poetry:

| Layer | Key packages (pinned versions) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Deep learning core | `torch 2.5.1`, `torchvision 0.20.1`, `torchaudio 2.5.1`, `triton 3.1.0` | Model computation and kernel compilation |
| Distributed / training ops | `pytorch-lightning 2.4.0`, `lightning 2.4.0`, `deepspeed 0.15.4`, `mpi4py 4.0.1` | Trainer loops, DDP, ZeRO stage 2, multi-node |
| CUDA runtime (bundled) | `nvidia-cublas-cu12 12.4.5.8`, `nvidia-cudnn-cu12 9.1.0.70`, `nvidia-nccl-cu12 2.21.5` (+ cupti/nvrtc/curand/cusolver/cusparse/nvtx at 12.4.x) | GPU libraries shipped as pip wheels |
| Single-cell bio stack | `scanpy 1.11.2`, `anndata 0.11`, `scvi-tools 1.3.1.post1`, `scikit-learn 1.5.2`, `scipy 1.14.1`, `numba 0.61.2` | Preprocessing, `AnnData` I/O, NB/ZINB distributions |
| Data & model assets | `datasets 3.0.0`, `huggingface-hub 0.26.5`, `transformers 4.47.0` | Tokenized dataset loading, checkpoint downloads |
| Tracking & sweeps | `wandb 0.17.9`, `optuna 4.1.0`, `ray 2.40.0`, `tensorboard 2.18.0` | Experiment logging, hyperparameter search |
| Evaluation metrics | `pot 0.9.4` (optimal transport), `evaluate`, `torchmetrics 1.4.1` | MMD/EMD/OT distances, perplexity, MSE |
| Documentation (optional group) | `sphinx ^8.2.3`, `sphinx-rtd-theme ^3.0.2`, `myst-nb ^1.3.0`, `sphinx-autobuild` | Building the readthedocs site |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L263-L271), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L216-L235), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L159-L170), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L57-L91), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L192-L222), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L306-L310), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L120), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L139)

The following diagram shows how these layers stack on top of your OS and Python installation, and which components activate only when a GPU is present:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph HOST["Your machine"]
        OS["Linux / macOS / Windows"]
        PY["Python ≥ 3.11"]
    end
    subgraph VENV["Poetry virtualenv (locked by poetry.lock)"]
        subgraph BIO["Bioinformatics layer"]
            SC["scanpy · anndata · scvi-tools"]
        end
        subgraph DL["Deep learning layer"]
            PL["PyTorch Lightning 2.4.0"]
            DS["DeepSpeed 0.15.4 (optional: ZeRO-2)"]
            T["PyTorch 2.5.1 + Triton 3.1.0"]
        end
        subgraph OPS["Operations layer"]
            WB["wandb 0.17.9 (offline by default)"]
            HF["huggingface-hub · datasets"]
        end
    end
    subgraph CUDA["CUDA runtime wheels (GPU only)"]
        NV["cuBLAS 12.4 · cuDNN 9.1 · NCCL 2.21.5"]
    end
    OS --> PY --> VENV
    DL --> CUDA
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L159-L170), [README.md](README.md#L66-L70)

## Hardware Requirements

Hardware needs split cleanly by workload. **Preprocessing, tokenization, and inference notebooks run on CPU** — a machine with **≥ 32 GB RAM is recommended for the larger datasets**. No GPU is needed until you reach the training commands (`train-mask`, `train-decoder`), and **training requires a CUDA GPU**.

The GPU memory figures below were measured over a full training epoch on the LPS tutorial data at the default batch size of 64:

| Training stage | Peak GPU memory (batch size 64) |
|----------------|---------------------------------|
| Masking model  | 13.8 GB                         |
| Count decoder  | 15.8 GB                         |

In practice this means training at the default batch size runs on **24 GB GPUs (e.g. RTX 3090/4090) and larger**. On 16 GB cards the count-decoder stage sits close to the memory limit; if you hit an out-of-memory (OOM) error, lower the batch size via the `--batch_size` flag on the CLI (or `batch_size=` in the Python API). To reproduce the paper's results exactly, keep the default batch size of 64.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L43-L59), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L146)

For multi-GPU scaling, the training code **automatically uses all visible GPUs** (`devices=-1` when more than one GPU is detected), with **DDP as the default strategy**; **DeepSpeed (ZeRO stage 2)** is available via `--parallel_distribution deepspeed`, which also reduces per-GPU memory. Single-node execution is the default (`--num_node 1`), and there is an explicit `--single_device` escape hatch that forces one GPU without DDP/DeepSpeed. Device selection itself is automatic: the trainer sets `accelerator = 'gpu'` if `torch.cuda.is_available()`, otherwise it falls back to CPU — which is why the CPU-only workflows above work unchanged.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S["Start training run"] --> Q{"torch.cuda.is_available()?"}
    Q -->|"No"| CPU["accelerator='cpu' — preprocessing / inference only"]
    Q -->|"Yes"| N{"GPU count > 1 and not --single_device?"}
    N -->|"No"| ONE["devices=1, strategy='auto'"]
    N -->|"Yes"| ALL["devices=-1 — all visible GPUs"]
    ALL --> PD{"--parallel_distribution"}
    PD -->|ddp default| DDP["DDPStrategy"]
    PD -->|deepspeed| Z2["DeepSpeedStrategy stage=2 — lower per-GPU memory"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L64), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L656-L688), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L147-L158)

There is also device-adaptive behaviour worth knowing about on data-center hardware: at model construction the trainer checks the GPU name and, on **A100 or NVIDIA H100 80GB** devices, sets `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision` (default `'medium'`) and prints which GPU is in use; on any other setup it simply reports "CUDA is not available, using CPU for training" when applicable. No configuration is required — this is automatic tuning for tensor-core-capable accelerators.

Sources: [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L43-L52)

For reference, the repository's own HPC job scripts document the resource envelopes the authors used on a LSF cluster. The CPU unit-test job requests 1 core and 10 GB RAM with the `cuda-12.1.1` module loaded; the hyperparameter sweep job requests **4 exclusive GPUs, 8 CPU cores, and 50 GB RAM** on a GPU partition:

| Reference job | Queue | Cores | RAM | GPUs | CUDA module |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `run_test.sh` (unit tests) | `cpu-interactive` | 1 | 10 GB | — | `cuda-12.1.1` |
| `run_sweep.sh` (wandb sweep) | `gpu-lotfollahi` | 8 | 50 GB | 4 (exclusive process) | `cuda-12.1.1` |

Sources: [run_test.sh](perturbgen/run_test.sh#L1-L25), [run_sweep.sh](perturbgen/run_sweep.sh#L1-L26)

> [!TIP]
> Experiment logging to Weights & Biases is **offline by default**, deliberately so that runs never hang on wandb authentication on machines without internet access (e.g., firewalled compute clusters). Offline runs can be uploaded later with `wandb sync`; to log online, either `export WANDB_MODE=online` or pass `--wandb_mode online` per run, and use `--wandb_mode disabled` to switch logging off entirely. Direct your runs to your own account with `--wandb_entity <your-team>`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L66-L81), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L625-L638)

## Verifying the Installation

Once installed, the fastest sanity check is the CLI itself. Running `perturbgen` should print the command group with these subcommands — `tokenise` (data preprocessing/tokenisation), `train-mask` (masking model), `train-decoder` (count decoder model), and `extract-embedding` (load a checkpoint and extract embeddings). If this help text appears, the package, its dependencies, and the entry point are all wired correctly.

```shell
$ perturbgen
Usage: perturbgen [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
Commands:
  tokenise           Data preprocessing, tokenisation
  train-mask         Training the masking model
  train-decoder      Training the count decoder model
  extract-embedding  Load checkpoint and extract the embeddings
```

Sources: [installation.rst](docs/installation.rst#L55-L72), [__main__.py](perturbgen/__main__.py#L38-L72)

For a functional check of the training stack, the repository ships a unittest suite that the authors run on a CPU queue with 10 GB of RAM — `python -m unittest discover` over the `perturbgen/tests/` directory. A minimal GPU availability check before your first training run is one line: `python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.device_count())"`.

Sources: [run_test.sh](perturbgen/run_test.sh#L20-L25)

## Downloading Pretrained Assets (Optional)

The pretrained model checkpoint is distributed via Hugging Face at `huggingface.co/lotfollahi-lab/PerturbGen`. Note one installation-time pitfall: although a checkpoint file exists in `pretraining_cohort/` via Git LFS, `git lfs pull` may fail with a 403 bandwidth error — download the `.ckpt` from the Hugging Face link instead and save it in `pretraining_cohort/` **keeping its original filename**. That location is where training looks for the encoder by default, so no `--encoder_path` flag is needed afterwards.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L105-L112)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `CUDA out of memory` during training | Count-decoder stage peaks at 15.8 GB at batch size 64 | Lower `--batch_size`; or use `--parallel_distribution deepspeed` (ZeRO-2 lowers per-GPU memory) |
| Jupyter kernel stalls when training | `torch.compile` is on by default and can stall/deadlock inside a Jupyter kernel | The in-process API disables it automatically; via CLI pass `--compile False` and/or `--single_device True` |
| Run hangs at start waiting for wandb | Online wandb auth on a machine without internet | W&B is offline by default; explicitly set `--wandb_mode online` or `export WANDB_MODE=online` if you *want* online logging |
| "CUDA is not available, using CPU" during training | No usable GPU / missing CUDA 12.x driver | Verify driver with `nvidia-smi`; training needs a CUDA GPU, other workloads legitimately stay on CPU |
| `poetry install` resolves the wrong Python | Virtualenv picked up a non-3.11 interpreter | Re-run `poetry env use python3.11` before `poetry install` |
| `git lfs pull` fails with 403 | Bandwidth limits on the Git LFS-hosted checkpoint | Download from the Hugging Face repo and place the `.ckpt` in `pretraining_cohort/` |
| `mpi4py` fails to build in Docker | Native MPI headers missing | The Dockerfile already installs `libopenmpi-dev`; replicate this on bare-metal pip installs |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L56-L64), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L148-L158), [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L43-L52), [Dockerfile](Dockerfile#L6), [README.md](README.md#L111-L112)

## Where to Go Next

You now have a working environment and know what hardware each workload demands. The natural reading progression from here: if you have not yet run anything, start with the [Quick Start](2-quick-start), then move to the [Tutorial Notebooks Walkthrough](4-tutorial-notebooks-walkthrough) to see the installed toolchain in action. When you begin training in earnest, the deeper operational pages become relevant: how dataset and checkpoint paths are resolved ([Configuration System and Path Management](17-configuration-system-and-path-management)), scaling beyond one GPU ([Distributed Training with DDP and DeepSpeed](19-distributed-training-with-ddp-and-deepspeed)), configuring the W&B logging you just learned about ([Experiment Tracking with Weights and Biases](20-experiment-tracking-with-weights-and-biases)), the exact CLI flags behind `perturbgen` ([CLI Command Reference](22-cli-command-reference)), fetching the released checkpoint ([Pretrained Checkpoints and Hugging Face Assets](23-pretrained-checkpoints-and-hugging-face-assets)), and running the test/benchmark suite on your new environment ([Test and Benchmark Suite](26-test-and-benchmark-suite)).


# Tutorial Notebooks Walkthrough



This page walks through the six Jupyter notebooks shipped in `docs/examples/`, which together form a complete PerturbGen analysis workflow on the LPS immune-response time-course dataset. Each notebook is a self-contained, executable lesson — from raw public data download all the way to interpreting in silico perturbation results. The notebooks assume familiarity with Python-based scientific computing (Scanpy/AnnData) and single-cell data, and they are organized in the docs via the `Tutorial` toctree so they render as a connected narrative on the documentation site. By the end of this walkthrough you will know exactly which notebook to run, in what order, and what each one produces for the next stage.

Sources: [tutorial.rst](/docs/tutorial.rst#L1-L17), [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](/docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L7-L17)

![PerturbGen architecture](https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen/blob/main/docs/architecture.png?raw=true)

## The Six-Notebook Landscape

The tutorial toctree in `docs/tutorial.rst` lists the notebooks in the following order: `preprocessing_curation`, `cell_gene_embeddings`, `gene_program_discovery`, `train_and_perturb`, `perturbation`, and `post_perturbation_analyses`. Functionally they split into **two tracks**: a *released-model track* (analyze without training anything, using checkpoints downloaded from Hugging Face) and a *training track* (build your own model end-to-end with the Python API). Both tracks converge on the same final artifact — a post-perturbation AnnData that the analysis notebook consumes.

Sources: [tutorial.rst](/docs/tutorial.rst#L10-L17), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](/docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L5-L16), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L5-L16)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PRE["1. preprocessing_curation<br/>public + private LPS data → clean AnnData<br/>(Ensembl IDs, raw counts)"]

    subgraph RA["Track A · Released model — no training needed"]
        EMB["2. cell_gene_embeddings<br/>download HF checkpoint → cell + gene embeddings"]
        GPD["3. gene_program_discovery<br/>cluster gene embeddings → programs + enrichment"]
        PERT["5. perturbation<br/>released IL1B model → in silico knockout"]
    end

    subgraph RB["Track B · Your own model — full Python API"]
        TP["4. train_and_perturb<br/>tokenize → train masking → train count → perturb"]
    end

    POST["6. post_perturbation_analyses<br/>DEGs, perturbation effect, enrichment"]

    PRE -->|"cleaned AnnData"| EMB
    PRE -->|"cleaned AnnData"| TP
    EMB -->|"lps_cell_gene_embeddings/"| GPD
    GPD -->|"identifies IL1B as candidate"| PERT
    PERT -->|"lps_perturbation/*.h5ad"| POST
    TP -->|"lps_6h_perturbation/*.h5ad"| POST
```

The table below summarizes each notebook's role, required model assets, and hardware needs — use it to decide which track fits your situation:

| # | Notebook | Purpose | Model source | Hardware | Key output |
|---|----------|---------|-------------|----------|------------|
| 1 | `preprocessing_curation` | Merge public + private LPS data; harmonize gene IDs and cell types | None (data only) | CPU | Clean AnnData, raw counts, Ensembl `var` index |
| 2 | `cell_gene_embeddings` | Extract cell and time-resolved gene embeddings | Released masking checkpoint (Hugging Face) | CUDA GPU | `lps_cell_gene_embeddings/` h5ad with `obsm` + `varm` |
| 3 | `gene_program_discovery` | De novo gene program discovery + enrichment | Consumes embeddings from notebook 2 | CPU | Gene programs, UMAPs, enrichment plots |
| 4 | `train_and_perturb` | Full API workflow: tokenize → train → perturb | Pretrained `scmaskgit` encoder + your training | CUDA GPU (24 GB fits `batch_size=64`, ~16 GB peak) | Trained checkpoints + post-perturbation h5ad |
| 5 | `perturbation` | In silico IL1B knockout with the released manuscript model | Released count-decoder checkpoint (Hugging Face) | CUDA GPU | `lps_perturbation/*.h5ad` |
| 6 | `post_perturbation_analyses` | Quantify perturbation effects: DEGs, cell-type response | Consumes output of notebook 5 (or 4) | CPU | Barplots, DEG tables, enrichment |

Sources: [tutorial.rst](/docs/tutorial.rst#L10-L17), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L42-L52), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](/docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L18-L45), [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L48-L52)

## Shared Assets: What Every Notebook Depends On

Three asset categories recur across the notebooks. First, the **released model assets** live in the Hugging Face repository `lotfollahi-lab/PerturbGen`: notebooks download a specific checkpoint (`hf_hub_download`) together with the *exact tokenized dataset that checkpoint was trained on* (`snapshot_download`) — token IDs are defined by the tokenization, so a checkpoint is only valid with its matching tokenized data. Second, the **tokenizer reference files** shipped inside the package (`gene_median`, `token_dict`, `gene_mapping`) are resolved through `perturbgen.configs.paths` constants, so notebooks never hardcode their locations. Third, a **gene-ID mapping file** `docs/examples/reference/mart_export.txt` — an Ensembl BioMart export of `HGNC symbol → Gene stable ID` pairs (~86k rows) — supports symbol↔Ensembl harmonization during preprocessing.

Sources: [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](/docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L18-L45), [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L48-L60), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L54-L82), [mart_export.txt](/docs/examples/reference/mart_export.txt#L1-L15)

## Notebook 1: Preprocessing and Curation

This notebook prepares the LPS datasets — both the public source and private data — and demonstrates how to merge them into a training-ready AnnData. It starts by downloading the public LPS dataset from the EBI Biostudies archive (dataset E-MTAB-10026, a ~7.2 GB `h5ad` file) using `gdown`, then loads it with Scanpy and investigates the object to identify LPS-stimulated samples versus healthy control cells. This is the natural first notebook for anyone bringing their own data, and its conventions (raw counts in `.X`, Ensembl IDs as the `var` index) are exactly what the later API notebooks expect.

Sources: [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](/docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L7-L17), [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](/docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L25-L78)

The curation steps follow a reproducible pattern you can copy for your own cohort: copy `full_clustering` into an `obs['cell_type']` column, filter out cell types with fewer than 50 cells to remove statistically fragile categories, and verify the `obs['time_after_LPS']` column — the ordered time-point categories (`normal` < `90m_LPS` < `10h_LPS` in the public data) that drive PerturbGen's trajectory modeling. The gene annotation uses Ensembl stable IDs alongside HGNC symbols (~19k genes in the shown `var` table), which is the identifier scheme the tokenizer requires.

Sources: [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](/docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L760-L959)

For the deeper statistical rationale behind pairing cells across time points, continue to [Cell Pairing and Data Curation](14-cell-pairing-and-data-curation); the identifier scheme is covered in [Geneformer-Style Gene Tokenization](9-geneformer-style-gene-tokenization).

## Notebook 2: Cell and Gene Embeddings (Released Model)

This notebook extracts cell embeddings and time-resolved gene embeddings from the **released PerturbGen model used for the embedding analyses in the manuscript** — the masking model trained on LPS data with the unstimulated `normal` state as source and 90 min, 6 h, and 10 h as targets. No training happens here: the checkpoint and its tokenized data are downloaded from Hugging Face, the model is rebuilt with the checkpoint's exact configuration (`n_hvg=2000`, `n_layers=6`, `d_model=768`, `max_len=797`, `tgt_vocab_size=2002`, cosine mask scheduler, time conditioning), and embeddings are produced in a single `model.get_embeddings()` call.

Sources: [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](/docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L5-L16), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](/docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L47-L80)

The output AnnData has a precise contract that notebook 3 depends on: **cell embeddings** are stored in `obsm["cls_embeddings"]`, while **gene embeddings** are extracted separately per time point (via `gene_embs_condition="time_after_LPS"`) and stored in `varm` (`90m_LPS`, `6h_LPS`, `10h_LPS`). The notebook writes everything to `lps_cell_gene_embeddings/` and explicitly hands off to the next notebook.

Sources: [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](/docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L62-L84)

The embedding mechanics themselves — how the masking model's representations become cell/gene vectors — are explained in [Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction](11-cell-and-gene-embedding-extraction).

## Notebook 3: Gene Program Discovery

This notebook treats gene embeddings as a framework for *de novo gene program discovery*: genes grouped into the same program may represent coordinated biological functions and serve as candidate perturbation targets. It loads the `*inference_embs*.h5ad` written by notebook 2 — an AnnData with 69,433 cells × 2,000 genes, cell embeddings under `obsm["cls_embeddings"]`, and per-timepoint gene embeddings under `varm` — then runs standard Scanpy workflows (`normalize_total`, `log1p`, `neighbors`, `UMAP`) on the cell embeddings for visualization.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L5-L15), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L37-L77)

The key conceptual move is a **transposition**: each gene becomes an *observation*, and its features are the 768-dimensional learned embedding vector rather than expression values. The notebook stacks all time-point gene-embedding matrices into one AnnData (`{gene}_{timepoint}` rows), drops all-zero gene–timepoint vectors, and applies standard single-cell tooling — neighborhood graphs, clustering, and `gseapy` enrichment — to the embedding space. This is precisely the analysis that surfaced the cytokine/chemokine program with IL1B as its leading gene, motivating the perturbation experiments in notebooks 4 and 5.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L263-L320), [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L15-L20)

Program-discovery methodology is treated in depth in [Gene Program Discovery](12-gene-program-discovery).

## Notebook 4: Train and Perturb — The End-to-End Python API

This is the flagship tutorial: it trains PerturbGen on the in vivo LPS challenge with the **6 h state as source and 10 h as target**, then knocks out **IL1B** at 6 h and predicts how the 10 h state changes — all in-process, no shell calls. The notebook header states the five-step API contract: `pg.tokenize` → `pg.PerturbGen` → `train_masking` → `train_count` → `save`/`embed`/`perturb`. Prerequisites are a preprocessed AnnData (QC'd, Ensembl IDs, raw counts), the tokenizer reference files, the pretrained `scmaskgit` encoder checkpoint (used by default from `pretraining_cohort/` in the repository, downloadable from Hugging Face if `git lfs pull` fails), and a CUDA GPU.

Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L5-L52)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["pg.tokenize(adata)<br/>CPU · pairs cells source→target"] --> B["pg.PerturbGen(dir)<br/>build model config"]
    B --> C["model.train_masking()<br/>GPU · ckpt per epoch"]
    C -->|"masking_ckpt (metric-best<br/>or chosen epoch)"| D["model.train_count()<br/>GPU · frozen encoder + CountDecoder"]
    D --> E["model.save() / load()<br/>manifest: ckpts + hyperparams"]
    C --> F["model.get_embeddings()<br/>uses masking ckpt"]
    D --> G["model.perturb()<br/>uses count ckpt"]
    F --> H["gene_program_discovery"]
    G --> I["post_perturbation_analyses"]
```

Step through the stages with their verified behaviors:

| API call | Stage | Hardware | Key details |
|----------|-------|----------|-------------|
| `pg.tokenize(adata_path, dataset=..., reference_time='6h_LPS', time_point_order=[...])` | Tokenize + pair cells | CPU | Writes the `.dataset` layout; HVG selection defaults to `hvg_flavor='seurat_v3'` over Geneformer-tokenizable genes |
| `pg.PerturbGen(TOKENIZED_DIR, source=..., pred_tps=[...])` | Build model | CPU | Ships with frozen pretrained `scmaskgit` encoder; pass `encoder_path=` to override |
| `model.train_masking(output_dir=...)` | Stage 1 training | GPU | Checkpoint saved **every epoch**; returns metric-best (perplexity) checkpoint; ~91.5 M params total, only ~19.7 M trainable |
| `model.train_count(output_dir=..., masking_ckpt=...)` | Stage 2 training | GPU | Initializes `CountDecoder` from your chosen masking epoch; ~95.7 M total, ~4.3 M trainable (encoder frozen) |
| `model.save(dir)` / `pg.PerturbGen.load(dir)` | Persist | CPU | Manifest stores tokenized dir, source, hyperparameters, and both checkpoint paths |
| `model.get_embeddings(...)` | Analysis | GPU | Embeddings come from the **masking** model; `gene_embs_condition` splits gene embeddings per column value |
| `model.perturb(genes=[...], count_ckpt=...)` | Prediction | GPU | Uses the trained count-decoder checkpoint; writes post-perturbation h5ad to `output_dir` |

Sources: [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L84-L115), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L327-L350), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L560-L645), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L648-L693), [train_and_perturb.ipynb](/docs/examples/train_and_perturb.ipynb#L695-L745)

> [!TIP]
> The two-stage training design gives you an explicit decision point: because `train_masking` saves a checkpoint per epoch, you choose *which* masking epoch feeds the count decoder (the notebook demonstrates initializing from epoch 8 while perturbing with count epoch 2). Inspect training curves — e.g., in Weights & Biases — before locking in the handoff; the default is simply the metric-best checkpoint.

The configuration values flowing into these calls (`GENE_MEDIAN_PATH`, `TOKEN_DICT_PATH`, `GENE_MAPPING_PATH`, `TOKENIZED_DIR`) are managed by the package's path system described in [Configuration System and Path Management](17-configuration-system-and-path-management); the two training stages are dissected in [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training).

## Notebook 5: In Silico Perturbation (Released Model)

This notebook runs an in silico perturbation with the **released IL1B model from the manuscript**, downloaded from Hugging Face — the count-decoder checkpoint (which embeds the masking model it was trained from) plus its matching tokenized data (`90m_LPS` source, targets 6 h and 10 h). It reproduces the paper's experimental logic, illustrated below: gene-program discovery across the LPS trajectory highlighted a cytokine/chemokine program with IL1B emerging as a mechanistic candidate, and PerturbGen then simulates an IL1B knockout at the 90-minute source to see how the disruption propagates to 6 h and 10 h.

Sources: [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L5-L52), [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L62-L112)

![Manuscript perturbation schematic](https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen/blob/main/docs/_static/fig2.png?raw=true)

The notebook doubles as the practical reference for `model.perturb()` arguments — experiments change without touching model code:

| Argument | Values | Meaning |
|----------|--------|---------|
| `genes` | Ensembl ID (recommended) or symbol; accepts a **list** | Which genes to perturb; a list enables multi-gene/combinatorial knockouts. `ENSG00000125538` = IL1B |
| `where` | `'source'` (default) / `'target'` | `'source'` edits the source state and propagates downstream along the trajectory; `'target'` perturbs the predicted state directly |
| `pred_tps` | Indices into the dataset's ordered time points (1 → 6 h, 2 → 10 h for the released model) | Which downstream time points to generate, for both control and perturbed runs |
| `pert_tps` | Only with `where='target'`; required for knockout-type modes there | Which target time point(s) to edit before predicting |
| `mode` | `'knockout'` / `'pad'` / `'delete'` / `'overexpress'` | How the gene token is edited (see below) |
| `n_samples` | Integer (e.g. 3) | Generative samples per condition |
| `extra_config` | `{section: {key: value}}` | Escape hatch for YAML config options without a dedicated argument |

Sources: [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L114-L236)

The four **perturbation modes** map directly onto biological interpretations — loss-of-function versus gain-of-function:

| Mode | Token edit | Biological analogy | Intensity |
|------|-----------|--------------------|-----------|
| `'knockout'` | Replace with `[MASK]` — model infers consequences from context | CRISPR KO / knockdown | Default, recommended |
| `'pad'` | Replace with `[PAD]` — removed from the active sequence | Complete absence from expressed gene set | Stronger knockout assumption |
| `'delete'` | Token removed from the sequence entirely (sequence shortens) | Strongest deletion; robustness stress-test | Strongest |
| `'overexpress'` | Token promoted to the top rank of the ranked gene sequence | CRISPRa / activation — rank encodes relative expression | Gain-of-function |

Sources: [perturbation.ipynb](/docs/examples/perturbation.ipynb#L188-L215)

> [!TIP]
> The notebook carries a critical warning: a **source knockout only has an effect if the gene is expressed in the source state** — cells lacking the gene token in the source are filtered, and batches left with no qualifying cells are skipped. IL1B is LPS-induced and near-zero in the unstimulated `normal` baseline, which is why the released IL1B model uses `90m_LPS` as its source; pointing a perturbation at `normal` would skip nearly all batches and yield empty, irreproducible results. Always verify expression of your target gene in the chosen source before running.

The complete mode taxonomy and their mechanistic grounding are detailed in [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes).

## Notebook 6: Post-Perturbation Analyses

This final notebook examines transcriptomic changes after in silico perturbation, consuming the h5ad written by notebook 5 (or 4). The output AnnData follows a documented three-layer contract: **`.X` holds the perturbed counts** (raw), **`layers['pred_counts']`** holds reconstructed pre-perturbation counts, **`layers['true_counts']`** holds the original observed counts, plus a per-cell `mean_cos_similarity` metric. Because all counts are raw, the notebook normalizes and log-transforms before any downstream analysis.

Sources: [post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb](/docs/examples/post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb#L9-L16), [post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb](/docs/examples/post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb#L44-L85)

The analysis pipeline then proceeds in three verifiable steps. First, it reorganizes the object into perturbed/unperturbed counterparts using `status` and `status_time` annotations (`perturbed_6h_LPS` vs `unperturbed_6h_LPS`, etc.) and concatenates them into one comparison AnnData. Second, it computes the **"perturbation effect"**: per cell type and time point, a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (`sc.tl.rank_genes_groups`) compares perturbed against unperturbed cells, counting significant DEGs (`pvals_adj < 0.05`), visualized as a cell-type-ranked barplot — the myeloid lineage (CD14+/CD16+ monocytes, dendritic cells) shows the strongest effect and is subsetted for deeper analysis. Third, Ensembl IDs are mapped back to gene symbols for interpretability, followed by `gseapy` enrichment on the perturbation-driven changes.

Sources: [post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb](/docs/examples/post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb#L44-L100), [post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb](/docs/examples/post_perturbation_analyses.ipynb#L102-L190)

How these predictions are scored at the population level (MMD, EMD, optimal transport) is covered in [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport).

## Recommended Path Through the Documentation

For beginners we suggest this progression: run the notebooks in the toctree order above while reading along in the docs. After finishing this walkthrough, continue with [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview) to understand what the checkpoints contain, then [Quick Start](2-quick-start) recap and [Installation and Hardware Requirements](3-installation-and-hardware-requirements) if you are still setting up. When you reach the analysis notebooks, deepen each topic with its dedicated deep-dive page: [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes), [Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction](11-cell-and-gene-embedding-extraction), [Gene Program Discovery](12-gene-program-discovery), and [Pretrained Checkpoints and Hugging Face Assets](23-pretrained-checkpoints-and-hugging-face-assets) for troubleshooting checkpoint downloads. For reproducibility-oriented users, [Test and Benchmark Suite](26-test-and-benchmark-suite) shows how the same workflows are validated programmatically.

Sources: [tutorial.rst](/docs/tutorial.rst#L6-L17)

## Common Pitfalls and Practical Notes

| Pitfall | Symptom | Fix (as documented in the notebooks) |
|---------|---------|--------------------------------------|
| Checkpoint/tokenized-data mismatch | Garbage or failed model load | Download the tokenized dataset shipped alongside each released checkpoint; token IDs are defined by that tokenization |
| Perturbing a gene not expressed in the source | "No cells" messages, empty/skipped batches | Choose a source where the gene is expressed (IL1B example uses `90m_LPS`, not `normal`) |
| Reusing a non-empty `output_dir` for `perturb()` | Previously computed genes silently skipped | Use a fresh `output_dir` per experiment |
| GPU out-of-memory during training/perturbation | CUDA OOM error | `batch_size=64` fits 24 GB cards (~16 GB peak); lower the batch size |
| Raw counts fed directly to analysis | Distorted DEG/enrichment results | `normalize_total` + `log1p` both perturbed and predicted counts before analysis |
| Kernel restart after tokenization | Lost `TOKENIZED_DIR`/`SOURCE` variables | The notebook defines these paths before the tokenize cell precisely so a restart doesn't force re-tokenization |


# Architecture Overview



PerturbGen is a foundation model for predicting how perturbations reshape dynamic cellular trajectories — given a tokenized single-cell dataset, it predicts gene expression at future time points and supports in silico gene perturbations across those transitions. This page maps the repository's architectural layers from first principles: how the codebase is partitioned, how data flows from raw AnnData through tokenization into a two-stage masked-generative model, and how the perturbation, configuration, and training-infrastructure layers are composed. It is the entry point for the Deep Dive section; each architectural subsystem documented here has a dedicated page that goes deeper.

![PerturbGen architecture](https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/Perturbgen/blob/main/docs/architecture.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L16), [docs/architecture.png](docs/architecture.png)

## The Three-Tier Repository Layout

The repository is not a single package — it is a three-tier system in which each top-level directory owns one stage of the model's lifecycle. `pretraining_cohort/` owns the upstream pretraining data pipeline (bronze→silver harmonization, median calculation, tokenization) plus the pretrained encoder checkpoint that ships with the repo via Git LFS. `scmaskgit/` owns the base masked-generative transformer (`scmoscf` in `Modules/T_model.py`) — the architecture trained during pretraining. `perturbgen/` is the application package that wraps the pretrained `scmaskgit` encoder as a frozen feature extractor and adds the decoder, count-decoder, and perturbation machinery around it.

| Tier | Directory | Responsibility | Key artifacts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pretraining cohort | `pretraining_cohort/` | Cohort harmonization, median aggregation, tokenization pipeline | Encoder checkpoint `.ckpt`, `preprocessing/`, `tokenization/` |
| Base model | `scmaskgit/` | Masked-generative transformer (`scmoscf`), its own `PositionalEncoding`, losses, metrics | `Modules/T_model.py`, `src/` |
| Application | `perturbgen/` | Fine-tuning, perturbation, tokenization pipeline, CLI, Python API, configs | `Model/`, `Modules/`, `Perturb/`, `pp/`, `configs/`, `model.py` |

Sources: [scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1-L120), [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L407-L449), [pretraining_cohort/](pretraining_cohort#L1-L1)

## Visual Project Structure

The `perturbgen/` package itself follows a strict subsystem decomposition. Each directory is a layer with a single direction of dependency: `pp/` (tokenization) feeds `Dataloaders/` (pairing and batching), which feeds `Model/` and `Perturb/` (Lightning trainers), which are orchestrated by `train.py`, `val.py`, the click-based CLI in `__main__.py`, and the scvi-tools-style Python API in `model.py`.

```
perturbgen/
├── __main__.py            # click CLI: tokenise, train-mask, train-decoder, extract-embedding
├── model.py               # scvi-tools-style Python API (PerturbGen class + tokenize())
├── train.py / val.py      # Lightning orchestration entry points
├── pp/                    # Geneformer-style tokenization + shipped vocab/median pickles
│   ├── GF_tokenisation.py # Tokenization pipeline main()
│   ├── tokenizer.py       # TranscriptomeTokenizer
│   └── *.pkl              # gene medians, token dict, Ensembl mapping (gc95M)
├── Dataloaders/
│   └── datamodule.py      # PerturbGenDataset + PerturbGenDataModule (src/tgt pairing)
├── Modules/
│   └── transformer.py     # PerturbGen, CountDecoder, Encoder, scmaskgitwrapper, PositionalEncoding
├── Model/
│   └── trainer.py         # PerturbGenTrainer (masking), CountDecoderTrainer (count)
├── Perturb/
│   ├── trainer.py         # PerturberTrainer (in silico perturbation)
│   ├── transformer.py     # PerturberMasking, PerturberCountDecoder
│   └── val.py
├── src/                   # losses, metrics (MMD/EMD/OT), GF utils, shared utils
├── configs/               # paths.py + eval/ + sweep/ YAMLs
└── batch_job_script/      # per-dataset sweep scripts (hspc, lps, eb, sko, cytoimmgen)
```

Sources: [perturbgen/__main__.py](perturbgen/__main__.py#L42-L66), [perturbgen/model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L1-L33), [perturbgen/train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L11-L24)

## Layered Architecture

Every request — whether it arrives through the CLI, the sweep shell scripts, or the in-process Python API — traverses the same vertical stack. The critical design decision is at the boundary between the base model tier and the application tier: `perturbgen.Modules.transformer` imports `scmoscf` directly from `scmaskgit.Modules.T_model` and wraps it in `scmaskgitwrapper`, which loads the shipped pretrained checkpoint, freezes every parameter, and only ever exposes its `dec_embedding` output. All learning in the application tier happens in the decoder stack on top of this frozen encoder.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Interfaces["Interface layer"]
        CLI["__main__.py<br/>(click CLI)"]
        API["model.py<br/>(PerturbGen class)"]
        SWEEP["run_sweep.sh +<br/>batch_job_script/"]
    end

    subgraph Orchestration["Orchestration layer"]
        TRAIN["train.py<br/>train_mode: masking | count"]
        VAL["val.py / Perturb/val.py"]
    end

    subgraph DataLayer["Data layer"]
        PP["pp/GF_tokenisation.py<br/>TranscriptomeTokenizer"]
        DM["Dataloaders/datamodule.py<br/>PerturbGenDataset +<br/>PerturbGenDataModule"]
    end

    subgraph ModelLayer["Model layer (PyTorch Lightning)"]
        MT["Model/trainer.py<br/>PerturbGenTrainer<br/>CountDecoderTrainer"]
        PT["Perturb/trainer.py<br/>PerturberTrainer"]
        MOD["Modules/transformer.py<br/>PerturbGen · CountDecoder<br/>PositionalEncoding"]
        PTRANS["Perturb/transformer.py<br/>PerturberMasking · PerturberCountDecoder"]
    end

    subgraph BaseTier["Base model tier (frozen)"]
        ENC["scmaskgitwrapper<br/>→ scmoscf (frozen, eval)"]
        CKPT["pretraining_cohort/<br/>*.ckpt"]
    end

    subgraph Utilities["Shared utilities"]
        SRC["src/<br/>losses · metric · mmd ·<br/>optimal_transport · gf_utils"]
        CFG["configs/paths.py"]
    end

    CLI --> TRAIN
    API --> TRAIN
    API --> PP
    SWEEP --> CLI
    TRAIN --> DM
    TRAIN --> MT
    VAL --> PT
    PP --> DM
    MT --> MOD
    PT --> PTRANS
    PTRANS --> MOD
    MOD --> ENC
    CKPT --> ENC
    MT -.-> SRC
    MOD -.-> CFG
```

Sources: [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L14-L19), [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L407-L449), [perturbgen/train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L560-L731), [perturbgen/configs/paths.py](perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L1-L35)

## The PerturbGen Transformer: Frozen Encoder Plus Masked Decoder

Inside `Modules/transformer.py`, the `PerturbGen` module composes four components. A `PositionalEncoding` layer provides **time-aware positional encoding** in four selectable modes (`time_pos_sin`, `comb_sin`, `sin_learnt`, `time_pos_learnt`) — the sinusoidal `time_pe`/`pos_pe` pair is what allows interpolation and extrapolation to time steps never seen during training. A `token_embedding` maps the Geneformer-style vocabulary to `d_model`-dimensional vectors. The encoder branch is switchable: `encoder='scmaskgit'` instantiates the frozen pretrained wrapper, while `encoder='Transformer_encoder'` trains a fresh `Encoder` from scratch. Finally, a stack of timm-derived `Block`s (self-attention → cross-attention against the encoded source/context → MLP) projects into `decoder_fc`, a linear head over the target vocabulary.

The frozen encoder itself is a 12-layer, `d_model=768`, 8-head, 4096-token transformer (`scmoscf`) loaded from `pretraining_cohort/*.ckpt`. The wrapper handles two checkpoint layouts — standalone scmaskgit checkpoints keyed `transformer.*` and nested PerturbGen checkpoints keyed `transformer.encoder_layers.model.*` — strips the appropriate prefix, then sets `requires_grad=False` and `eval()` mode on every parameter.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SRC["src tokens"] --> ENC["scmaskgitwrapper<br/>(scmoscf, frozen)"]
    ENC --> ENCOUT["enc_output<br/>(dec_embedding)"]
    TGT["tgt tokens<br/>(partially masked)"] --> TE["token_embedding"]
    TE --> PE["PositionalEncoding<br/>time_pos_sin (default)"]
    PE --> DEC["Block × num_layers<br/>self-attn → cross-attn<br/>→ MLP"]
    ENCOUT -->|"context<br/>(cross-attention)"| DEC
    DEC --> FC["decoder_fc<br/>(linear → tgt vocab)"]
    FC --> OUT["dec_logits ·<br/>dec_embedding ·<br/>labels"]
```

A second-order performance concern shapes this module's forward pass: the frozen encoder output and the cross-attention context embeddings are invariant across MaskGIT's 18 demasking iterations (only the target time step's tokens change between iterations), so both are cached using an `O(1)` key built from `data_ptr()`, shape, and stride rather than an expensive full-tensor comparison.

Sources: [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L24-L120), [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L407-L449), [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L688-L760), [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1140-L1150)

> [!TIP]
> The encoder checkpoint is auto-resolved from `configs.paths.ENCODER_CKPT_PATH`, so downloading the Hugging Face `.ckpt` into `pretraining_cohort/` (keeping its filename) is all that's needed — no `--encoder_path` flag. The wrapper also explicitly detects Git LFS pointer files (<1 KB starting with `version https://git-lfs`) and fails with an actionable download hint instead of a cryptic tensor-shape error.

## Two-Stage Training Pipeline

Training is deliberately split into two sequential stages, both orchestrated by `train.py` under one `--train_mode` flag. The **masking stage** (`PerturbGenTrainer`) trains the decoder as a MaskGIT-style masked-token model against token IDs, monitored by `val/perplexity`. The **count stage** (`CountDecoderTrainer`) then trains a regression head from the frozen embedding space to actual expression counts, monitored by `val/mse` and configured for ZINB or negative-binomial loss (`--loss_mode`). `main()` returns the `ModelCheckpoint.best_model_path` of each stage so callers can chain them without guessing by filename.

| Aspect | Stage 1: Masking | Stage 2: Count decoder |
|---|---|---|
| Lightning module | `PerturbGenTrainer` | `CountDecoderTrainer` |
| Objective | MLM loss over masked token IDs | ZINB / NB / MSE regression to counts |
| Monitor metric | `val/perplexity` (min) | `val/mse` (min) |
| Default LR / weight decay | `cellgen_lr=1e-4` / `cellgen_wd=1e-4` | `count_lr=5e-5` / `count_wd=1e-2` |
| Input | Tokenized `src`/`tgt` datasets | Tokenized datasets + raw count matrices + condition encodings |
| torch.compile | Enabled by default (CPU-disable via `--compile False`) | Not compiled |

Sources: [perturbgen/train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L63-L70), [perturbgen/train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L560-L731), [perturbgen/Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L91-L150), [README.md](README.md#L45-L58)

## Perturbation as an Inheritance Layer

In silico perturbation is implemented not as a separate subsystem but as a shallow inheritance chain layered on top of both training stages. `PerturberMasking` extends `PerturbGen` with a guided `generate()` method implementing iterative parallel demasking: a mask scheduler (`uniform`, `pow`, `cosine`, `log`, `exp`) controls how many tokens are remasked per iteration, confidence scores rank tokens, top-k filtering plus temperature-annealed Gumbel sampling produce predictions, and a `topk-margin` mode derives uncertainty scores from the gap between the top-2 logits. On the trainer side, `PerturberTrainer` extends `CountDecoderTrainer` and adds the perturbation configuration surface: `perturbation_mode` (`mask`, `pad`, `delete`, `overexpress`), `perturbation_sequence` (`src` or `tgt` — where the edit is applied), gene-to-token ID resolution through the pickled mapping dictionaries, and `pert_tps` validation against `pred_tps`.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class PerturbGen {
        +PositionalEncoding pos_embedding
        +Embedding token_embedding
        +scmaskgitwrapper encoder_layers
        +ModuleList decoder_block
        +Linear decoder_fc
        +forward(...) all_outputs
    }
    class CountDecoderTrainer {
        <<LightningModule>>
        +training_step()
        +validation_step()
    }
    class PerturbGenTrainer {
        <<LightningModule>>
        +MaskGIT masking loss
    }
    class PerturberMasking {
        +generate(18 iterations,<br/>mask_scheduler)
    }
    class PerturberCountDecoder {
        +count-space perturbation
    }
    class PerturberTrainer {
        <<LightningModule>>
        +perturbation_mode
        +perturbation_sequence
        +genes_to_perturb
    }
    PerturbGen <|-- PerturberMasking
    PerturbGenTrainer <|-- CountDecoderTrainer
    CountDecoderTrainer <|-- PerturberTrainer
    PerturberTrainer ..> PerturberMasking : uses
    PerturberTrainer ..> PerturberCountDecoder : uses
```

Sources: [perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L19-L150), [perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L15-L100), [perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1300-L1420), [perturbgen/model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L57-L64)

> [!TIP]
> The masking stage caches cross-attention context embeddings per `(src data_ptr, shape, target time step)` because they are provably invariant across the 18 demasking iterations — only the target time step's token IDs mutate during generation. Training and normal inference deliberately bypass this cache.

## Configuration and Path Management

Path management is centralized in `configs/paths.py`, which derives `ROOT` and `REPO_DIR` from the file's own location and side-effect-creates the `data/`, `T_perturb/res/`, and `T_perturb/tokenized_data/` directories at import time. The shipped preprocessing assets in `pp/` — the gene median dictionary, token dictionary, and Ensembl mapping (`*_gc95M.pkl`) — are wired as module-level defaults, meaning tokenization runs with zero path arguments on a fresh clone. Entry points perform `os.chdir(ROOT)` at import; the Python API neutralizes this with a `_preserve_cwd()` context manager so notebook working directories survive calls into the CLI-shaped internals.

Sources: [perturbgen/configs/paths.py](perturbgen/configs/paths.py#L1-L35), [perturbgen/model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L40-L49), [perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L28-L32), [perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L63-L76)

## Cross-Cutting Training Infrastructure

Four infrastructure concerns are handled uniformly across trainers. **Distribution**: Lightning strategy selection defaults to DDP (`find_unused_parameters=False`), with DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 2 available via `--parallel_distribution deepspeed`; multi-GPU runs use all visible devices (`devices=-1`), while the in-process Python API forces a single-device, notebook-safe strategy because multi-process DDP cannot launch inside a Jupyter kernel. **Experiment tracking**: Weights & Biases logging defaults to `offline` mode (read from `WANDB_MODE`), and `--wandb_mode disabled` skips `wandb.init()` entirely to avoid headless-kernel hangs. **Compilation**: the masking model is `torch.compile`d by default; checkpoints are saved with the `._orig_mod.` prefix stripped and re-inserted on load via `_restore_compiled_keys` for strict resume. **Device precision**: `set_matmul_precision_for_device` downgrades float32 matmul precision to `medium` specifically on A100/H100 hardware.

Sources: [perturbgen/train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L660-L713), [perturbgen/train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L106-L130), [perturbgen/Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L54-L71), [README.md](README.md#L60-L92)

## Dual Interface: CLI and Python API

The same orchestration is exposed through two interfaces. The click CLI in `__main__.py` defines four commands in a deliberate pedagogical order (`tokenise`, `train-mask`, `train-decoder`, `extract-embedding`), each forwarding raw arguments to the corresponding `main()` function — the hidden `tokenize` alias exists for US-spelling users. The Python API in `model.py` wraps the same entry points in-process: `pg.tokenize()` mirrors the tokenization CLI argument-by-argument, and the `PerturbGen` class chains `train_masking()` → `train_count()` → `perturb()` with a mode-alias table mapping friendly names (`knockout` → `mask`, `source` → `src`) onto the underlying perturbation enums. The API auto-detects `n_hvg`, `max_len`, and `tgt_vocab_size` from the tokenized-data layout rather than requiring them explicitly.

Sources: [perturbgen/__main__.py](perturbgen/__main__.py#L42-L89), [perturbgen/model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L1-L64), [perturbgen/model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L125-L200)

This overview established the vertical skeleton. The natural deep-dive order mirrors the data flow: start with how genes become tokens, then how the base model was trained, then how fine-tuning and perturbation work on top of it.

2. [scMASKGIT Masked Generative Encoder](6-scmaskgit-masked-generative-encoder) — the frozen base model tier in detail
