# scMASKGIT Masked Generative Encoder



This page dissects the masked generative encoder at the core of the `scmaskgit` subpackage — the `scmoscf` module in `scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py`. The model transplants the **MaskGIT** paradigm (masked token modeling with confidence-based iterative parallel decoding) from image synthesis to single-cell transcriptomics: a cell is represented as a Geneformer-style sequence of gene tokens, a random subset is masked under a scheduler during training, and at inference an entirely masked cell is progressively demasked over a fixed number of parallel decoding iterations. We cover the architecture topology, the token protocol, the training-time masking algorithm, the iterative decoding loop, guided generation, and the embedding interface exposed to downstream consumers (count regression and perturbation analyses).

## Architectural Role and Design Lineage

The module header states it is "mostly copy-paste from timm library" (the Vision Transformer reference implementation), but the model it builds, `scmoscf`, is explicitly documented as a "Seq2Seq model for cell generation using masked language modeling adopted from MaskGIT" ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1-L4), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L504-L510)). Unlike autoregressive generators, the encoder is a **single-stack, bidirectional (non-causal) transformer**: there is no separate decoder and no causal attention mask. Every gene position attends to every other position, which is precisely what makes MaskGIT-style parallel decoding possible — all token predictions for one iteration are produced in a single forward pass, then refined over successive iterations. The `Block` layers are constructed without a `context_dim`, so they operate in pure self-attention mode ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L352-L359)), and SDPA attention is invoked with `is_causal=False` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L258)).

A distinctive biological adaptation: because cells are unordered sets of gene tokens rather than spatial image patches, "position" in the sequence encodes token rank (expression magnitude) rather than spatial location, and a dedicated **time-axis embedding** marks the pseudotime/time-step condition the cell is being generated for. The `PositionalEncoding` module supports four modes (`time_pos_sin`, `comb_sin`, `sin_learnt`, `time_pos_learnt`) and adds a per-time-step embedding to token embeddings ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L32-L146)). The full treatment of the time axis is deferred to [Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding); for this page, note only that the default forward pass calls `self.pos_embedding(src_embedding, 1)` before the attention stack ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L784-L785)).

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1-L4), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L504-L510), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L352-L359), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L32-L146), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L784-L785)

## Model Topology: Token Embedding → Bidirectional Attention Stack → Logit Head

The `scmoscf` constructor assembles four components ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L478-L591)):

1. **Token embedding** — `nn.Embedding(total_vocab_size, d_model, padding_idx=pad_token)` where `total_vocab_size = tgt_vocab_size + n_total_tps`. The vocabulary is the gene token space extended by one token per modeling time step; padding index 0 gets a zero vector ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L572-L575)).
2. **Positional encoding** — the four-mode `PositionalEncoding` module configured by `pos_encoding_mode` (default `'time_pos_sin'`) ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L552-L557)).
3. **Decoder stack** — `nn.ModuleList` of `Block` modules (self-attention + GELU MLP, residual connections with LayerNorm), stacked `num_layers` times ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L576-L588), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L308-L371)).
4. **Logit head** — a single `nn.Linear(d_model, tgt_vocab_size)` projecting each position to the gene vocabulary ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L589)).

The `call_decoder` method runs the stack, optionally collects per-layer self-attention weights (averaged across layers and cast to `float16`), applies the logit head, and — critically for downstream pages — computes `mean_embedding` via `mean_nonpadding_embs`, a mask-aware mean pool over token embeddings that serves as the **cell-level representation** ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L702-L736), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L727-L735)). The training/eval branch in `forward` is the switch between the two regimes: while `self.training`, tokens pass through `generate_mask` in `'MASKGIT'` mode with the configured scheduler; in eval mode, `labels=None` and tokens flow through unmasked ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L774-L783)).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph TRAIN["Training — masked token prediction"]
        A["GF gene-token sequence<br/>[batch, seq_len]"] --> B["generate_pad<br/>pad := (ids == 0)"]
        B --> C["generate_mask(mode='MASKGIT')<br/>t ~ U(0,1); ratio = scheduler(t)<br/>sampled positions → mask token"]
        C --> D["token_embedding<br/>vocab = 25426 genes + 3 time tokens"]
        D --> E["PositionalEncoding<br/>time PE + position PE"]
        E --> F["decoder_block × num_layers<br/>bidirectional self-attention"]
        F --> G["decoder_fc → logits<br/>[batch, seq, 25426]"]
        G --> H["CrossEntropy on masked<br/>labels = -100 elsewhere"]
    end
```

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L478-L591), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L702-L736), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L774-L783), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L308-L371)

## Token Space and Special-Token Protocol

The encoder relies on a small, strict token-ID protocol that both training masking and generation decoding depend on. Integer IDs below the vocabulary extension are gene tokens from the Geneformer tokenizer; the reserved IDs are shown below.

| Token ID | Role | Enforcement points |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | Padding (also `padding_idx` of the embedding) | `generate_pad` masks all logic at `ids == 0`; excluded from masking and pooling ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L573-L575), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L679-L680)) |
| `1` | `[MASK]` (`self.mask_token = 1`) | Written by `generate_mask` during training; counts as "tokens to decode" during generation ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L570), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1255-L1256)) |
| `tgt_vocab_size … +n_total_tps` | Per-time-step condition tokens (CLS-style, position 0) | Appended to embedding table; never masked — CLS mask row forced to `False` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L572), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L682-L686)) |

Two protocol details matter for correctness. First, the CLS/time-step token at position 0 is protected in every masking path: the MASKGIT branch concatenates a `zeros((batch, 1))` boolean mask so position 0 is never remasked ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L682-L686)), and during generation the prompt position is frozen by setting its score to `-inf` before iteration begins ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1251-L1252)). Second, random-token sampling in the BERT branch uses `torch.randint(2, self.tgt_vocab_size, ...)` with an explicit comment that `+1` excludes pad and CLS from random replacement ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L660-L663)).

> [!TIP]
> The mask token doing double duty is an implementation subtlety worth internalizing: `generate_sequence` computes `total_tokens = torch.sum(tmp_ids == 1, dim=1)` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1255-L1256)) — i.e., the number of remaining mask tokens *is* the decoding budget. Any preprocessing step that leaves a literal `1` in the sequence will corrupt this count.

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L570-L575), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L682-L686), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L660-L663), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1251-L1256)

## The Training Objective: Variable-Rate Random Masking

The `generate_mask` method implements two masking regimes, selectable by `mask_mode` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L593-L689)). The **BERT** branch is the canonical 80/10/10 corruption (MASK / random / original), adapted from the HuggingFace data collator ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L631-L664)). However, `scmoscf.forward` always calls it with `mask_mode='MASKGIT'`, so the second branch is the operative training path ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L775-L781)).

The MASKGIT branch implements **variable-rate masking**: instead of a fixed corruption ratio, each sample draws a random time `t ~ U(0,1)` per batch (`rand_time = uniform((batch,))`), converts it to a mask ratio through `noise_schedule(rand_time, method=mask_scheduler, total_tokens=seq_len-1)`, and masks `round(sample_length × ratio)` positions, clamped to a minimum of 1 ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L665-L688)). Which positions get masked is decided by `argsort` of uniform random values — a permutation-based uniform sample over non-pad, non-CLS positions. The scheduler is configurable across `'uniform'`, `'pow'`, `'cosine'`, `'log'`, `'exp'` (documented at the generation call sites; cosine is the default, matching MaskGIT's finding that cosine difficulty-weighting trains best) ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L495), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L993-L995)). Unmasked positions receive label `-100` so cross-entropy ignores them — the loss is computed **only** on masked positions ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L688)).

| Property | BERT mode | MASKGIT mode (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Mask fraction | Fixed (`mlm_probability`, default 0.3) | Random per sample: `scheduler(t)`, `t ~ U(0,1)` |
| Corruption mix | 80% MASK / 10% random / 10% original | 100% MASK token |
| Position choice | Bernoulli per position | Permutation of uniform randoms (exact count) |
| Protected positions | CLS (pad excluded via probability fill 0) | CLS + pad via `rand_int[pad]=1` trick |
| Training signal | Position-wise denoising | Difficulty-scaled denoising aligned with iterative decoding |

The design rationale is train/inference symmetry: at generation time the model must reconstruct a sequence from an arbitrary partial context (every ratio from ~0% to ~100% masked), so the training distribution must cover that entire spectrum. A random `t` per sample plus the cosine schedule approximates exactly that curriculum. This is also why `mlm_probability` is effectively inert in the default configuration — it only parameterizes the BERT branch.

> [!TIP]
> The BERT branch contains latent bugs that are masked (pun intended) by the default path: `tgt_input_id[masked_indices] = self.mask_token` replaces **all** selected positions with MASK, so the 80/10/10 comment is not honored in the current code, and the `sin_learnt`/`time_pos_learnt` forward branches reference an undefined `tgt_time_step_` variable ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L128-L146)). Treat non-default modes as unverified; the shipped configuration (`MASKGIT` + `time_pos_sin`) is the exercised, validated path.

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L593-L689), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L631-L664), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L665-L688), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L775-L781), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L495)

## Confidence-Based Iterative Parallel Decoding

Inference inverts the training objective. `CountDecoder.generate` initializes a fully masked target sequence — `ids` filled with `mask_token`, position 0 seeded with the input's CLS token, positions beyond `sequence_length` zeroed — and hands it to `generate_sequence` with `demask_fn=self.pretrained_model` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1037-L1042), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1045-L1058)). The `generate_sequence` loop ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1191-L1334)) is the canonical MaskGIT decoding algorithm adapted for set-structured tokens:

1. **Iterate** over `torch.linspace(0, 1, iterations)` zipped with `reversed(range(iterations))` — iteration fraction rises, `steps_until_x0` falls ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1258-L1264)).
2. **Compute the remask budget** from the scheduler: `rand_mask_prob = noise_schedule(ratio=iteration, ...)`; the number of tokens to re-hide is `unmasked_count × rand_mask_prob` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1266-L1276)).
3. **Remask the least-confident tokens**: `torch.topk(scores, ...)` selects positions with the highest `scores` (confidence deficit) and they are overwritten with the mask token ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1277-L1284)).
4. **Predict all positions in one forward pass** through the encoder; logits are sliced past the prompt ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1292-L1300)).
5. **Suppress already-decoded gene IDs** in the logits so a token already committed elsewhere in the cell cannot be re-emitted in this iteration ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1313-L1315)).
6. **Sample**: `top_k` filtering at `topk_filter_thres=0.9`, then `gumbel_sample` with a temperature annealed as `starting_temperature × (steps_until_x0 / iteration)` — high randomness early, near-greedy late ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1316-L1320)).
7. **Update confidence scores** as `scores = 1 − softmax(logits)[pred_id]` and freeze committed tokens when `can_remask_prev_masked=False` (the default) by filling non-masked positions' scores with `-inf` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1322-L1333)).

Defaults mirror the MaskGIT paper's optimum: `iterations=18` (commented "optimal of iterations in MaskGIT"), `temperature=2.0` (recommended range 2.0–3.0), `topk_filter_thres=0.9`, `mask_scheduler='cosine'` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L962-L967)). After the loop, the final decoder output's non-padding embeddings are mean-pooled into a cell embedding and pushed through the count head ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1061-L1068)) — the consumer contract is covered in [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    S["Start: all gene positions = MASK<br/>(CLS prompt at pos 0, frozen)"] --> T["Iteration i ∈ linspace(0,1), T=18<br/>budget_i = unmasked × cosine(i)"]
    T --> U["Remask lowest-confidence positions<br/>(top-k by score deficit)"]
    U --> V["One bidirectional forward pass<br/>→ logits for all positions"]
    V --> W["Suppress already-decoded gene IDs<br/>top-k filter 0.9 · Gumbel sample<br/>temperature annealed ∝ (1 − i/T)"]
    W --> X["Commit predictions<br/>scores := 1 − p(token)"]
    X --> Y{"i < 1 ?"}
    Y -- "yes" --> T
    Y -- "no" --> Z["Mean-pool non-pad embeddings<br/>→ cell embedding → count head"]
```

This decoding scheme carries two orders-of-magnitude advantages over autoregressive generation of a 2,048-token cell: only 18 forward passes total (vs. one per token), and each pass is fully parallel across the sequence and batch. The repository even ships dedicated benchmarks for this behavior (`perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py`, `perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py`), detailed in [Test and Benchmark Suite](26-test-and-benchmark-suite).

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1191-L1334), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1258-L1284), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1292-L1333), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L962-L967), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1037-L1058), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1061-L1068)

## Guided Generation with Gene-Prompt Logit Boosting

`guided_generate` extends the decoding loop for **in-silico perturbation of known gene programs**: it accepts `unique_gene_list` and `shared_gene_list` dictionaries and biases the generative trajectory toward those genes. Inside `generate_sequence`, when both lists are provided, the raw logits are boosted before filtering — `logits[:, :, unique_genes] += 5` and `logits[:, :, shared_genes] += 2` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1302-L1307)). Because boost happens pre-`top_k` and pre-softmax, it raises both the probability of these tokens being sampled and their confidence scores, making the model commit to them early and keep them.

The guided path also restructures decoding itself: for `time_step == 1`, a first pass decodes only the first `prompt_length = 10` positions over `iterations=10`, effectively "seeding" the cell with the guided genes as a prefix prompt; those tokens are then unmasked into the buffer (`ids_[:, prompt_length:] = 1` forces them into the to-decode set? — no: the returned ids are written back and the remaining positions continue through a full `iterations` decode) ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1129-L1157)). This two-stage prompting trades a small extra compute cost for stronger adherence to the requested gene list. The perturbation semantics built on this entry point — knockout overexpression, combinatorial conditions — are documented in [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes).

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1071-L1189), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1302-L1307), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L1129-L1157)

## Attention Mechanics: SDPA with Recoverable Weights

The `CrossAttention` module is a unified self/cross-attention primitive with two execution paths ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L176-L305)). The `'sdpa'` path routes through `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` under an explicit kernel constraint — `sdpa_kernel(backends=[FLASH_ATTENTION, EFFICIENT_ATTENTION])` — for memory-efficient long-sequence attention over up to 2,048 gene tokens ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L250-L252)). The `'normal'` path is a materialized-softmax einsum implementation that always returns attention weights ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L222-L235)).

When `return_attn=True` under SDPA, flash kernels cannot expose attention matrices, so the code employs an identity-matrix trick: it passes `torch.eye(seq_len)` as the *value* tensor, so SDPA's output is the attention matrix itself; a second manual `out_ @ v` then recovers the real output ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L247-L248), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L285-L288), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L260-L264)). The collected per-block self-attention maps are averaged across layers and cast to `float16` in `call_decoder` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L722-L725)) — these are the tensors consumed by attention-based gene program discovery, treated fully in [Gene Program Discovery](12-gene-program-discovery). Note the attention-weight recovery path is substantially more expensive (it defeats fused kernels) and should be reserved for analysis runs.

> [!TIP]
> The attention-recovery trick (identity as value) silently doubles the memory traffic of the attention block — do not enable `return_attn` in sweep or training configurations. The averaged layer weights are also `float16`, which matters if you later threshold or cluster them at high precision.

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L176-L305), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L222-L235), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L250-L252), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L285-L288), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L722-L725)

## Class Interaction Map

The module-level relationships below show how the encoder composes internally and how it is consumed by the count-decoding wrapper in the same file. The `Encoder` class (a vanilla `torch.nn.TransformerEncoder` variant with the same embedding/PE front-end) coexists as an alternative encoder body ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L374-L475)).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class PositionalEncoding {
        +mode: time_pos_sin | comb_sin | sin_learnt | time_pos_learnt
        +forward(x, tgt_time_step)
    }
    class Block {
        +self_attn: CrossAttention
        +feed_forward: Mlp
        +forward(x, tgt_mask)
    }
    class CrossAttention {
        +normal_attention()
        +sdpa_attention(FLASH/EFFICIENT)
    }
    class scmoscf {
        +mask_token = 1
        +generate_mask(mode='MASKGIT')
        +call_decoder() → dict
        +forward(src_input_id)
    }
    class CountDecoder {
        +pretrained_model: scmoscf
        +count_decoder: CountHead
        +generate(iterations=18)
        +guided_generate(unique/shared genes)
        +generate_sequence(demask_fn)
    }
    class CountHead {
        +loss_mode: mse | zinb | nb
    }
    scmoscf *-- PositionalEncoding
    scmoscf *-- "num_layers" Block
    Block *-- CrossAttention
    Block *-- Mlp
    CountDecoder o-- scmoscf : demask_fn
    CountDecoder *-- CountHead
```

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L478-L591), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L861-L956), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L374-L475), [__init__.py](scmaskgit/Modules/__init__.py#L1)

## Configuration Reference

Constructor defaults for `scmoscf` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L481-L502)) and generation-time defaults for `generate` ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L962-L967)):

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `tgt_vocab_size` | 25426 | Gene token vocabulary size (Geneformer tokenizer output space) |
| `d_model` | 256 | Token embedding / hidden dimension |
| `num_heads` | 8 | Attention heads per block |
| `num_layers` | 1 | Number of self-attention blocks |
| `d_ff` | 2048 | Attention head inner dim; MLP hidden sizing |
| `max_seq_length` | 2048 | Maximum tokens per cell (drives positional PE length) |
| `mlm_probability` | 0.3 | Mask fraction (BERT branch only; inert under MASKGIT) |
| `pred_tps` / `n_total_tps` | [1, 2, 3] / 3 | Target time steps; vocab extension size |
| `mask_scheduler` | `'cosine'` | Mask-ratio schedule: uniform, pow, cosine, log, exp |
| `pos_encoding_mode` | `'time_pos_sin'` | Time + position encoding variant |
| `pad_token` / `mask_token` | 0 / 1 | Reserved token IDs |
| `iterations` (generation) | 18 | Decoding refinement steps |
| `temperature` (generation) | 2.0 | Gumbel sampling temperature, annealed; range 2.0–3.0 |
| `topk_filter_thres` | 0.9 | Fraction of logits retained pre-sampling |
| `can_remask_prev_masked` | False | Whether committed tokens may be re-hidden |

Scaling notes for advanced users: the depth default (`num_layers=1`) is intentionally minimal — sweep configurations in `perturbgen/configs/sweep/` and the pretraining checkpoint naming convention (`..._pow_tp_1-2-3_s_42...` in `pretraining_cohort/`) indicate that depth, scheduler family (`pow` vs `cosine`), and time-step sets are the primary swept axes (see [Hyperparameter Sweeps and Batch Jobs](18-hyperparameter-sweeps-and-batch-jobs) and [Pretrained Checkpoints and Hugging Face Assets](23-pretrained-checkpoints-and-hugging-face-assets)).

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L481-L502), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L962-L967)

## Where This Fits and Where to Go Next

The masked generative encoder is the first stage of a two-phase training scheme: it learns the token-space distribution of cells via masked prediction, after which its pooled `mean_embedding` output is frozen and a count head (ZINB/NB/MSE) is trained on top for expression regression ([T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L796-L858)). The embedding also serves as the export surface for cell/gene representation extraction ([Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction](11-cell-and-gene-embedding-extraction)).

Recommended reading order from here: **[Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training)** for the second training stage that wraps this encoder; **[Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding)** for the `tgt_time_step` conditioning semantics referenced throughout this page; **[Geneformer-Style Gene Tokenization](9-geneformer-style-gene-tokenization)** for how raw counts become the input token sequences; and **[In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes)** for how `generate` and `guided_generate` are orchestrated into perturbation prediction.


# Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training



Perturbgen's pretraining recipe decouples **what a cell is** (discrete gene-token identity) from **how much a cell expresses** (continuous per-gene counts). Stage 1 trains a MaskGIT-style masked generative backbone (`CellGenTrainer` wrapping the `scmoscf` transformer) with cross-entropy over randomly corrupted token sequences. Stage 2 freezes that backbone entirely and trains a lightweight `CountDecoder`/`CountHead` that regresses gene-expression counts from pooled cell embeddings, using MSE, ZINB, or NB losses. This page explains both stages as implemented in the `scmaskgit` training package, from the masking operator down to the distributional count loss.

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L62-L130), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L478-L591)

## Design Rationale: Why Decouple Token Identity from Count Regression

The two stages answer two fundamentally different prediction problems. Stage 1 is a **discrete denoising task**: given a sequence of Geneformer-style gene tokens with a random subset replaced by `[MASK]`, predict the original token identity at each masked position. This forces the transformer to learn cell-state semantics in embedding space. Stage 2 is a **continuous regression task**: pool the (uncorrupted) sequence into a single cell embedding and predict the full count vector, optionally under a negative-binomial-style observation model that respects count-data overdispersion and dropout.

The decoupling has a concrete architectural payoff: during Stage 2 inference (and later in-silico perturbation), the frozen backbone performs MaskGIT iterative parallel decoding to synthesize target-cell token sequences, and only afterwards does the trained count head convert the pooled embedding into calibrated counts. Training the head on frozen features guarantees that count calibration never distorts the generative decoder learned in Stage 1.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph S1["Stage 1 — Masking (CellGenTrainer)"]
        A["Tokenized cell sequences"] --> B["MaskGIT corruption<br/>(noise_schedule ratio)"]
        B --> C["scmoscf transformer<br/>+ time/pos encoding"]
        C --> D["CrossEntropyLoss<br/>on masked positions only"]
    end
    subgraph S2["Stage 2 — Count Decoder (CountDecoderTrainer)"]
        E["Load masking checkpoint<br/>freeze all params"] --> F["CountDecoder forward<br/>(no masking)"]
        F --> G["mean non-padding embedding<br/>per time step"]
        G --> H["CountHead: MSE / ZINB / NB<br/>+ conditioned theta"]
    end
    D -->|"ckpt_masking_path"| E
```

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L62-L212), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L275-L371), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L861-L948), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L958-L975)

## Stage 1: MaskGIT-Style Masked Token Prediction

### Trainer and model composition

`CellGenTrainer` is a PyTorch Lightning `LightningModule` that instantiates `scmoscf` with a vocabulary of gene tokens plus per-time-step task tokens (`total_vocab_size = tgt_vocab_size + n_total_tps`), a stack of decoder blocks, and a final `decoder_fc` projection back to the token vocabulary. The only training objective is a plain `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` assigned to `self.masking_loss`; perplexity (`torchmetrics.text.Perplexity`, ignoring index `-100`) is tracked alongside as a diagnostic. Optimization is a single Adam optimizer over all transformer parameters with configurable `weight_decay` and `initial_lr`, monitored on `train/masking_loss`.

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L62-L130), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L162-L169), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L572-L591)

### The masking operator: BERT vs MASKGIT

The masking itself lives in `scmoscf.generate_mask`, which supports two regimes selectable via `mask_mode`. The **BERT** regime is the classic 80/10/10 corruption (mask / random token / keep), applied to a fixed `mlm_probability` fraction of positions, with CLS and padding positions excluded. The **MASKGIT** regime — the default for this pipeline — draws an independent masking ratio per sample: `rand_time ~ Uniform(0,1)` is mapped through a `noise_schedule` (methods: `uniform`, `pow`, `cosine`, `log`, `exp`) into a probability, which is multiplied by the sample's actual sequence length and rounded with a floor of one masked token. Positions to mask are then chosen uniformly at random via `rand_int.argsort`, so each cell in a batch is corrupted at a different rate. Crucially, `labels` are set to `-100` at all non-masked positions, so the cross-entropy loss and perplexity are computed over masked tokens only.

| Property | BERT mode | MASKGIT mode |
|---|---|---|
| Mask ratio | Fixed per batch (`mlm_probability`) | Per-sample, sampled from `noise_schedule` |
| Input corruption | 80% `[MASK]`, 10% random, 10% original | 100% replaced by mask token |
| Position selection | i.i.d. Bernoulli per position | Uniform without replacement (`argsort` trick) |
| Excluded positions | CLS + padding | CLS + padding (set `rand_int = 1`) |
| Typical use | MLM-style encoders | MaskGIT-style parallel iterative decoding |

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L593-L689), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L997-L999), [utils.py](scmaskgit/src/utils.py#L29-L56)

### Stage 1 forward pass and training step

In `scmoscf.forward`, masking runs only under `self.training`; the corrupted ids are embedded via `token_embedding` (with `padding_idx=0`), receive time-aware positional encoding, and flow through the decoder blocks. The head returns `dec_logits`, the `labels`, and `mean_embedding` — a mean over non-padding token embeddings. The Lightning `training_step` flattens logits and labels, applies cross-entropy, and logs `train/masking_loss` and `train/perplexity` (the latter under `torch.no_grad()` with `sync_dist=True` for DDP-correct aggregation). The validation step mirrors this and logs `val/loss` and `val/perplexity`, which is the monitored metric for checkpoint selection.

> [!TIP]
> The mask-scheduler choice is recorded in the checkpoint filename (e.g., `..._m_pow_tp_1-2-3_s_42-...ckpt` in `pretraining_cohort/` means scheduler `pow`, prediction time steps 1–2–3, seed 42), so a trained checkpoint is self-describing with respect to its Stage 1 corruption policy.

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L738-L793), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L702-L736), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L171-L248), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L23-L30)

## Stage 2: Count Decoder Training

### Frozen backbone and task tokens

`CountDecoderTrainer` reconstructs a fresh `scmoscf`, restores Stage 1 weights from `ckpt_masking_path` via `modify_ckpt_state_dict` (stripping the `transformer.` prefix) with `strict=False`, then sets `requires_grad = False` on **every** backbone parameter. The frozen module is handed to `CountDecoder`, which owns the trainable `CountHead`. A second optional checkpoint (`ckpt_count_path`) restores a previously trained count head — again with `strict=False`. The trainer also registers one extra vocabulary id per time step (`cls_token_{i} = total_vocab_size + (i - 1)`) as a buffer; in `forward`, these task tokens are prepended to each target sequence before the decoder runs, letting one model serve multiple prediction horizons.

> [!TIP]
> The `strict=False` load tolerates buffers registered after the checkpoint was saved (e.g., positional-encoding tables or CLS-token buffers), which is what allows Stage 2 checkpoints to be re-loaded into later perturbation-time trainers without schema churn.

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L275-L371), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L392-L402), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L447-L465)

### From embeddings to counts: CountHead modes

`CountDecoder.forward` invokes the frozen backbone with masking disabled (`not_masked=True`) — no MaskGIT corruption during Stage 2 training — and pools each time step's output into `mean_embedding` (mean over non-padding tokens, despite the `cls_embedding` naming). `CountHead` then applies an MLP followed by L2 normalization and branches on `loss_mode`:

| Loss mode | Output heads | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `mse` | `count_lognorm` = Linear → ReLU | Regresses log-normalized counts directly |
| `zinb` | `count_mean` = Linear → Softmax; `count_dropout` = Linear (zi_logits) | Mean as a fraction of library size; zero-inflation logits |
| `nb`  | `count_mean` = Linear → Softmax | Overdispersed counts without zero inflation |

The softmax parameterization makes `count_mean` a per-gene expression fraction; at loss time it is scaled by the target library size (`batch_size_factor`) to recover an absolute mean, following the standard scVI-style size-factor decode.

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L796-L858), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L931-L948), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L544-L547)

### Conditioned dispersion and the count loss

For `zinb`/`nb` modes, dispersion is not a free per-gene vector but is **conditioned on experimental batch**: the trainer holds `theta ∈ R^{n_genes × n_conditions_combined}` and `compute_dispersion` multiplies a one-hot encoding of each cell's combined condition (`combined_batch`) through `theta`, exponentiating the result to obtain per-gene dispersion. `compute_count_loss` then loops over every prediction time step in `pred_tps`: for `mse` it sums squared errors on log-normalized counts; for `zinb` it evaluates the log-likelihood of true counts under a `ZeroInflatedNegativeBinomial(mu, theta, zi_logits)` from scvi-tools; for `nb` under a plain `NegativeBinomial`. Per-time-step losses are summed into a scalar. When `n_samples > 1`, predictions are drawn from the fitted distribution and averaged rather than reported as the posterior mean.

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L467-L494), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L496-L572)

### Training loop and diagnostics

The Stage 2 `training_step` logs `train/loss` and, under `torch.no_grad()`, a batch-wise `train/mse` against true counts. At each epoch end, the accumulated true/predicted counts are concatenated and a Pearson correlation is logged (`train/pearson`) — the canonical quality signal for count reconstruction. The validation step computes the same loss with distributional sampling enabled and logs `val/loss`, `val/mse`, and epoch-level Pearson correlation.

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L652-L699), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L701-L734)

## Orchestration, Checkpoints, and Reproducibility

A single entry point, `scmaskgit/train.py`, drives both stages via the `--train_mode` flag (`masking` or `count`), which selects `CellGenTrainer` vs `CountDecoderTrainer` and the matching `CellGenDataModule`. The masking stage is wired with model hyperparameters (`d_model=768`, `num_heads=8`, mask scheduler, prediction/context time steps, positional-encoding mode) and persisted through a `ModelCheckpoint` whose filename encodes the run id, learning rate, weight decay, batch size, positional mode, mask scheduler, time steps, and seed. Logging goes to a Weights & Biases project named `Moscf`; large runs use `DDPStrategy(find_unused_parameters=True)` with `bf16-mixed` precision across all visible GPUs. The repository ships a concrete Stage 1 artifact following this convention in `pretraining_cohort/`.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class CellGenTrainer {
        +scmoscf transformer
        +CrossEntropyLoss masking_loss
        +Perplexity perplexity
        +forward(batch)
        +training_step(batch)
    }
    class CountDecoderTrainer {
        +CountDecoder decoder
        +Parameter theta
        +compute_dispersion(batch)
        +compute_count_loss(outputs, batch)
        +training_step(batch)
    }
    class CountDecoder {
        +scmoscf pretrained_model
        +CountHead count_decoder
        +forward(src, tgt_dict)
        +generate(...)
    }
    class scmoscf {
        +generate_mask(...)
        +call_decoder(...)
        +dec_logits / labels / mean_embedding
    }
    class CountHead {
        +loss_mode
        +forward(x) count_outputs
    }
    CellGenTrainer *-- scmoscf : owns + trains
    CountDecoderTrainer *-- CountDecoder : owns
    CountDecoderTrainer ..> CountDecoderTrainer : theta (dispersion)
    CountDecoder *-- scmoscf : frozen backbone
    CountDecoder *-- CountHead : trainable head
```

Sources: [train.py](scmaskgit/train.py#L42-L50), [train.py](scmaskgit/train.py#L301-L324), [train.py](scmaskgit/train.py#L350-L387), [train.py](scmaskgit/train.py#L390-L438)

## Stage 1 vs Stage 2 at a Glance

| Dimension | Stage 1 — Masking | Stage 2 — Count Decoder |
|---|---|---|
| Trainer class | `CellGenTrainer` | `CountDecoderTrainer` |
| Trainable params | Full `scmoscf` backbone | `CountHead` + optional `theta` only |
| Input corruption | MASKGIT per-sample ratios (or BERT) | None (`not_masked=True`) |
| Loss | `CrossEntropyLoss` over masked tokens, `-100` ignored | MSE / ZINB / NB log-likelihood, summed over `pred_tps` |
| Key metrics | masked loss, perplexity | loss, MSE, Pearson correlation |
| Optimization | Adam, `initial_lr`, `weight_decay`, monitor `train/masking_loss` | `lr`, `weight_decay` hyperparameters on head |
| Artifact | masking checkpoint (`ckpt_masking_path`) | count-head checkpoint (`ckpt_count_path`) |
| Role downstream | MaskGIT iterative decoding backbone | Count calibration for generated cells |

Sources: [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L62-L169), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L275-L409), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L496-L572), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L931-L948)

The mathematical details of the distributional losses belong to [ZINB and Negative Binomial Losses](24-zinb-and-negative-binomial-losses). For running these stages at scale — sweeps, DDP, and W&B tracking — continue with [Hyperparameter Sweeps and Batch Jobs](18-hyperparameter-sweeps-and-batch-jobs), [Distributed Training with DDP and DeepSpeed](19-distributed-training-with-ddp-and-deepspeed), and [Experiment Tracking with Weights and Biases](20-experiment-tracking-with-weights-and-biases); for how the frozen Stage 1 backbone is reused at inference, see [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes).


# Time-Aware Positional Encoding



This page explains how PerturbGen injects **which time point is being predicted** into its token representations. A single MaskGIT-style encoder must produce a *different* transcriptomic distribution for day 1, day 2, and day 3 of a perturbation time course, yet it shares one set of weights and one token embedding table across all of them. The `PositionalEncoding` module solves this by combining a **time-point encoding** (identifies the target time step) with a **slot-position encoding** (identifies the token's index in the sequence), and it offers four interchangeable modes controlled by a single CLI/config parameter. This page documents the module's construction, its per-encoder index-offset conventions, how `tgt_time_step` flows through training and generation, and the interpolation/extrapolation trade-offs between sinusoidal and learnt variants.

## Why a Time Axis in Positional Encoding

PerturbGen models a source cell state and one or more target cell states measured at successive time points after a perturbation. The target time steps are declared via `pred_tps` (default `[1, 2, 3]`) and `n_total_tps`, and the model maintains `self.total_tps = list(range(1, n_total_tps + 1))` as its canonical time-point index space. During generation, the model loops over these time points and produces a separate de-noised sequence per time point — each loop iteration explicitly tags the request with a `tgt_time_step`. The positional encoding is the mechanism that makes the *same* transformer block behave differently for `t=1` versus `t=3`, because the time identity is added directly to the token embeddings before any attention layer sees them. This design is what allows one checkpoint to serve multi-step prediction instead of training one model per time point.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L591-L696), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L94-L124)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Token IDs<br/>tgt_input_ids_t{t}"] --> B["token_embedding<br/>(nn.Embedding)"]
    B --> C["+ time_pe[:, t_offset]<br/>one d_model vector<br/>broadcast over all tokens"]
    C --> D["+ pos_pe[:, :seq_len]<br/>varies per slot index"]
    D --> E["Transformer blocks<br/>(self-attn + FFN)"]
    E --> F["dec_logits / dec_embedding<br/>time-point-specific output"]
    style C fill:#e8f0fe
    style D fill:#e8f0fe
```

Both additions happen **once, before the encoder stack** — the time information is baked into the input representations rather than injected per layer. The diagram above shows the `time_pos_sin` composition; the other modes swap *how* the two components are computed, not *where* they are added.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L670-L676), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L130-L161)

## The `PositionalEncoding` Module at a Glance

`PositionalEncoding` lives in `perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py` and is instantiated once per model. Its constructor takes four key arguments: `d_model` (embedding width), `length` (maximum sequence length for slot encoding), `n_time_steps` (size of the time axis), `encoder` (`'scmaskgit'` or `'Transformer_encoder'`), and `mode` (one of the four encoding strategies). The module is shared by the production `PerturbGen` model, the legacy `scmoscf` base model in `scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py` (which carries an equivalent copy), and the alternative `Encoder` class — all three wire it in identically as `self.pos_embedding`.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L34-L79), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L670-L676), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L32-L146), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L552-L557)

A critical construction detail: **the time buffer is deliberately oversized**. When `mode='time_pos_sin'`, the module builds two registered buffers — `time_pe` of shape `[1, n_time_steps + Δ, d_model]` and `pos_pe` of shape `[1, length, d_model]`. For the `scmaskgit` encoder, `Δ = +2`; for `Transformer_encoder`, `Δ = +1`. At forward time, `tgt_time_step` is shifted by a per-encoder offset before indexing the time buffer. The code comments mark this as *"adjust for src embedding starting at 0"*: the extra slots reserve room below the trained time-point indices so the shifted lookups never underflow the table.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L81-L93), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L130-L138)

> [!TIP]
> Because time and position tables are created with `register_buffer` (not `nn.Parameter`), the sinusoidal variants are **non-trainable but checkpointed**: they are serialized into the `.ckpt` state dict and follow the model across devices via Lightning's `.to()` semantics. The learnt variants instead use `nn.Embedding`, whose weights *are* trained — this is why switching modes changes both the parameter count and what a pretrained checkpoint can load cleanly.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L87-L112), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L127-L128)

## Four Encoding Modes Compared

The `mode` parameter selects between four strategies, all producing the same mathematical contract: `x + time_encoding + position_encoding` (except `comb_sin`, which fuses the two into one table).

| Mode | Time component | Position component | Trainable params | Time interpolation/extrapolation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `time_pos_sin` (default) | Sinusoidal buffer, indexed by `tgt_time_step` | Sinusoidal buffer, sliced to `seq_len` | None | Yes — closed-form function of the index |
| `comb_sin` | Fused: one sinusoid over the flattened `(time × position)` grid | Fused into the same table | None | Yes |
| `sin_learnt` | Sinusoidal buffer | `nn.Embedding(length, d_model)` | Position table | Yes — time stays closed-form |
| `time_pos_learnt` | `nn.Embedding(n_time_steps, d_model)` | `nn.Embedding(length, d_model)` | Both tables | No — unseen time indices have untrained entries |

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L87-L114), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L63-L67)

The `comb_sin` mode deserves a precise description: it builds a **single** sinusoidal table of size `n_time_steps * length` and treats the `(time, position)` pair as one linear index. At forward time it slices the contiguous block `[tgt_time_step * length : tgt_time_step * length + seq_len]`, so time step `t` occupies the `t`-th strip of one long positional axis rather than adding a separate time vector.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L94-L98), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L143-L147)

## The Default Mode: `time_pos_sin`

The sinusoidal generator reproduces the classic Transformer formula: for position `p` and dimension pair `(2i, 2i+1)`, it writes `sin(p · div_term)` into even columns and `cos(p · div_term)` into odd columns, where `div_term = exp(arange(0, d_model, 2) · −log(10000)/d_model)`. The result is stored with a leading batch dimension (`pe.unsqueeze(0)`) so it broadcasts cleanly against `[batch, seq, d_model]` activations.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L116-L125)

At forward time, the mode performs three verifiable steps:

1. **Offset the time index** according to the encoder type (table below).
2. **Look up the time vector**: `time_pe = self.time_pe[:, tgt_time_step_].unsqueeze(0)` — a single `d_model` vector, broadcast across the whole sequence, identical for every token in the batch sample.
3. **Add the slot encoding**: `pos_pe = self.pos_pe[:, :x.size(1)]` — sliced to the actual sequence length, varying per token.

The final expression is `return x + time_pe + pos_pe`. The legacy copy in `scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py` implements the identical semantics with an explicit `expand(batch, seq, -1)` instead of implicit broadcasting.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L130-L142), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L121-L126)

## Encoder-Specific Time Index Offsets

The mapping from a logical time point (`1, 2, 3, …`) to a physical buffer row differs per encoder family:

| Encoder | Buffer size | Forward offset `tgt_time_step → tgt_time_step_` | Rationale (from code comments) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scmaskgit` | `n_time_steps + 2` | `+1` | Src embedding occupies the reserved slots below the target range |
| `Transformer_encoder` | `n_time_steps + 1` | `0` (unchanged) | Src embedding starts at index 0; one extra slot for the src step |
| `GF_frozen` / `GF_fine_tuned` | `n_time_steps` | `−1` | Geneformer-style encoders use 0-indexed time steps |

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L81-L85), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L130-L138)

Two call sites make these conventions concrete. The alternative `Encoder` class always encodes at `tgt_time_step=0` (its forward has no time-step argument to thread), while the legacy `scmoscf` base model hardcodes `pos_embedding(src_embedding, 1)` in its forward pass — with the `scmaskgit` `+1` offset this resolves to buffer row 2. The production `PerturbGen` model instead threads the real target time step through, as described next.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L570-L577), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L784-L785)

## Time-Step Flow in Training and Generation

During generation, `PerturberMasking.generate` iterates over `self.pred_tps` and dispatches one full MaskGIT iterative-denoising run per time point. Each call passes `tgt_time_step=time_step` down into `generate_sequence`, so every demask iteration for that time point re-applies the same `time_pe` row — the logits the decoder produces are explicitly conditioned on the requested time point, and results are keyed back into per-time-step outputs (`'count_output_t{t}'`, `'cls_embedding_t{t}'`).

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L94-L124), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L30-L79)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["generate(src, tgt_input_id_dict)"] --> L{"for time_step<br/>in pred_tps"}
    L -->|"t = 1"| M1["Mask all target tokens<br/>ids = mask_token"]
    L -->|"t = 2"| M2["Mask all target tokens"]
    L -->|"t = 3"| M3["Mask all target tokens"]
    M1 --> G1["generate_sequence(<br/>tgt_time_step=1)"]
    M2 --> G2["generate_sequence(<br/>tgt_time_step=2)"]
    M3 --> G3["generate_sequence(<br/>tgt_time_step=3)"]
    G1 --> P1["+ time_pe[row(t=1)] + pos_pe<br/>→ iterative demasking"]
    G2 --> P2["+ time_pe[row(t=2)] + pos_pe"]
    G3 --> P3["+ time_pe[row(t=3)] + pos_pe"]
    P1 --> O["outputs keyed by time step<br/>'count_output_t{t}'"]
    P2 --> O
    P3 --> O
```

An efficiency property documented directly in the model code: because the context embeddings depend only on the encoder output and the fixed `tgt_time_step` — not on the evolving masked sequence — they are **computed once per predicted time point and cached across all ~18 MaskGIT demask iterations** (`_ctx_cache_key` / `_ctx_cache_output`). This is safe precisely *because* the time encoding is constant within a generation loop.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L742-L752)

> [!TIP]
> When reusing the legacy `scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py` copy of `PositionalEncoding` outside PerturbGen, note that its forward pass only fully implements `time_pos_sin`: the `comb_sin`, `sin_learnt`, and `time_pos_learnt` branches reference a variable `tgt_time_step_` that is never assigned in that class (the `encoder` constructor argument was commented out there), so those branches will raise `NameError`. The canonical, mode-complete implementation is the `perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py` version.

Sources: [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L121-L146), [T_model.py](scmaskgit/Modules/T_model.py#L33-L47)

## Configuring the Encoding Mode

The mode is a first-class training parameter. In `train.py`, `--pos_encoding_mode` accepts exactly the four mode strings with `time_pos_sin` as default, and companion flags `--pred_tps` (default `[1, 2, 3]`) and `--context_tps` define the time-point index space the encoding table must cover.

| CLI argument | Default | Role in time-aware encoding |
|---|---|---|
| `--pos_encoding_mode` | `time_pos_sin` | Selects one of `time_pos_sin`, `comb_sin`, `sin_learnt`, `time_pos_learnt` |
| `--pred_tps` | `[1, 2, 3]` | Time points the model predicts; each gets its own `time_pe` row (offset applied) |
| `--context_tps` | `None` | Additional time points supplied as cross-attention context |
| `--mask_scheduler` | `pow` | Masking schedule (orthogonal to PE, but co-recorded in run names) |

Sources: [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L297-L303), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L243-L256), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L231-L236)

The checkpoint naming convention encodes the encoding choice so runs are self-describing. The filename template appends `..._tp_{time_steps_str}_s_{args.seed}_pos_{args.pos_encoding_mode}_m_{args.mask_scheduler}` — which is exactly how the shipped pretraining checkpoint `pretraining_cohort/20250709_..._ptime_pos_sin_m_pow_tp_1-2-3_s_42-epoch=00.ckpt` decomposes: sinusoidal time+position encoding (`pos_sin`), power-scheduled masking (`m_pow`), predicted time points 1–3 (`tp_1-2-3`), seed 42. Sweeps treat the mode as a tunable dimension too — for example, the HSPC masking sweep pins `positional_encoding: 'time_pos_learnt'` while varying layers and learning rates.

Sources: [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L600-L602), [sweep-hspc-masking.yaml](perturbgen/configs/sweep/sweep-hspc-masking.yaml#L36-L37)

When loading a pretrained encoder, the mode is part of the architecture, not just the weights: the wrapper `scmaskgitwrapper` reconstructs `scmoscf` with default `pos_encoding_mode='time_pos_sin'` and then loads the checkpoint's `state_dict`, which contains the registered sinusoidal buffers. A checkpoint trained with a learnt mode therefore expects the matching `nn.Embedding` shapes at load time — mode changes between training and inference require retraining.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L401-L466)

## Interpolation, Extrapolation, and Mode Choice

The docstring states the governing constraint plainly: *"'time_pos_learn' cannot be used for time interpolation and extrapolation — the missing time step encoding is not available during training."* The asymmetry follows from the two construction mechanisms. Sinusoidal encodings are **closed-form functions of an integer index** — the same formula that fills rows 0–4 could fill row 7, so an unseen time step has a well-defined encoding by construction. Learnt encodings are **lookup tables**: an `nn.Embedding` row for a time index never visited during training holds an untrained random vector, so generating for `t=4` when only `t∈{1,2,3}` was trained would inject noise rather than signal.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L63-L67), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L116-L128)

The practical selection heuristic this implies: choose a sinusoidal time axis (`time_pos_sin`) when the deployment scenario may query time points beyond the training grid — the shipped pretraining checkpoint made exactly this choice. Choose `time_pos_learnt` when the time grid is fixed and closed, in exchange for the flexibility of learned, potentially sharper time separations — the trade-off explored by the HSPC sweep. Within-model comparisons of mode quality belong to the sweep/benchmark workflow rather than to any single configuration.

Sources: [sweep-hspc-masking.yaml](perturbgen/configs/sweep/sweep-hspc-masking.yaml#L36-L37), [train.py](perturbgen/train.py#L297-L303)

## Where to Go Next

This page sits inside the Model Design track of the Deep Dive section. For the surrounding context: the masked-generative training objective that consumes these time-conditioned logits is covered in [scMASKGIT Masked Generative Encoder](6-scmaskgit-masked-generative-encoder) and [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training); how gene identity reaches the token embedding table *before* time/position are added is covered in [Geneformer-Style Gene Tokenization](9-geneformer-style-gene-tokenization). To see the time axis in action — generating per-time-step counterfactual states via the `tgt_time_step` loop — continue to [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes). For hands-on mode selection and sweep setup, see [Configuration System and Path Management](17-configuration-system-and-path-management) and [Hyperparameter Sweeps and Batch Jobs](18-hyperparameter-sweeps-and-batch-jobs); for the checkpoint whose name encodes `pos_sin`, see [Pretrained Checkpoints and Hugging Face Assets](23-pretrained-checkpoints-and-hugging-face-assets).

# Geneformer-Style Gene Tokenization



Perturbgen represents every cell not as a numeric expression vector, but as a **rank-encoded sequence of gene tokens** — the tokenization scheme introduced by Geneformer. This page explains how raw single-cell counts are converted into model-ready token sequences: the rank-value encoding principle, the three shipped vocabulary assets, the `TranscriptomeTokenizer` class (ported from Geneformer), the `GF_tokenisation` end-to-end pipeline, and the dual token-ID space (Geneformer tokens vs. compact row IDs) that the rest of the framework consumes. After reading it, you will understand exactly what an `input_ids` sequence in a `.dataset` artifact means and how it was produced.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L1-L39), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L1-L35)

## The Rank-Value Encoding Principle

The core idea inherited from Geneformer is that **a cell is encoded by ranking its genes, not by storing their expression values**. For each cell, the pipeline (1) scales gene counts, (2) keeps only detected genes, and (3) sorts genes in descending order of scaled expression, emitting the corresponding gene token IDs in that order. Position in the sequence therefore implicitly encodes relative expression level, and the token values identify *which* gene sits at each rank. This is a deliberate departure from continuous-valued inputs: the transformer operates on a discrete vocabulary shared with the Geneformer foundation model, which is what enables Geneformer-based embedding extraction downstream (see [Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction](11-cell-and-gene-embedding-extraction)).

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L66-L83), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L520-L532)

The per-cell transformation can be summarized as follows:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Raw counts matrix X<br/>(genes × cells)"] --> B["Collapse duplicate Ensembl IDs<br/>(sum counts)"]
    B --> C["Restrict to vocabulary genes<br/>(protein-coding + miRNA)"]
    C --> D["Median-normalize:<br/>X / n_counts × 10,000 / gene_median"]
    D --> E["Mask undetected genes<br/>(keep nonzero entries)"]
    E --> F["Sort descending by<br/>scaled expression value"]
    F --> G["Sequence of gene token IDs<br/>in rank order"]
    G --> H["Truncate to model_input_size − 2"]
    H --> I["&lt;cls&gt; + rank-ordered tokens + &lt;eos&gt;"]
```

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L75-L83), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L656-L680)

Two module-level functions implement the ranking core. `rank_genes` computes `np.argsort(-gene_vector)` — a descending sort of the median-scaled values — and returns the token array reordered accordingly; `tokenize_cell` first applies a `np.nonzero` mask so that undetected genes never enter the sequence. Because only detected genes are ranked, sequence length is data-dependent (up to the vocabulary size), which is why padding and truncation logic exist downstream.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L66-L83)

> [!TIP]
> Token order *is* the expression signal. When a sequence must be truncated (e.g., `--max_len` below the longest cell), the **lowest-ranked genes — the least-expressed ones — are dropped first**, as the `apply_dim_overrides` warning documents. Choose truncation lengths with this loss profile in mind.

Sources: [utils.py](perturbgen/src/utils.py#L59-L83)

## Vocabulary and Normalization Assets

Tokenization is driven by three pickle dictionaries shipped inside `perturbgen/pp/`, all suffixed `gc95M` (Genecorpus-95M model series). The package's `__init__.py` exposes their paths as defaults so that both the pipeline script and the tokenizer resolve the same assets without configuration.

| Asset | Default file (`perturbgen/pp/`) | Maps | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token dictionary | `token_dict_gftokens_gc95M.pkl` | Ensembl ID → token ID | Defines the vocabulary; includes special tokens (`<cls>`, `<eos>`, IDs 0–3) |
| Gene median dictionary | `gene_median_dict_gftokens_gc95M.pkl` | Ensembl ID → non-zero median expression | Per-gene normalization factor computed across the Genecorpus pretraining corpus |
| Ensembl mapping | `ensembl_mapping_dict_gc95M.pkl` | Ensembl ID → canonical Ensembl ID | Collapses versioned/alias Ensembl IDs; duplicates are merged by summing counts |

Sources: [\_\_init\_\_.py](perturbgen/pp/__init__.py#L1-L7), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L35-L37)

At construction time, the tokenizer loads the median and token dictionaries and performs three invariant checks that intermediate developers should internalize: (1) when `special_token=True`, `<cls>` and `<eos>` must exist in the token dictionary (hard error otherwise); (2) when `special_token=False` but the dictionary *contains* those tokens, a warning reminds you that the 95M series expects them; and (3) the mapping dictionary is filtered to entries whose target exists in the token dictionary, guaranteeing every collapse target is tokenizable. A `genelist_dict` (every vocabulary gene → `True`) then acts as the vocabulary-membership filter applied to each input file's genes.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L351-L398)

The constructor defaults encode the 95M-series configuration: `model_input_size=4096`, `special_token=True`, `collapse_gene_ids=True`, `chunk_size=512`. The module docstring states the complementary contract: **95M series → `special_token=True`, `model_input_size=4096`; 30M series → `special_token=False`, `model_input_size=2048`.** Mixing these settings silently produces sequences incompatible with the intended checkpoint, so treat them as a matched pair (see [Pretrained Checkpoints and Hugging Face Assets](23-pretrained-checkpoints-and-hugging-face-assets)).

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L293-L335), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L319-L324)

## Gene ID Collapsing Before Ranking

Raw datasets frequently carry multiple Ensembl identifiers that resolve to the same gene (versioned IDs, deprecated accessions). The `sum_ensembl_ids` routine runs before any ranking and is available for both storage backends. In the **loom path**, it asserts the presence of `ensembl_id` row attributes and `n_counts` cell attributes, writes an `ensembl_id_collapsed` column via the mapping dictionary, and — when duplicates exist — streams the file in `chunk_size` blocks, grouping duplicate-gene rows and *summing their counts* into a `__dedup.loom` output. In the **h5ad path**, the same mapping is applied with `data.var.ensembl_id.str.upper().map(gene_mapping_dict)`; duplicate columns are aggregated per gene with sparse DataFrame sums and concatenated back onto the deduplicated AnnData.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L86-L202), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L204-L290)

If `collapse_gene_ids=False`, the routine switches to validation mode: it checks that the Ensembl IDs present in the token dictionary are unique within the file and raises `ValueError("Error: data Ensembl IDs non-unique.")` otherwise. This gives pipeline authors a cheap integrity gate — the check runs against the token dictionary keys, so only vocabulary-relevant IDs are validated.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L116-L127), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L228-L239)

## Per-Cell Normalization Math

Both file-format paths apply an identical three-factor normalization before ranking, with `target_sum=10_000`:

```
X_norm = (gene counts / cell n_counts) × 10,000 / gene_median[gene]
```

The first factor is library-size normalization (expressing each gene as counts-per-10k); the second divides by the gene's **non-zero median expression across the pretraining corpus**, which rescales genes onto a comparable dynamic range so the ranking reflects biologically meaningful prominence rather than raw detection frequency. In `tokenize_anndata`, this is implemented as `X_view / n_counts * target_sum / norm_factor_vector` on the sparse submatrix restricted to vocabulary genes; the loom path applies the same formula per scan chunk with `norm_factor_vector[:, None]` broadcasting.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L473-L532), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L595-L613)

Cell-level inclusion honors an optional `filter_pass` observation (or loom column attribute): cells with value `1` are tokenized, everything else is skipped. When the attribute is absent, a printed notice confirms that all cells are tokenized. Custom cell metadata declared in `custom_attr_name_dict` is carried alongside tokens through every chunk and reattached in the final dataset — this is how fields like `Time_point` and `cell_pairing_index` survive into the tokenized artifacts.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L489-L517), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L534-L541)

## Special Tokens and Sequence Formatting

The final dataset assembly happens in `create_dataset`. Sequences are stored under an `input_ids` feature together with an integer `length`. When `special_token=True` (the 95M configuration used throughout Perturbgen), formatting proceeds as: truncate the rank-ordered tokens to `model_input_size − 2` (4094), insert the `<cls>` token ID at position 0, and append the `<eos>` token ID at the end. Without special tokens, the sequence is simply truncated to `model_input_size`. A `keep_uncropped_input_ids` flag additionally preserves the full pre-truncation sequence as `input_ids_uncropped` with its own `length_uncropped` feature.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L632-L686)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Input["tokenize_files → per-file backend"]
        F1["*.loom"] --> T1["tokenize_loom"]
        F2["*.h5ad"] --> T2["tokenize_anndata"]
    end
    subgraph Assets["Loaded at __init__"]
        A1["gene_median_dict"]
        A2["gene_token_dict"]
        A3["gene_mapping_dict"]
    end
    T1 --> R["rank_genes / tokenize_cell"]
    T2 --> R
    Assets --> T1
    Assets --> T2
    R --> C["create_dataset<br/>+ &lt;cls&gt;/&lt;eos&gt;, length"]
    C --> S["HF Dataset → save_to_disk<br/>(.dataset)"]
```

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L437-L471), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L400-L435)

The entry point `tokenize_data` glues everything together: glob the data directory for the chosen format, dispatch per file, then `Dataset.from_dict` (or `Dataset.from_generator` when `use_generator=True` for memory-constrained corpora) and `save_to_disk` to `<output_prefix>.dataset`. These `.dataset` directories are exactly what the training data pipeline loads later — their on-disk structure is detailed in [Tokenized Dataset Layout](16-tokenized-dataset-layout).

Sources: [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L400-L435), [tokenizer.py](perturbgen/pp/tokenizer.py#L646-L654)

## The GF_tokenisation Pipeline

For perturbation fine-tuning datasets, `GF_tokenisation.py` orchestrates tokenization plus all the preprocessing that must happen around it. The pipeline is CLI-driven (`get_args`) and executes the following stages:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Read h5ad (raw counts)"] --> B{"--gene_filtering_mode"}
    B -->|hvg| C["HVG selection<br/>seurat_v3: raw counts<br/>seurat/cell_ranger: log-normalized"]
    B -->|all| D["Keep full vocabulary"]
    C --> E["Optional filters:<br/>cells ≥1000 genes, genes ≥10 cells,<br/>drop MT-/RPS/RPL/MRPS/MRPL"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Add n_counts + cell_pairing_index"]
    F --> G["filter_adata_for_GF_genes:<br/>subset to token dictionary"]
    G --> H["tokenid_mapping →<br/>token_id_to_row_id_dict"]
    H --> I["TranscriptomeTokenizer.tokenize_data<br/>→ dataset_{suffix}.dataset"]
    I --> J["Cell pairing across time points"]
    J --> K["dataset.map: input_ids → row IDs"]
    K --> L["Save src (GF token IDs) and<br/>tgt (row IDs) per time point"]
```

Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L213-L240), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L318-L338), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L440-L528)

Key preprocessing decisions worth noting for intermediate users:

- **Counts discipline.** The script guarantees raw counts land in `adata.layers['counts']` and that `adata.X` holds counts before tokenization — HVG flavors other than `seurat_v3` temporarily log-normalize (`normalize_total(1e4)` + `log1p`) for selection, then restore counts (`adata.X = adata.layers['counts']  # need raw counts`), because the tokenizer's median normalization assumes raw inputs.
- **HVG timing is a first-class option.** `--hvg_mode before_tokenisation` selects HVGs before the vocabulary subsetting; `after_tokenisation` runs the same scanpy HVG machinery on the GF-filtered AnnData. `--hvg_flavor seurat_v3` is the only flavor ranking on raw counts directly.
- **Dictionary-aware output naming.** Every artifact is suffixed with the filtering regime (e.g., `2000_hvg` or `all`), so `token_id_to_genename_2000_hvg.pkl` and `dataset_2000_hvg/` unambiguously belong together.
- **Mito/ribosomal removal** is opt-in (`--remove_mito_ribo_genes`) and matches gene-name prefixes `MT-`, `RPS`, `RPL`, `MRPS`, `MRPL`.

Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L237-L279), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L341-L400), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L301-L317)

The script instantiates the tokenizer exactly per the 95M contract — `model_input_size=4096`, `special_token=True`, `collapse_gene_ids=True` — with `custom_attr_name_dict` set to the requested `--var_list` plus the injected `cell_pairing_index`, so pairing metadata rides along into the `.dataset` artifact.

Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L436-L459)

## The Dual Token-ID Space: GF Tokens vs. Row IDs

This is the most consequential design decision in Perturbgen's tokenization layer. After tokenization, the pipeline maintains **two parallel representations of the same cell**:

| ID space | Content | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **GF token IDs** | Geneformer vocabulary IDs (incl. `<cls>`=0-range specials) | Source (control) cells when extracting Geneformer embeddings — the upstream model requires its native vocabulary |
| **Row IDs** | Compact contiguous indices 0…N−1 via `tokenid_mapping` | Target cells and transformer-mode inputs — the Perturbgen decoder indexes embedding rows with these |

`tokenid_mapping(adata_subset, token_dict_path)` returns the subset AnnData aligned to row IDs plus both directions of the mapping (`token_id_to_row_id_dict`, `row_id_to_gene_name`), which are persisted as `tokenid_to_rowid_{suffix}.pkl` and `token_id_to_genename_{suffix}.pkl`. The HF `dataset.map(map_input_ids_to_row_id, ...)` then rewrites every target example's `input_ids` from GF tokens to row IDs. The `--src_mode` flag governs the source side: with `Geneformer` (default) the source dataset keeps *original token IDs* — the code comments state that "Geneformer needs initial token ids to extract correct embeddings" — whereas `Transformer` stores the row-ID-mapped variant.

Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L402-L420), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L482-L488), [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L509-L527)

> [!TIP]
> Special token IDs are hard-coded as **{0, 1, 2, 3}**. The pipeline strips them from `token_dict` when building gene-name lookups, and evaluation code blanks them out before computing ROUGE — so any custom vocabulary must reserve IDs 0–3 for `<cls>`/`<eos>`/control tokens or these utilities will misinterpret gene IDs as specials.

Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L288-L299), [utils.py](perturbgen/src/utils.py#L274-L281)

Row IDs also define the model's input dimensionality. `apply_dim_overrides` detects `vocab` and `max_len` from the tokenized data and allows manual `--tgt_vocab_size` / `--max_len` overrides — with an explicit warning that shrinking the vocabulary makes condition tokens (numbered above the gene IDs) collide with gene tokens, and shrinking `max_len` truncates the lowest-ranked genes. This keeps checkpoints trained with fixed dimensions loadable across datasets.

Sources: [utils.py](perturbgen/src/utils.py#L59-L83)

## Batch Integration: Padding Utilities

Because rank-encoded sequences have variable length, batching pads them to a common length. `perturbgen/src/gf_utils.py` is a verbatim port of the relevant helpers from Geneformer's `perturber_utils.py` (Hugging Face `ctheodoris/Geneformer`, header-dated 2025-09-06). `pad_tensor` right-pads with `pad_token_id` via `torch.nn.functional.pad`; `pad_3d_tensor` handles a chosen non-batch dimension; and `pad_tensor_list` resolves the target length as either `dynamic` (longest member of the list), an explicit integer, or — with a logged warning — a fallback to `model_input_size`. Padded 1-D tensors are stacked; 3-D padded tensors are concatenated along dim 0.

Sources: [gf_utils.py](perturbgen/src/gf_utils.py#L1-L14), [gf_utils.py](perturbgen/src/gf_utils.py#L29-L62)

## Pretraining-Scale Tokenization

The `pretraining_cohort/` tree contains the recipe used to tokenize the harmonized pretraining corpus itself (see [Pretraining Cohort Harmonization Pipeline](15-pretraining-cohort-harmonization-pipeline)). Notably, this script imports the **upstream `geneformer` package's** `TranscriptomeTokenizer` rather than the vendored copy, supplying cohort-specific median, token-dictionary, and Ensembl-mapping files, `model_input_size=4096`, `nproc=32`, and custom attributes `{"tissue", "disease"}`. It walks the harmonized h5ad tree, calls `tokenize_data` with `use_generator=True` and `file_format='h5ad'`, disables HF datasets caching up front, and clears the HuggingFace cache directory after each file — a pragmatic memory-hygiene pattern for very large corpora.

Sources: [tokenization.py](pretraining_cohort/tokenization/tokenization.py#L1-L42)

## Key Pipeline Parameters Reference

The table below consolidates the most consequential CLI arguments of `GF_tokenisation.py` (defaults shown as shipped):

| Parameter | Default | Choices / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `--h5ad_path` | `./data/eb/EB.h5ad` | Input AnnData with raw counts + `ensembl_id` in `var` |
| `--dataset` | `eb_100M` | Artifact/folder naming stem |
| `--gene_filtering_mode` | `hvg` | `hvg` / `degs` / `all`; suffixes all outputs |
| `--hvg_mode` | `before_tokenisation` | `before_tokenisation` / `after_tokenisation` |
| `--hvg_flavor` | `seurat` | `seurat_v3` ranks raw counts; others log-normalize first |
| `--n_hvg` | `2000` | Top-N genes for HVG modes |
| `--exclude_non_GF_genes` | `False` | Drop AnnData genes absent from the GF token dictionary |
| `--remove_mito_ribo_genes` | `False` | Prefix filter: `MT-`, `RPS/RPL`, `MRPS/MRPL` |
| `--src_mode` | `Geneformer` | `Geneformer` keeps GF token IDs for source cells; `Transformer` uses row IDs |
| `--pairing_mode` | `random` | `stratified` / `random` / `mapping` (see [Cell Pairing and Data Curation](14-cell-pairing-and-data-curation)) |
| `--time_obs` | `Time_point` | Observation driving pairing and time encoding |
| `--reference_time` | `Day 00-03` | Control time point stored as the `src` dataset |
| `--model input paths` | shipped pickles | `--gene_median_path`, `--token_dict_path`, `--gene_mapping_path` default to `perturbgen/pp/` assets |
| `--nproc` | `4` | Processes for dataset mapping |

Sources: [GF_tokenisation.py](perturbgen/pp/GF_tokenisation.py#L37-L211), [\_\_init\_\_.py](perturbgen/pp/__init__.py#L1-L7)

## Where to Go Next

Tokenization is the contract between raw data and everything downstream. To continue along the Deep Dive track, the natural progression is [Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding) (how time tokens join the token sequence), then [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training) (how these sequences are consumed by the generative objective). For the artifacts tokenization produces, read [Tokenized Dataset Layout](16-tokenized-dataset-layout); for running the pipeline end-to-end, the command surface is documented in [CLI Command Reference](22-cli-command-reference) and the class API in [Python API Reference](21-python-api-reference).


# In Silico Perturbation Modes



This page explains how PerturbGen simulates genetic perturbations computationally — the core mechanism by which a pretrained model predicts how cell states respond to gene knockouts or overexpression without ever running a wet-lab experiment. The system is organized around two orthogonal axes — **what happens to the gene's tokens** (`perturbation_mode`) and **where in the input/output structure the edit is applied** (`perturbation_sequence`) — combined with a choice of decoding strategy (`validation_mode`). All logic lives in three files: the `PerturberTrainer` orchestration layer, the `PerturberMasking` generative wrapper, and the `PerturbGen.perturb()` high-level API.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L25-L45), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L486-L503), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L21-L43)

## The Perturbation Configuration Space

Every in-silico perturbation run is fully specified by the constructor arguments of `PerturberTrainer`. The two mandatory axes are `perturbation_mode` (one of `mask`, `pad`, `delete`, `overexpress`) and `perturbation_sequence` (`src` or `tgt`); if `validation_mode` is provided but either axis is missing, initialization fails immediately with an explicit error. Two additional controls refine the edit: `pert_tps` restricts the edit to specific predicted time steps (validated as a subset of `pred_tps`), and `exclude_src` replaces the entire source sequence with zeros to study target-side effects in isolation.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L46-L59), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L139-L147), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L368-L370)

Genes can be specified either by name (`genes_to_perturb`) or directly by token ID (`src_tokens_to_perturb` / `tgt_tokens_to_perturb`). Gene names are resolved through two pickled mapping dictionaries: `mapping_dict_path` yields `gene → target-row-ID`, and `tokenid_to_rowid_path` additionally yields `gene → original Geneformer token ID` for the source sequence. Both resolved token sets are registered as non-persistent buffers (`src_pert_tokens`, `tgt_pert_tokens`) so they automatically follow the model's device. The constructor prints a summary banner of the full perturbation configuration at startup, which is useful for verifying sweep jobs.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L62-L86), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L87-L137), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L150-L157)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CFG["PerturberTrainer config"] --> MODE{"perturbation_mode"}
    MODE --> M1[mask: replace with MASK token]
    MODE --> M2[pad: replace with PAD token]
    MODE --> M3[delete: remove + compact]
    MODE --> M4[overexpress: remove + prepend gene]
    CFG --> SEQ{"perturbation_sequence"}
    SEQ --> S1[src: edit encoder input]
    SEQ --> S2[tgt: edit decoder output]
    SEQ --> S3["['src','tgt']: edit both"]
    CFG --> VM{validation_mode}
    VM --> V1[inference: single forward pass]
    VM --> V2[generate: MaskGIT demasking]
    CFG --> TPS["pert_tps: subset of pred_tps<br/>(tgt edits only)"]
    CFG --> EX["exclude_src: zero out source"]
```

The diagram above maps the full decision space: a perturbation run picks one operation per axis. Note that `perturbation_sequence` is checked with membership tests (`'src' in perturbation_sequence`), so passing a list like `['src', 'tgt']` applies the edit to both sequences simultaneously.
