Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L87-L119), [delete_fcgr3a.yaml](perturbgen/configs/eval/HSPC/delete_fcgr3a.yaml#L44-L45)

## Token-Level Mechanics of the Four Modes

All four modes converge on a single dispatch point, `perturb_sequence(input_ids, token_to_perturb, replace_token, perturbation_mode, perturbation_sequence)`. The `mask` and `pad` modes are replacement operations: `torch.isin` builds a boolean mask over positions holding the perturbed gene's token, and those positions are overwritten in-place — with the learned `<mask>` token ID for `mask`, or the padding ID for `pad`. Because `mask` needs the vocabulary's `<mask>` entry, this mode additionally requires the mapping dictionary to be loaded; the forward pass raises a targeted error otherwise.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L269-L279), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L305-L328)

The `delete` and `overexpress` modes share a prefix: `delete_token` removes all occurrences of the perturbed gene and compacts the remaining non-padding tokens to the left, preserving sequence contiguity. `overexpress` then continues in one of two ways depending on the sequence: for target sequences, the gene's tokens are **prepended** at position 0; for source sequences, they are inserted **after the first token** (the CLS position), so the sequence occupies its original length via right truncation.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L242-L267), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L280-L303)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["perturb_sequence(input_ids, tokens)"] --> B{perturbation_mode?}
    B -->|mask| C["torch.isin → replace with &lt;mask&gt; ID"]
    B -->|pad| D["torch.isin → replace with PAD ID"]
    B -->|delete| E["delete_token:<br/>drop gene, compact left"]
    B -->|overexpress| E
    E --> F{perturbation_sequence?}
    F -->|tgt| G["Prepend gene tokens at index 0"]
    F -->|src| H["Insert after CLS token,<br/>truncate right to keep length"]
    C --> Z["Return edited input_ids"]
    D --> Z
    G --> Z
    H --> Z
```

| Mode | Token operation | Sequence length after edit | Modeling semantics | Cells retained in batch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mask` | Gene token → `<mask>` token | Unchanged | Knockout signal via the mask token the model was pretrained to decode from | Only cells expressing the gene |
| `pad` | Gene token → `<pad>` token | Unchanged | Knockout without the mask-token prior; masked-position conventions bypassed | Only cells expressing the gene |
| `delete` | Gene token removed, sequence compacted | Shortened | Hard ablation; no trace of the gene in context | Only cells expressing the gene |
| `overexpress` | Gene removed, then prepended at sequence head | Preserved (via truncation) | Forced expression regardless of baseline | **All cells** |

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L459-L501), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L269-L303)

> [!TIP]
> Choosing `mask` over `pad` matters: the masking model was pretrained to predict tokens hidden behind the `<mask>` ID, so `mask` keeps the perturbed sequence on-distribution for the encoder, while `pad` tests a distribution-shifted input — a useful ablation pair when auditing knockout robustness.

## Source vs Target: Where the Edit Lands

The `src` sequence is the encoder's input — the observed reference cell state — while each `tgt_input_ids_t{i}` sequence is the decoder's input representing a future time point. In `forward`, the replace token is resolved once per mode (`<mask>` ID or pad ID) and then the edit is applied per time step: if `pert_tps` is set, only those time steps' target sequences are edited; otherwise the edit hits every predicted time step. Condition tokens (e.g., cell-type embeddings produced by `concat_cond_tokens`) are concatenated *after* perturbation, so conditioning metadata is never perturbed.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L305-L388), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L359-L366)

The two axes answer different biological questions. A **source-side** edit (`perturbation_sequence: ['src']`) asks "what happens downstream if the reference state changes?" — the edit propagates through the encoder into every predicted time step, which is why released configs pair it with `exclude_src: false`. A **target-side** edit (`perturbation_sequence: ['tgt']`, combined with `pert_tps`) asks "what if this gene were disrupted specifically at time point t?" — one concrete example config perturbs the target at `pert_tps: [1]` out of predicted time points `[1, 2, 3]`, with `exclude_src: true` isolating the target pathway entirely.

Sources: [mask_src_inference_perturbation_IL1B.yaml](perturbgen/configs/eval/LPS/mask_src_inference_perturbation_IL1B.yaml#L33-L38), [delete_fcgr3a.yaml](perturbgen/configs/eval/HSPC/delete_fcgr3a.yaml#L38-L55)

## Validation Modes: Single-Pass Inference vs Iterative Generation

The `validation_mode` axis selects how the model decodes the perturbed state. In **`inference`** mode, `test_step` runs the model twice over the filtered batch: once with `perturbation=False` (the unperturbed reference) and once with `perturbation=True`; the latter is a single forward pass with `not_masked=True`, meaning the (edited but complete) target tokens are decoded directly — no generative loop. The count decoder, when enabled, additionally draws count predictions (`compute_count_loss` with `n_samples` samples averaged).

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L512-L521), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L390-L429)

In **`generate`** mode, the decoder instead reconstructs target sequences from scratch via `PerturberMasking.generate`: every target position starts as `<mask>`, and a MaskGIT-style loop of `iterations` (default 18, documented as the MaskGIT optimum) progressively demasks tokens. Each iteration samples a mask ratio from the configured noise schedule (`uniform`, `pow`, `cosine`, `log`, `exp`), remasks the lowest-confidence positions, predicts all masked positions in parallel, ranks candidates by confidence (`1 − softmax probability`), and anneals the Gumbel-sampling temperature linearly toward zero. Sampling is filtered by `topk_filter_thres` (default 0.9), and previously demasked tokens are frozen (`can_remask_prev_masked=False` by default).

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L30-L124), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L197-L263), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L522-L546)

> [!TIP]
> Generation is *guided*: on every demasking iteration, the logits for the perturbed gene's vocabulary entries are explicitly set to `−finfo.max` (`logits[:, :, genes_to_perturb] = max_neg_value`), so a knocked-out gene can never be re-sampled back into existence by the generative model — the edit is enforced, not merely suggested.

| Dimension | `validation_mode: inference` | `validation_mode: generate` |
|---|---|---|
| Target decoding | Single forward pass on edited tokens (`not_masked=True`) | Full MaskGIT demasking from all-mask init |
| Reference arm | Forward pass on unperturbed batch | `generate()` on unperturbed source (with gene suppression active) |
| Extra sampling params | None | `temperature` (2.0–3.0 range advised), `iterations`, `topk_filter_thres`, `mask_scheduler` |
| Sequence-level metric | Embedding/count comparisons | ROUGE-1 at lengths 25/100/max against observed tokens |
| Used by high-level API | **Always** (hard-coded) | CLI/config only |

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L522-L561), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L513-L518), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L36-L39)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Filter batch: keep cells<br/>expressing the target gene"] --> A["Apply token edit<br/>(mask / pad / delete / overexpress)"]
    A --> B{validation_mode}
    B -->|inference| C1["Forward, perturbation=False<br/>(reference outputs)"]
    B -->|inference| C2["Forward, perturbation=True<br/>not_masked=True"]
    C1 --> D["Per-gene & mean embedding deltas,<br/>predicted/perturbed counts"]
    C2 --> D
    B -->|generate| E1["generate(): unperturbed src<br/>+ genes_to_perturb logit suppression"]
    B -->|generate| E2["generate(): perturbed src"]
    E1 --> F["ROUGE vs observed target tokens"]
    E2 --> D
```

The diagram summarizes the dual-arm structure: both modes always compare a perturbed arm against an unperturbed arm; they differ in whether each arm is *decoded* (inference) or *generated* (MaskGIT). This comparison pipeline feeds the metric dictionary described below.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L457-L566)

## Cell Filtering and Embedding Realignment

For `mask`, `pad`, and `delete`, `test_step` filters the batch before any forward pass: it checks whether the perturbed gene's token appears in the source sequence, the target sequences (at `pert_tps`), or both, and drops cells with zero occurrences. This is a correctness requirement, not an optimization — perturbing a token that isn't present would produce a meaningless "unperturbed" arm. The consequence is important for experiment design: **a source knockout requires the gene to be expressed in the source state**, otherwise every cell is filtered out and the run produces nothing, as documented in the API docstring.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L459-L504), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L539-L541)

`overexpress` deliberately skips this filter and keeps all cells, since forced expression does not presuppose baseline expression. After the forward pass, `delete` and `overexpress` require one more piece of bookkeeping: because those modes change token positions, `dec_embedding` tensors of the true and perturbed arms are no longer column-aligned. The code builds a cross-sequence match mask (`true_ids` vs `perturbed_ids` via argmax matching) to realign embeddings position-by-position; for `overexpress`, the prepended gene tokens are first overwritten with the pad ID so comparisons exclude the artificially inserted positions.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L492-L496), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L568-L598)

> [!TIP]
> When interpreting overexpression results, remember the comparison is fair by construction: the `len(tgt_pert_tokens)` prepended positions are masked out of `perturbed_ids` *before* embedding realignment, so reported deltas reflect downstream transcriptional response, not the artificial token insert itself.

## Running Perturbations: API, CLI, and Configs

The high-level entry point is `PerturbGen.perturb(genes, mode, where, ...)`. It translates user-facing aliases into the underlying trainer vocabulary — `"knockout"` maps to the `mask` mode via `_MODE_ALIASES`, and `"source"`/`"target"` map to `src`/`tgt` via `_WHERE_ALIASES` — then assembles the full YAML config consumed by `perturbgen/Perturb/val.py` and invokes it in-process. Two guardrails are enforced: target-side knockout/delete/pad runs must pass `pert_tps`, and a trained count-decoder checkpoint must be available (via `count_ckpt` or a prior `train_count()` call).

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L57-L66), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L486-L575), [test_api_perturb.py](perturbgen/tests/test_api_perturb.py#L42-L61)

| `perturb()` parameter | Type / default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `genes` | `Sequence[str]` | Gene names (e.g., Ensembl IDs) to perturb; `[]` allowed with `perturb_genes_file` |
| `mode` | `"knockout"` (default) | Alias for `mask`; also `"overexpress"`, `"delete"`, `"pad"` |
| `where` | `"source"` (default) | `"src"` edits the encoder input; `"target"`/`"tgt"` edits decoded time points |
| `pert_tps` | `None` | Target time points to edit; **required** when `where="target"` with non-overexpress modes |
| `n_samples` | `3` | Count-decoder draws per cell, averaged into predicted counts |
| `context_mode` | `False` | Keeps the decoder from attending to observed cells of other time points during perturbation |
| `extra_config` | `None` | Escape hatch: `{section: {key: value}}` for `data`/`trainer`/`datamodule`/`model` options the API doesn't expose; keys the API already manages are rejected |

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L486-L542), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L543-L575), [test_api_perturb.py](perturbgen/tests/test_api_perturb.py#L63-L100)

Two API behaviors deserve attention. First, `perturb()` always runs `validation_mode="inference"`; passing non-default `temperature`/`iterations` triggers a warning because those only configure MaskGIT generation — the parameters are retained purely for backward compatibility. Second, `extra_config` supports cluster-targeted perturbation: passing `{"data": {"perturb_genes_file": ..., "perturb_colname": ..., "perturb_cluster": [...]}}` with `genes=[]` perturbs all genes assigned to the given cluster in a precomputed gene-embedding CSV; the file path is made absolute automatically to survive the entry point's working-directory change.

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L513-L563), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L524-L557)

The standalone CLI (`perturbgen/Perturb/val.py`) reads the same config schema and adds batch-operations conveniences: it loads a CSV of candidate genes and filters by cluster membership, intersects genes with the mapping dictionary, **resumes interrupted runs by skipping genes whose output file (pattern `adata_g{gene}_ssrc`) already exists**, normalizes/log-transforms target AnnData when `loss_mode` is `mse`, and auto-selects mixed precision (`bf16-mixed` on A100/H100, `16-mixed` otherwise, `32` on CPU). Released configs follow the naming convention `{mode}_{sequence}_{validation_mode}_perturbation_{GENE}.yaml` — e.g., `mask_src_inference_perturbation_IL1B.yaml` knocks out IL1B (`ENSG00000125538`) in the source sequence with the count decoder enabled (`loss_mode: zinb`, `n_samples: 2`).

Sources: [val.py](perturbgen/Perturb/val.py#L31-L38), [val.py](perturbgen/Perturb/val.py#L67-L132), [val.py](perturbgen/Perturb/val.py#L102-L146), [mask_src_inference_perturbation_IL1B.yaml](perturbgen/configs/eval/LPS/mask_src_inference_perturbation_IL1B.yaml#L19-L50)

## What a Perturbation Run Reports

Each `test_step` accumulates a metric dictionary comparing the perturbed arm to the reference arm: mean and per-gene cosine similarity of decoder embeddings, `delta_probs` and `delta_gene_probs` (token-level probability shifts), Wasserstein distance between count distributions, plus paired tensors of true vs. perturbed CLS embeddings, gene-mean embeddings, background embeddings, and observed/predicted/perturbed counts. In generate mode, ROUGE-1 scores at sequence lengths 25, 100, and `max_seq_length` quantify how faithfully free generation reconstructs the observed transcriptome.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L200-L224), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L547-L561)

Per-gene predicted AnnData objects are written under the configured `output_dir`, one file per perturbed gene. Downstream — differential expression on these h5ads, or distributional evaluation of count predictions — belongs to the analysis layer rather than the perturbation mechanics themselves.

Sources: [val.py](perturbgen/Perturb/val.py#L102-L122), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L15-L22)

## Where to Go Next

- To understand *why* the `<mask>` token and the MaskGIT demasking loop behave as they do, read [scMASKGIT Masked Generative Encoder](6-scmaskgit-masked-generative-encoder) and [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training).
- For the interpretation of `delta_probs`, Wasserstein distances, and count distributions, continue to [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport).
- For the full parameter surface of `PerturbGen.perturb()` and `tokenize()`, see [Python API Reference](21-python-api-reference); for YAML-driven batch perturbation workflows, see [CLI Command Reference](22-cli-command-reference) and [Configuration System and Path Management](17-configuration-system-and-path-management).
- For an end-to-end worked example — tokenization, training, then running `perturb()` in a notebook — follow [Tutorial Notebooks Walkthrough](4-tutorial-notebooks-walkthrough).

# Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction



This page covers how PerturbGen extracts **cell embeddings** (a fixed-length vector per cell) and **time-resolved **gene embeddings** (one vector per gene per condition) from a trained masking model. It documents the high-level `PerturbGen.get_embeddings()` API, the validation pipeline it triggers, and the internal mechanics that turn transformer hidden states into AnnData files ready for downstream analyses such as gene program discovery. Throughout, we follow the released LPS embedding workflow from `docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb` as the canonical example.

Sources: [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L8-L13), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L382-L398)

## What Gets Extracted: Two Embedding Families

PerturbGen's masking model is a transformer that processes tokenized gene-expression sequences; the embedding extraction step exposes its internal representations without running generative sampling. **Cell embeddings** are the pooled sequence representations (`outputs[t]['mean_embedding']`) collected per cell per time point — they summarize each cell's identity and state in a single `d_model`-dimensional vector. **Gene embeddings** are derived from the decoder-side token embeddings (`outputs[t]['dec_embedding']`), excluding any classifier-free-guidance condition tokens, and are averaged across all cells in which a gene is non-padded/non-zero, grouped by a conditioning variable such as `time_after_LPS`. This yields one gene-embedding matrix per unique condition value, enabling trajectory-aware gene geometry analyses.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L433-L446), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L501-L511), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L85-L88)

The conceptual relationship between the model internals and the two embedding families is summarized below:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph MaskingModel["Masking Transformer (PerturbGen nn.Module)"]
        FWD["forward(batch)"] --> OUT["outputs per time step t"]
        OUT --> MEAN["mean_embedding"]
        OUT --> DEC["dec_embedding<br/>(minus condition tokens)"]
    end
    MEAN -->|"per cell, per t"| CELL["Cell embeddings<br/>obsm['cls_embeddings']"]
    DEC -->|"return_gene_embeddings()"| GENE["per-gene token vectors"]
    GENE -->|"mean over non-zero cells<br/>grouped by gene_embs_condition"| COND["Gene embeddings<br/>one set per condition value → varm"]
```

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L405-L446), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L85-L88)

## High-Level API: `PerturbGen.get_embeddings()`

The public entry point follows the library's scvi-tools-style in-process API: `import perturbgen as pg; model = pg.PerturbGen(...)`, then call `model.get_embeddings(...)`. The method requires only a **masking checkpoint** — the count decoder is not needed for embedding extraction — and returns the output directory containing the embedding AnnData files. Two validation rules are enforced before anything runs: a masking checkpoint must exist (from `train_masking()` or passed explicitly as `masking_ckpt=`), and `return_gene_embs=True` requires `gene_embs_condition` to name an `obs` column whose values define the gene-embedding groups.

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L1-L27), [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L382-L411), [__init__.py](perturbgen/__init__.py#L3-L5)

| Parameter | Type | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `output_dir` | `str` | `"embeddings"` | Directory where embedding AnnData files are written |
| `masking_ckpt` | `str \| None` | `None` | Path to the masking checkpoint; defaults to the one stored by `train_masking()` |
| `return_cell_embs` | `bool` | `True` | Extract pooled per-cell embeddings |
| `return_gene_embs` | `bool` | `True` | Extract per-gene embeddings (requires `gene_embs_condition`) |
| `gene_embs_condition` | `str \| None` | `None` | `obs` column whose unique values define one gene-embedding set each (e.g. `time_after_LPS`) |
| `batch_size` | `int` | `64` | DataLoader batch size for the test pass |
| `n_workers` | `int` | `4` | DataLoader workers |

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L382-L398)

The canonical usage, from the released-checkpoint notebook, downloads both the checkpoint and the exact tokenized dataset it was trained on — token IDs are defined by the tokenization, so a checkpoint must be paired with its training data — and then extracts both embedding families in one call:

```python
model = pg.PerturbGen(
    TOKENIZED_DIR, source="normal", n_hvg=2000,
    n_layers=6, d_ff=32, d_model=768,
    pred_tps=[1, 2, 3],
    var_list=["cell_type_harmonized", "cell_pairing_index", "time_after_LPS"],
    cond_list=["time_after_LPS"],
    mask_scheduler="cosine", context_mode=True,
    max_len=797, tgt_vocab_size=2002,
)
EMB_DIR = model.get_embeddings(
    output_dir=EMB_DIR,
    masking_ckpt=MASKING_CKPT,
    return_cell_embs=True,
    return_gene_embs=True,
    gene_embs_condition="time_after_LPS",
)
```

Sources: [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L31-L47), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L66-L77), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L97-L104)

## Execution Pipeline: From API Call to AnnData on Disk

Internally, `get_embeddings()` does not reimplement inference; it assembles a CLI-style argument vector and invokes `perturbgen.val.main(argv)` **in process** (with the caller's working directory preserved, since `val.py` changes to the repo root on import). The critical flags it sets are `--test_mode masking`, `--split False`, `--return_embeddings`, `--return_gene_embs`, `--generate False`, plus notebook-safety switches: `--single_device True` (avoids DDP, which cannot launch inside a Jupyter kernel) and `--wandb_mode disabled` (avoids a headless `wandb.init()` hang). Model architecture hyperparameters (`d_model`, `num_layers`, `d_ff`, `pred_tps`, `cond_list`, `mask_scheduler`, `pos_encoding_mode`) and data paths are forwarded from the model's stored hparams and paths.

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L412-L458), [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L29-L30)

The orchestration then flows through the Lightning module system:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant API as PerturbGen.get_embeddings()
    participant VAL as perturbgen/val.py main()
    participant DM as PerturbGenDataModule
    participant LT as PerturbGenTrainer (Lightning)
    participant PL as pl.Trainer.test()

    API->>VAL: argv (--test_mode masking, --generate False)
    VAL->>DM: tokenized .dataset + paired h5ads
    VAL->>LT: test_kwargs incl. return_embeddings, gene_embs_condition
    Note over LT: compile_model=False (strict ckpt load)
    PL->>LT: load masking ckpt, run test loop
    LT->>LT: test_step → collect mean_embedding + dec_embedding
    LT->>LT: on_test_epoch_end → mean gene embs per condition
    LT->>API: writes *_inference_embs_*.h5ad under output_dir
```

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L454-L458), [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L565-L607), [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L724-L740)

Two implementation details in `val.py` matter for reproducibility. First, for masking mode the trainer is instantiated with `gene_names` taken from the target AnnData's `var['gene_name']`, and a `conditions` directory is prepared for the per-condition gene-embedding outputs. Second, the module is deliberately built **uncompiled** (`compile_model=False`): checkpoints are saved with `torch.compile`'s `._orig_mod.` prefix stripped, so they only load cleanly under Lightning's strict `ckpt_path` load into an uncompiled module — numerically identical, but a prerequisite for checkpoint compatibility.

Sources: [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L590-L607), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L61-L72)

## Inside the Trainer: `test_step` and Epoch-End Aggregation

Within `PerturbGenTrainer`, `test_step` runs one forward pass per batch (`generate=False` here, so observed target tokens are decoded directly — no MaskGIT iterative sampling). For each predicted time step `t`, three things happen: (1) if `return_gene_embs`, `return_gene_embeddings()` maps the decoder token embeddings (sliced past the condition tokens with `[:, cond_length:, :]`) back to genes using the `gene_to_rowid` mapping, optionally restricted to marker genes; (2) the per-condition accumulators `sum_gene_embs[condition]` and `count_gene_embs[condition]` are updated by masking cells to each condition value of `gene_embs_condition` and summing non-zero token positions; and (3) pooled cell embeddings (`mean_embedding`), true counts, cell indices, and all `var_list` metadata are appended to `test_dict`.

> [!TIP]
> Despite the key name, the cell embedding stored under `cls_embeddings` is actually `outputs[t]['mean_embedding']` — the padding-aware mean-pooled sequence representation, not a dedicated CLS token. Code reading checkpoints should not assume a literal classification-token vector.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L405-L431), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L436-L485), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L501-L511), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L43)

At `on_test_epoch_end`, the gene-embedding accumulators are finalized as a **non-zero mean** — each gene's vector is `sum / count` where `count` tallies only positions where the gene's token embedding was non-zero, and positions with zero count are left at zero. `return_prediction_adata()` then serializes everything into AnnData file(s) named `{date}_inference_embs_t{pred_tps}_{encoder}_m{mask_scheduler}` under `output_dir`. In the released workflow, these files carry cell embeddings in `obsm["cls_embeddings"]` and the per-condition gene embeddings in `varm`, which is exactly the format consumed by the gene program discovery notebook.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L513-L560), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L85-L88)

| Output artifact | Content | AnnData location | Granularity |
|---|---|---|---|
| `obsm["cls_embeddings"]` | Pooled per-cell vectors (`mean_embedding`) | Cell-level | One vector per cell per predicted time point |
| `varm` (per condition) | Averaged gene token embeddings | Gene-level | `n_genes × d_model` per unique value of `gene_embs_condition` |
| `obs` metadata | `var_list` columns + `batch` + `cell_idx` | Cell-level | Preserved for downstream grouping/plots |

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L501-L511), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L535-L560), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L85-L88)

## Practical Constraints and Troubleshooting

| Constraint | Consequence if violated | Where enforced |
|---|---|---|
| Masking checkpoint required | `ValueError` directing you to `train_masking()` or `masking_ckpt=` | [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L400-L404) |
| `gene_embs_condition` set when `return_gene_embs=True` | `ValueError` explaining gene embeddings are extracted per unique value of the column | [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L405-L411) |
| Checkpoint paired with its training tokenization | Token IDs mismatch → meaningless embeddings | [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L19-L23) |
| Model dims must match checkpoint (`max_len`, `tgt_vocab_size`, `d_model`, ...) | Strict state-dict load failure | [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L54-L57) |
| Uncompiled module for inference | Compiled checkpoints only load into uncompiled modules (prefix-stripped state dicts) | [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L602-L606), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L61-L72) |
| Notebooks must use `single_device=True` / `wandb_mode=disabled` | DDP cannot launch in a Jupyter kernel; `wandb.init()` hangs headless | [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L420-L421), [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L674-L677) |
| CPU fallback supported | `accelerator='gpu' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'` | [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L700-L701) |

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L400-L421), [val.py](perturbgen/val.py#L602-L606)

> [!TIP]
> The released embedding-analysis checkpoint on Hugging Face (`lps/embedding/20250714_2311_..._pos_sin_m_cosine_tp_1-2-3_s_0-epoch=07.ckpt`) already encodes the manuscript settings — `normal` source, targets 90 min / 6 h / 10 h, cosine masking scheduler, time conditioning — so reproducing the paper's embeddings is purely an inference exercise with no training.

Sources: [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L38-L46), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L54-L57)

## Where Embeddings Fit in the Larger Workflow

Embedding extraction sits between training and analysis: it consumes the stage-1 masking model and produces the artifacts consumed by downstream discovery. The notebook explicitly hands off its `EMB_DIR` to `gene_program_discovery`, which mines the per-condition gene embeddings for programs. Note that only `train_masking` (stage 1) is needed — `train_count` and the perturbation modes operate on a separate pathway.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["train_masking()<br/>(stage 1: masking model)"] --> B["get_embeddings()<br/>(this page)"]
    B --> C["Cell embeddings<br/>obsm['cls_embeddings']"]
    B --> D["Gene embeddings per condition<br/>varm"]
    C --> E["Cell-state analyses"]
    D --> F["Gene Program Discovery"]
    A --> G["train_count() → perturb()<br/>(separate pathway)"]
```

Sources: [model.py](perturbgen/model.py#L382-L398), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L46), [cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb](docs/examples/cell_gene_embeddings.ipynb#L110-L112)

## Next Steps

- Turn the extracted gene embeddings into interpretable programs: [Gene Program Discovery](12-gene-program-discovery)
- Understand the model whose hidden states you are extracting: [scMASKGIT Masked Generative Encoder](6-scmaskgit-masked-generative-encoder) and [Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding)
- Train your own masking checkpoint before extracting embeddings: [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training)
- Download released checkpoints and tokenized datasets: [Pretrained Checkpoints and Hugging Face Assets](23-pretrained-checkpoints-and-hugging-face-assets)
- Apply interventions instead of passive extraction: [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes)


# Gene Program Discovery



Gene program discovery in PerturbGen treats the model's learned **gene embeddings** as a de novo representation of gene function: genes whose embeddings cluster together in latent space are interpreted as *gene programs* — coordinated biological functions that can serve as candidate targets for downstream perturbation studies. This page walks through the complete workflow implemented in `docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb`: loading the embedding AnnData produced by the upstream extraction step, re-shaping gene embeddings into a gene-as-observation matrix, clustering them with Leiden, annotating clusters via enrichment analysis, and validating programs by scoring them back in the original cell space.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L10-L21)

## Conceptual Model: From Embeddings to Programs

The workflow rests on a single representational insight: PerturbGen's masking encoder produces one 768-dimensional embedding per gene **per timepoint**, conditioned on the cellular context (time-aware positional encoding, see [Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding)). If a gene's embedding encodes its functional role in that context, then proximity in embedding space should encode functional similarity. The discovery pipeline therefore reuses the standard single-cell toolkit in an inverted geometry — instead of cells as observations, **genes become observations** and embedding coordinates become features:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Trained masking<br/>model checkpoint"] --> B["get_embeddings()<br/>per-timepoint extraction"]
    B --> C["AnnData<br/>n_obs = cells × timepoints<br/>varm: gene embeddings<br/>obsm: cls_embeddings"]
    C --> D["Transpose & stack<br/>gene-timepoint = observation<br/>768-dim vector = features"]
    D --> E["QC: drop all-zero vectors"]
    E --> F["neighbors + UMAP"]
    F --> G["Leiden clustering<br/>cluster = gene program"]
    G --> H["Enrichr annotation<br/>GO / Reactome"]
    H --> I["score_genes()<br/>program score in cell space"]
    I --> J["Biological validation<br/>cell-type & timepoint stratification"]
```

Each Mermaid node maps to a concrete code step documented below; read the diagram left-to-right as the data's transformation chain, from model weights to biological annotation.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L10-L21), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L335-L336)

## Prerequisite: The Embedding Artifact

Gene program discovery is downstream of the embedding extraction covered in [Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction](11-cell-and-gene-embedding-extraction). The `PerturbGen.get_embeddings()` API wraps `perturbgen/val.py` with `--test_mode masking --return_embeddings --return_gene_embs`, requiring a trained masking checkpoint and — critically for this page — a `gene_embs_condition` column: **gene embeddings are extracted per unique value of that column** (e.g. `gene_embs_condition='time_after_LPS'` yields one embedding matrix per LPS timepoint).

Sources: [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L382-L458), [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L399-L411), [val.py](/perturbgen/val.py#L86-L97)

The resulting AnnData has a dual layout that the discovery notebook exploits. The notebook loads the latest `*inference_embs*.h5ad` from the extraction output directory:

| AnnData slot | Contents | Role in program discovery |
|---|---|---|
| `obs` | `cell_pairing_index`, `time_after_LPS`, `cell_type_harmonized`, `batch`, `cell_idx` | Context metadata for the cells |
| `var` | `token_id` (one row per gene, Ensembl IDs as index) | Keyed against the original dataset for symbol mapping |
| `obsm['cls_embeddings']` | Cell embeddings (average of that cell's gene embeddings) | Cell-space UMAP baseline |
| `varm['<timepoint>']` | Per-gene embedding matrix for each conditioned timepoint (`90m_LPS`, `6h_LPS`, `10h_LPS`) | **Raw material for program discovery** |

In the LPS example the object contains 69,433 cell observations × 2,000 genes with three timepoint-conditioned gene embedding matrices in `varm`.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L66-L77), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L91-L105)

## Step-by-Step Workflow

### 1. Cell-Embedding Baseline and Gene Symbol Mapping

Before touching gene embeddings, the notebook establishes two reference points. First, it builds a neighborhood graph and UMAP directly on `cls_embeddings` (`sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep='cls_embeddings')`) so downstream program scores can be interpreted against the embedding-derived cell landscape. Second, it loads the **original full dataset** (`adata_full`) for two purposes: mapping the Ensembl gene IDs in the embedding object to readable gene symbols (`adata.var['gene_symbol'] = adata.var.index.map(adata_full.var['gene_symbol-0'])`), and providing a normalized/log-transformed expression UMAP for optional visual comparison.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L112-L140), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L163-L166), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L317-L328)

> [!TIP]
> The gene embedding AnnData stores Ensembl IDs because tokens are keyed to the Geneformer vocabulary (see [Geneformer-Style Gene Tokenization](9-geneformer-style-gene-tokenization)). The symbol lookup must come from the *original* h5ad, not from any derived object — the embedding object never carries `gene_symbol` itself.

### 2. Transposing the Geometry: Genes as Observations

The pivotal transformation stacks the `varm` matrices across timepoints into a new AnnData where each row is a **gene–timepoint pair** named `f"{g}_{tp}"`, and `X` is the vertically concatenated 768-dimensional embedding vectors:

```python
gene_symbols = adata.var['gene_symbol'].values
timepoints = list(adata.varm.keys())
all_embeddings, obs_names, obs_timepoints, obs_genes = [], [], [], []

for tp in timepoints:
    embedding = adata.varm[tp]
    all_embeddings.append(embedding)
    obs_names.extend([f"{g}_{tp}" for g in gene_symbols])
    obs_genes.extend(gene_symbols)
    obs_timepoints.extend([tp] * len(gene_symbols))

new_adata = ad.AnnData(X=np.vstack(all_embeddings),
                       obs=pd.DataFrame({"gene_symbol": obs_genes,
                                         "timepoint": obs_timepoints},
                                        index=obs_names))
```

This inversion is what makes the standard scanpy pipeline (`neighbors` → `umap` → `leiden`) applicable to gene embeddings without modification.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L335-L369)

### 3. QC: All-Zero Vectors

Some gene–timepoint pairs produce embedding vectors that are identically zero (37 in the example run). These carry no positional information and distort graph construction, so they are detected with `(new_adata.X == 0).all(axis=1)` and removed before clustering.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L376-L411)

### 4. Latent-Space Visualization and Leiden Clustering

With clean vectors, the notebook computes `sc.pp.neighbors(new_adata)` and `sc.tl.umap(new_adata)`, then colors the UMAP by `timepoint` to check whether embeddings organize by time. **Gene programs are identified by applying Leiden clustering to the gene embedding space** — `sc.tl.leiden(new_adata, resolution=1, key_added='r1')` — with each resulting cluster representing a coherent program. Resolution 1 is the notebook's default starting point; adjust it to control program granularity.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L418-L433), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L459-L490)

### 5. Annotating Programs with Enrichment Analysis

Cluster annotation uses `gseapy.enrichr` against `GO_Biological_Process_2025` and `Reactome_Pathways_2024` for `organism='Human'` with `cutoff=0.5`, keeping the top 5 terms per cluster sorted by Adjusted P-value:

| Parameter | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `gene_sets` | `GO_Biological_Process_2025`, `Reactome_Pathways_2024` | Two complementary ontologies: process-level and pathway-level |
| `organism` | `Human` | Gene symbol namespace |
| `cutoff` | `0.5` | Adjusted P-value inclusion threshold |
| Output | Top 5 terms per cluster | Stored in a `results[cluster]` dict |

The notebook's worked example finds cluster 6 dominated by interleukins and chemokines and annotates it **cytokine signaling** — the notebook recommends predefined gene sets as guidance for annotating programs generally.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L497-L525), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L531-L533)

### 6. Closing the Loop: Scoring Programs in Cell Space

Discovery only becomes useful when the program maps back onto cells. The notebook selects cluster 6's gene symbols, intersects them with `adata_full.var_names` (after re-keying `var_names` to gene IDs), and computes a z-score signature with `sc.tl.score_genes(adata_full, gene_list=genes_present, score_name='Cytokine Signaling')`. Clusters are then mapped to mechanism-of-action labels via a `cluster_map` dict into a `MoA` column, defaulting unmapped clusters to `'Others'`.

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L531-L561), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L570-L575)

The validation visuals follow directly: a highlighted UMAP of the gene embedding space with program genes circled and labeled (IL1RN, IL1B, PTX3, IL32, IL7R, CXCL8, CXCL3, CXCL9 via seaborn + `adjust_text`), a boxplot of the program score stratified by harmonized cell type, and — since the cytokine program was strongly myeloid-enriched — a subset to CD14+/CD16+ monocytes and dendritic cells to trace the program score across LPS timepoints (`90m`, `6h`, `10h`, `normal`).

Sources: [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L610-L677), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L684-L761), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L768-L799)

## Workflow Parameters at a Glance

| Stage | Function / Call | Key parameters | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extraction (upstream) | `PerturbGen.get_embeddings()` | `gene_embs_condition='time_after_LPS'` | One gene embedding matrix per timepoint in `varm` |
| Re-shaping | manual `varm` stacking | — | Gene-timepoint pairs as obs; 768-dim features |
| QC | boolean mask on `X` | — | Removes 37 all-zero vectors in example |
| Graph | `sc.pp.neighbors(new_adata)` | defaults | Graph over embedding space |
| Clustering | `sc.tl.leiden(..., resolution=1, key_added='r1')` | `resolution` | Granularity of programs |
| Annotation | `gp.enrichr(...)` | `gene_sets`, `organism`, `cutoff=0.5` | Biological labels per program |
| Scoring | `sc.tl.score_genes(adata_full, ...)` | `gene_list`, `score_name` | Z-score program activity per cell |

Sources: [model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L405-L411), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L489-L491), [gene_program_discovery.ipynb](/docs/examples/gene_program_discovery.ipynb#L510-L525)

> [!TIP]
> Gene embeddings are timepoint-conditioned by construction, so every gene appears once per extracted condition (e.g. three rows per gene for the LPS cohort). Leiden therefore clusters *gene-timepoint* units: a gene that shifts context between 90m and 10h can legitimately appear in different programs — treat the `timepoint` covariate as part of the program identity, not noise.

## Where to Go Next

This pipeline consumes artifacts built in [Cell and Gene Embedding Extraction](11-cell-and-gene-embedding-extraction) and shares its latent space with [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes) — a natural follow-up is perturbing the candidate target genes your programs nominate and measuring the effect with [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport). For the full runnable version of every snippet on this page, see [Tutorial Notebooks Walkthrough](4-tutorial-notebooks-walkthrough); for the embedding API signatures, see [Python API Reference](21-python-api-reference).


# Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport



Perturbgen validates in-silico perturbation predictions by comparing **distributions**, not individual cells. Because a generative model can produce a valid cell state through many different trajectories, deterministic per-cell losses (MSE) are insufficient to certify that predicted populations match true perturbed populations. This page explains the three distributional evaluation families — **Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)**, **Earth Mover's Distance (EMD)**, and **Optimal Transport (OT) Wasserstein distances** — covering their mathematical foundations, the exact code paths that implement them, and how they are orchestrated inside the PyTorch Lightning evaluation hooks. All implementations are adapted from proven sources: the [conditional-flow-matching](https://github.com/atong01/conditional-flow-matching) project for the primitive solvers, CPA for AnnData-aware MMD/EMD, CellFlow for energy distance, and CFGen for the aggregate distribution-distance report.

## Metric Architecture: A Three-Layer Design

The evaluation stack follows a strict separation of concerns that mirrors how the rest of the codebase separates primitives from orchestration. At the bottom, `perturbgen/src/mmd.py` and `perturbgen/src/optimal_transport.py` contain pure tensor mathematics with no domain assumptions — kernel functions and OT solvers that operate on raw tensors. The middle layer, `perturbgen/src/metric.py`, lifts these primitives into single-cell semantics: it understands `AnnData` objects, condition keys, differentially expressed gene (DEG) subsets, and sparse matrix handling. The top layer is the Lightning integration in `perturbgen/Model/trainer.py`, where preprocessing (PCA projection, z-scoring, seeded subsampling), logging, and CSV persistence happen inside `on_validation_epoch_end` and `on_test_epoch_end` hooks.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph L3["Layer 3 — Lightning Integration"]
        A1["Model/trainer.py<br/>on_validation_epoch_end<br/>val/emd"]
        A2["Model/trainer.py<br/>on_test_epoch_end<br/>CSV + wandb logging"]
    end
    subgraph L2["Layer 2 — Task Metrics (AnnData-aware)"]
        B1["evaluate_mmd<br/>multiscale RBF MMD"]
        B2["evaluate_emd<br/>per-gene 1D Wasserstein"]
        B3["compute_distribution_distances<br/>4-metric report"]
        B4["lin_reg_summary<br/>mean-expression regression"]
    end
    subgraph L1["Layer 1 — Primitives (pure tensors)"]
        C1["src/mmd.py<br/>linear_mmd2 / poly_mmd2<br/>mix_rbf_mmd2"]
        C2["src/optimal_transport.py<br/>wasserstein (POT)"]
        C3["scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance"]
        C4["sklearn rbf_kernel"]
    end
    A1 --> B2
    A2 --> B1 & B2 & B3 & B4
    B1 --> C4
    B2 --> C3
    B3 --> C1 & C2
```

This layering has a practical consequence: you can reuse the primitives for novel evaluations (e.g., comparing latent embeddings) without touching AnnData plumbing, while the task layer guarantees consistent per-condition decomposition and DEG-focused analysis across all metrics.

Sources: [mmd.py](perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L1-L190), [optimal_transport.py](perturbgen/src/optimal_transport.py#L1-L62), [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L1-L40), [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L29-L35)

## Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)

MMD is a kernel two-sample test statistic (Gretton et al., 2012): it measures the distance between **mean embeddings** of two distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Formally, MMD² = E[k(x, x′)] + E[k(y, y′)] − 2·E[k(x, y)], which equals zero if and only if the two distributions coincide. Perturbgen implements three complementary MMD estimators, each selected for a different evaluation regime.

### Primitive estimators (`src/mmd.py`)

The file adapted from conditional-flow-matching provides a **linear-time MMD** (`linear_mmd2`), which exploits the identity h(z_i, z_j) = [f(x_i) − f(y_i)]ᵀ[f(x_j) − f(y_j)] for a linear kernel — useful when evaluating very large sample counts where quadratic kernel matrices are prohibitive. The **polynomial MMD** (`poly_mmd2`) computes (α·f(x)ᵀf(y) + c)^d with d=2 by default, again in linear time. The full quadratic estimators (`mix_rbf_mmd2`, `_mmd2`) build an explicit Gaussian RBF kernel matrix over the concatenated samples, supporting both **biased** (divide by m²) and **unbiased** (drop diagonal, divide by m(m−1)) estimators; `mix_rbf_mmd2_and_ratio` additionally normalizes by a closed-form variance estimate, producing a scale-free test statistic.

Sources: [mmd.py](perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L12-L30), [mmd.py](perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L40-L58), [mmd.py](perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L80-L82), [mmd.py](perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L126-L190)

### Multiscale RBF MMD on AnnData (`metric.py`)

The primary MMD used in Perturbgen reports is `mmd_loss_calc`, which uses scikit-learn's `rbf_kernel` with a single bandwidth gamma and applies the **unbiased diagonal-removal correction**: `sum_Kxx = (ΣK_xx − Σdiag) / (n(n−1))`, analogously for `K_yy`, with `K_xy` averaged directly. Removing the diagonal is critical for unbiasedness — self-similarity terms (k(x_i, x_i) = 1) otherwise bias the statistic toward zero, which would understate distributional mismatch in small-cell-count perturbation conditions.

The orchestration function `evaluate_mmd` wraps this into a **multiscale** estimate: it averages MMD across bandwidths `gammas = [2, 1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.005]`, spanning both coarse (large-scale mean shifts) and fine (local variance changes) structure. The function supports three dimensions of analysis: (1) per-condition evaluation by looping over `condition_key` values and computing MMD separately for each perturbation; (2) DEG-focused evaluation via `de_genes_dict`, computing a restricted `mmd_deg` on differentially expressed genes only; and (3) sample-size control through `n_cells`, which subsamples the true AnnData and aligns `pred_adata` to the same cell indices before computing — required for a valid two-sample comparison. Sparse matrices are densified (`X.toarray()`) since `rbf_kernel` requires dense input.

> [!TIP]
> The `mmd_deg` call inside `evaluate_mmd` passes DEG-restricted tensors to `mmd_loss_calc` **without** an explicit `gamma` argument in the DEG branch — verify the default behavior matches your bandwidth expectation before comparing `mmd` and `mmd_deg` columns numerically; they may use different kernel scales.

Sources: [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L101-L135), [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L139-L198), [mmd.py](perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L134-L161)

## Earth Mover's Distance (EMD): Per-Gene Marginals

In Perturbgen's nomenclature, **EMD** refers to the 1D Wasserstein-1 distance computed independently per gene. Rather than comparing the joint cell × gene distribution, `evaluate_emd` loops over every gene column `i` and calls `scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance(true_X[:, i], pred_X[:, i])`, then reports the **mean across genes**. This measures how well the model reproduces each gene's marginal expression distribution — the shape of the histogram of counts for, say, *B2M* across the cell population — which captures distributional properties (variance, multimodality, tail behavior) that a mean-only metric like `lin_reg_summary` cannot.

Like `evaluate_mmd`, the AnnData-aware variant supports per-condition decomposition (`emd` per condition) and a DEG-restricted variant (`emd_deg` computed only on DE gene columns). The tensor-native sibling `compute_emd(pred_counts, true_counts)` performs the identical per-column loop on raw `torch.Tensor` batches, detaching and moving to CPU first — this is the variant invoked during **validation** for cheap, in-loop monitoring. Both densify sparse inputs defensively inside the loop.

> [!TIP]
> EMD per gene is computed on the **raw count/expression space**, not PCA space — so `test/emd` (logged during testing) reflects gene-space fidelity, while the `*_PCA` distribution distances reflect embedding-space fidelity. Comparing them diagnoses *where* the model's error lives: good PCA scores with poor gene-space EMD indicate accurate global structure but noisy per-gene marginals.

Sources: [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L199-L249), [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L252-L266)

## Optimal Transport: Joint-Space Wasserstein Distances

The `wasserstein` function in `src/optimal_transport.py` computes the true **p-Wasserstein distance** between two multivariate samples using the POT (Python Optimal Transport) library. It solves the discrete OT problem with **uniform marginals** (`ot.unif`), a cost matrix built from pairwise Euclidean distances (`torch.cdist`), and offers two solvers:

| Solver | `method` | Algorithm | Trade-off | Key parameter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exact | `"exact"` or `None` | `ot.emd2` — linear program | Exact solution; super-cubic worst-case complexity; `numItermax=1e7`, `numThreads='max'` | — |
| Entropic | `"sinkhorn"` | `ot.sinkhorn2` — entropic regularization | Approximate; fast, GPU-friendly scaling behavior | `reg=0.05` (entropy weight) |

The `power` argument (restricted to 1 or 2) selects the transport cost exponent: the function squares the cost matrix for `power=2` and takes the square root of the LP result afterward (since `emd2` returns squared cost sums for a squared cost matrix). Multi-dimensional inputs with dim > 2 are flattened to [n_samples, −1], making the function agnostic to whether you compare raw expression, PCA coordinates, or latent embeddings.

The aggregate report function `compute_distribution_distances` (adapted from CFGen) combines this OT solver with the linear/poly MMD primitives into a single four-metric dictionary — `1-Wasserstein`, `2-Wasserstein`, `Linear_MMD`, `Poly_MMD` — computed in one pass. Because `linear_mmd2` computes `f_of_X − f_of_Y` element-wise, the function **clips both tensors to `min_size`** (the smaller of the two batch sizes) before calling the MMD primitives; misaligned sample counts would otherwise raise shape errors.

Sources: [optimal_transport.py](perturbgen/src/optimal_transport.py#L13-L62), [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L327-L361)

### Related: Energy Distance

`metric.py` also ships `compute_e_distance` and a JAX-jitted variant `compute_e_distance_fast` (adapted from CellFlow), computing the energy distance `2δ − σ_X − σ_Y` from pairwise squared Euclidean statistics. This provides a fast, kernel-free alternative to MMD with similar sensitivity to distributional shape; the JAX `@jax.jit` decorator makes it suitable for batched, repeated evaluation in sweep pipelines.

Sources: [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L20-L62)

## Execution Pipeline: Where Metrics Run in Lightning

The metrics are wired into two Lightning hooks on `PerturbGenTrainer` (inherited by `CountDecoderTrainer` and `PerturberTrainer`). During **validation**, only the lightweight EMD runs: `on_validation_epoch_end` concatenates accumulated true/prediction count tensors across batches, subsamples to at most 10,000 cells using a **seeded generator** (`torch.Generator().manual_seed(42)`), and logs `val/emd` with `sync_dist=True` for correct aggregation under DDP.

During **testing** (`on_test_epoch_end`, generation mode), the full battery executes in a fixed preprocessing order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Assemble pred_adata<br/>true counts in 'counts' layer"] --> P1["scale_pca on both Adatas"]
    P1 --> P2["Z-score PCA coords<br/>→ obsm['X_pca_scaled']"]
    P2 --> P3["Subsample to ≤10k cells<br/>true_adata aligned by obs index"]
    P3 --> M1["compute_distribution_distances<br/>on X_pca_scaled"]
    M1 --> L1["log each metric + '_PCA' suffix"]
    P3 --> M2["evaluate_emd<br/>gene space"]
    M2 --> L2["log test/emd"]
    P3 --> M3["evaluate_mmd n_cells=10000<br/>+ lin_reg_summary"]
    M3 --> L3["Concat all DataFrames<br/>→ metrics CSV in output_dir"]
    L1 --> L3
    L2 --> L3
```

The PCA-space computation deserves attention: both predicted and true data are independently PCA-projected via `scale_pca`, then each coordinate matrix is z-scored `(coords − mean) / std` before `compute_distribution_distances` runs the four OT/MMD metrics on the scaled coordinates. Results are logged with a `_PCA` suffix (e.g., `1-Wasserstein_PCA`). The non-generative test path (direct count prediction without the masked iterative decoding loop) skips all distribution metrics and persists only `lin_reg_summary` to `test_metrics.csv` — distribution metrics require *sampled* populations to be meaningful.

The entry point for perturbation-specific evaluation is `perturbgen/Perturb/val.py`, which loads a YAML config (e.g., `configs/eval/HSPC/mask_src_inference_perturbation_B2M.yaml`), constructs a `PerturberTrainer` (which inherits the full metric pipeline from `CountDecoderTrainer`), and invokes `trainer.test(...)` — the hook above then executes automatically. Config-driven knobs such as `output_dir` determine where the timestamped metrics CSV lands.

> [!TIP]
> The 10,000-cell cap appears twice with different mechanisms: validation uses `torch.randint` with an explicit seeded generator (reproducible across DDP ranks), while testing uses `sc.pp.subsample` (which respects the global numpy seed set by `evaluate_mmd`'s `np.random.seed(seed)`). If you need bitwise-reproducible metric CSVs, pin both seeds and keep cell counts below the cap.

Sources: [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L1075-L1102), [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L1209-L1280), [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L1282-L1302), [Perturb/val.py](perturbgen/Perturb/val.py#L219-L282), [Perturb/trainer.py](perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L18-L19)

## Metric Comparison Matrix

| Metric | Function | Comparison space | Granularity | Library/backend | Provenance | Reported as |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linear MMD | `linear_mmd2` | Joint (cells × features), linear kernel | Whole population | PyTorch | conditional-flow-matching | `Linear_MMD_PCA` |
| Polynomial MMD | `poly_mmd2` | Joint, poly kernel (d=2) | Whole population | PyTorch | conditional-flow-matching | `Poly_MMD_PCA` |
| Multiscale RBF MMD | `evaluate_mmd` | Joint, 6 RBF bandwidths | Per condition (+DEG variant) | scikit-learn `rbf_kernel` | CPA | `mmd`, `mmd_deg` |
| 1D Wasserstein / EMD | `evaluate_emd` | Per-gene marginal (1D) | Mean over genes, per condition | `scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance` | CPA | `emd`, `emd_deg`, `test/emd` |
| Batch EMD | `compute_emd` | Per-gene marginal (1D) | Mean over genes | scipy (tensor-native) | — | `val/emd` |
| W₁ / W₂ (joint OT) | `wasserstein` via `compute_distribution_distances` | Joint (cells × features) | Whole population | POT (`ot.emd2` / `ot.sinkhorn2`) | CFGen | `1/2-Wasserstein_PCA` |
| Energy distance | `compute_e_distance(_fast)` | Joint, pairwise squared distances | Whole population | JAX (jitted) | CellFlow (Peidli 2024) | (utility, not logged by default) |
| Linear regression | `lin_reg_summary` | Per-gene mean expressions | Population (gene vector) | `scipy.stats.linregress` | — | slope, R², RMSE |

## Interpreting the Metrics Together

Each metric answers a different question about perturbation fidelity, and they are deliberately complementary. **MMD** (joint space) asks: "are the predicted and true populations indistinguishable as multivariate distributions under a kernel?" — it is sensitive to covariance structure and higher moments, and the multiscale bandwidths make it robust to both global shifts and local density changes. **Wasserstein (OT)** asks: "what is the minimum cost of transporting predicted cells onto true cells?" — it carries geometric meaning and is well-behaved for distributions with disjoint support (a known MMD failure mode with narrow kernels). **EMD** (per gene) asks: "does each gene's marginal expression profile match?" — it isolates per-gene fidelity that joint metrics can wash out when errors are anti-correlated across genes. The companion `lin_reg_summary` (slope ≈ 1, R², RMSE on per-gene mean expressions) anchors the distributional metrics with an interpretable, mean-focused reference point.

For advanced users extending the suite: new metrics should follow the established contract observed in `metric.py` — accept `AnnData` (or tensors), densify sparse inputs, support `condition_key` decomposition, and return a `pd.DataFrame` indexed by condition — so the DataFrame concatenation in `on_test_epoch_end` and the CSV/wandb persistence work without modification.

Sources: [metric.py](perturbgen/src/metric.py#L269-L324), [Model/trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L1246-L1280)

## Next Steps

- To understand how the predictions feeding these metrics are produced (masked iterative decoding vs. direct inference), see [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes).
- For the exhaustive benchmark suite that exercises these metrics end-to-end, see [Test and Benchmark Suite](26-test-and-benchmark-suite).
- To customize where metric CSVs and checkpoints are written, see [Configuration System and Path Management](17-configuration-system-and-path-management).
- Metric values are also surfaced to experiment tracking; for wandb integration details, see [Experiment Tracking with Weights and Biases](20-experiment-tracking-with-weights-and-biases).
- For the architectural context in which these evaluations sit (two-stage masking/count decoder), see [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).

# Cell Pairing and Data Curation



This page documents the two data-engineering foundations that make PerturbGen's supervised perturbation training possible: **data curation** (transforming heterogeneous raw scRNA-seq datasets into a harmonized, model-ready AnnData object) and **cell pairing** (the index-aligned linkage between control "source" cells and perturbed "target" cells across multiple time points). Curation is demonstrated end-to-end in the LPS preprocessing notebook, while pairing is implemented in the `PerturbGenDataset`/`PerturbGenDataModule` classes that every training and evaluation job consumes. Together they enforce a strict contract: for every cell index `i`, the model must always receive the same donor's baseline state and that same donor's perturbed states at each modeled time step.

## The Curation Workflow: From Public Repositories to a Unified Cohort

The curation notebook `preprocessing_curation.ipynb` prepares the LPS (lipopolysaccharide stimulation) dataset by merging a public cohort with a private one, then harmonizing metadata so both cohorts can be trained on jointly. The notebook's stated purpose is "the preparation of LPS datasets, including both public and private sources, and demonstrates how to merge them for training the PerturbGen model" [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L8-L17).

The complete pipeline proceeds in seven stages, each removing one source of heterogeneity:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Download public dataset<br/>E-MTAB-10026 · 647,366 × 24,929] --> B[Filter conditions<br/>keep only LPS + Healthy]
    B --> C[Standardize metadata<br/>time · donor_id · study · life_stage · tissue]
    C --> D[Restore raw counts<br/>adata.X = layers raw]
    D --> E[Subset features<br/>Gene Expression only]
    E --> F[Map gene symbols to<br/>Ensembl IDs via mart_export.txt]
    F --> G[Concatenate public + private<br/>224,150 × 13,826]
    G --> H[Harmonize cell type labels<br/>cell_type_harmonized]
    H --> I[Enforce timepoint completeness<br/>drop cell types missing any timepoint<br/>15 final cell types]
```

### Stage 1 — Acquisition and Condition Filtering

The public cohort is downloaded from the EBI Biostudies archive (study E-MTAB-10026, file `covid_portal_210320_with_raw.h5ad`, ~7.19 GB), yielding an AnnData object of 647,366 cells × 24,929 genes with rich `obs` fields including `sample_id`, `Status`, `full_clustering`, and `Collection_Day` [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L54-L77), [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L128-L131).

Before any pairing logic can run, the cohort must be restricted to cells relevant to the perturbation experiment. The notebook inspects the available conditions via `value_counts()` — revealing `Covid` (527,286), `Healthy` (97,039), `Non_covid` (15,157), and `LPS` (7,884) cells — extracts the patient IDs belonging to LPS and Healthy donors, then subsets the AnnData with `adata.obs['Status'].isin(['LPS','Healthy'])`. This isolates the stimulated cells and their matched unperturbed donors while discarding unrelated disease cohorts [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L179-L218).

### Stage 2 — Metadata Standardization

PerturbGen's training configuration references cells by *predictable* obs keys, so the notebook normalizes five metadata dimensions into a common schema:

| Obs field | Curation action | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `time_after_LPS` | `nan` → `'normal'`, suffixed values → `'90m_LPS'`, `'10h_LPS'`; cast to ordered `Categorical` | Time-step keys drive `tgt_dataset_t{t}` lookup |
| `donor_id` | Copied from `patient_id` | Donor identity for condition encodings |
| `study` | Hardcoded cohort tag (e.g. `'Public_Emily2021'`) | Batch/condition covariate at merge time |
| `development_stage` | Age intervals mapped to ordered life stages (`Adult`, `Old`, ...) | Harmonized covariate across cohorts |
| `tissue` | Constant `'blood'` | Consistent tissue annotation |

The time column is the most critical: unperturbed cells carry `nan` timestamps, which are relabeled `'normal'` so every cell carries a valid categorical time key, ordered as `['normal', '90m_LPS', '10h_LPS']` [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L225-L253), [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L286-L298). Life-stage harmonization uses an explicit mapping dictionary that collapses six age intervals into an ordered categorical, and the tissue field is assigned wholesale [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L352-L379).

### Stage 3 — Raw Counts Restoration and Feature Subsetting

Two invariants matter downstream: (1) the model operates on **raw counts**, not normalized values, and (2) only gene expression modalities are tokenized. The notebook therefore overwrites the processed matrix with the raw layer — `adata.X = adata.layers['raw'].copy()` — and verifies the maximum count is an untransformed float value [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L388-L411). It then subsets the `var` axis to features where `feature_types == 'Gene Expression'`, excluding antibody-capture or other modalities present in multiome-style public releases [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L453-L455).

> [!TIP]
> The gene-symbol → Ensembl-ID mapping file `mart_export.txt` is **pinned inside the repository** at `docs/examples/reference/mart_export.txt` (Ensembl BioMart, GRCh38.p14, 86,368 genes) rather than fetched at runtime. Because symbol-to-ID mappings drift between Ensembl releases, regenerating this file from a different release would match a different gene set and silently change which genes are retained — the checked-in file guarantees byte-identical gene matching with the tutorial.

This mapping is loaded with `pd.read_csv("reference/mart_export.txt")` and used to annotate `ensembl_id` per gene [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L463-L478).

### Stage 4 — Cohort Merging and Cell Type Harmonization

After the private cohort receives identical metadata treatment, both cohorts are concatenated into a single AnnData: `adata = adata1.concatenate(adata2)`, producing **224,150 cells × 13,826 genes**. The merged time-point distribution becomes `normal` (148,742), `6h_LPS` (43,810), `10h_LPS` (20,890), and `90m_LPS` (10,708) — note the private cohort contributes a `6h` time point absent from the public one [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L2004-L2056).

Merging exposes the central curation problem: the merged `cell_type` field contains **~60 distinct raw labels** that describe overlapping populations under different naming conventions (e.g., `CD14mono`, `CD14_mono`, `CD83_CD14_mono`, `CD14mono_M1`, `Int.mono` all denote CD14 monocytes) [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L2069-L2140). The notebook resolves this with an explicit `cell_type_mapping` dictionary that projects every raw label onto a canonical vocabulary — collapsing monocytes, CD4 T cell subtypes, CD8 subtypes, NK subsets, B cell subsets, and plasma cell variants into 20 canonical classes — and writes the result to a new `cell_type_harmonized` obs column, falling back to the raw label for unmapped entries [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L2177-L2254).

### Stage 5 — Timepoint Completeness Enforcement

Because the model predicts a perturbation response *per cell type per time step*, a cell type observed in only a subset of time points cannot contribute complete training pairs. The notebook runs a group-by check — for each harmonized cell type, it collects the set of observed time points and verifies that the full time-point universe is a subset. Five cell types fail the check (`ASDC`, `HSC_CD38pos`, `HSC_Erythroid`, `ILC1_3`, `Red_Blood_Cell`) and are explicitly removed, leaving **15 fully-paired cell types** spanning 224,150 curated cells [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L2271-L2290), [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L2315-L2356).

This completeness check is the curation-side twin of the pairing invariant described below: it guarantees every (cell type, time step) combination has both control and perturbed cells available for index-aligned pairing.

## The Cell Pairing Architecture: Index-Aligned src/tgt Tensors

Cell pairing in PerturbGen is **positional, not identity-based**. The `PerturbGenDataset` stores a source dataset (control/baseline cells) and a dictionary of target datasets keyed by time step — `tgt_dataset_t1`, `tgt_dataset_t2`, ... — and asserts that row `i` of the source corresponds to row `i` of every target. The constructor's split logic applies the *same* `split_indices` to source and all targets (`self.src_dataset.select(split_indices)` and per-time-step `select`), so subsetting for train/val/test preserves the alignment [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L22-L79).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Curated["Curated AnnData (obs order = pairing order)"]
        C0["normal cells"]
        C1["90m_LPS cells"]
        C2["10h_LPS cells"]
    end
    subgraph PGD["PerturbGenDataset"]
        S["src_dataset<br/>(input_ids tokens)"]
        T1["tgt_dataset_t1"]
        T2["tgt_dataset_t2"]
        SC["src_counts"]
        TC["tgt_counts_dict"]
    end
    C0 -->|"select(split_indices)"| S
    C1 -->|"select(split_indices)"| T1
    C2 -->|"select(split_indices)"| T2
    S ---|"__getitem__(ind)"| T1
    S ---|"__getitem__(ind)"| T2
    SC --> TC
```

Two integrity mechanisms enforce this contract at runtime. First, a **length invariant** warns when `src` and `tgt` differ in size and clamps iteration length to the minimum — `self.dataset_length = min(src_len, tgt_len)` — preventing silent index-out-of-range errors when a cohort has asymmetric coverage [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L80-L89). Second, `__getitem__` returns the source and *all* target time steps for a single index in one dict (`src_dataset[ind]` plus `tgt_dataset_t{t}[ind]` for each modeled time step), so a training sample is always a complete paired tuple, never an unpaired fragment [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L127-L148).

**Time steps** define how many targets pair with each source. The `PerturbGenDataModule` exposes three complementary settings: `pred_tps` (the time steps the model is trained to predict, e.g. `[1, 2]`), `context_tps` (additional observed time steps usable as conditioning context at test time), and `n_total_tps` (the universe of time points in the cohort) [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L151-L227). During test-stage setup, the dataset includes `pred_tps + context_tps` — with an explicit comment that this restriction exists "to avoid data leakage" — so evaluation never loads target states the model is not supposed to have seen [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L272-L293).

## Conditioning, Balanced Sampling, and Batch Assembly

Pairing alone is not enough when cohorts are imbalanced — the merged LPS cohort has 148,742 control cells but only ~10,700 at the rarest perturbation time point. The dataset computes **inverse-frequency label weights** from one or more `sampling_keys` (arbitrary obs columns, e.g. cell type + time point), combining the weight tensors of source and each target time step by element-wise mean, and the training dataloader feeds these into a `WeightedRandomSampler` (with replacement, seeded for reproducibility) instead of naive shuffling [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L91-L125), [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L295-L313).

The `collate` function then assembles model-ready tensors from each paired tuple, performing four transformations worth knowing when debugging shape mismatches:

| Collate output key | Transformation | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| `src_input_ids` | Pad token sequences to `max_len` (default 2048) via `pad_tensor_list` with `<pad>` token ID | Length also records true per-cell length in `src_length` |
| `tgt_input_ids_t{t}` | Strip `<cls>` and `<eos>` tokens from target sequences | Explicitly does *not* assume CLS is the first token |
| `tgt_counts_t{t}` | Concatenate per-cell raw counts (dense-ifying CSR matrices if needed) | Feeds the count decoder objective |
| `tgt_size_factor_t{t}` | Row sums of the target count matrix | Library size factor computed once per sample |

Condition tensors (`conditions`, `conditions_combined`) ride alongside when `condition_encodings` are supplied, carrying the donor/batch covariates curated in Stage 2 into the model [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L331-L398).

> [!TIP]
> The dense conversion of sparse CSR matrices happens **once per sample** in collate — the code deliberately reuses a single `_dense` array to derive both the counts tensor and the size factor, halving the sparse-to-dense cost on the hot path. If you extend the collate function, preserve this reuse pattern; recomputing `.toarray()` per derived tensor is the most common performance regression in custom dataloaders here.

## How Curation and Pairing Meet

The two halves of this page connect through **obs ordering**. The curation notebook's final `adata_filtered` (224,150 cells, 15 harmonized cell types, complete across all four time points) is later tokenized so that, for every donor, the `normal` row index matches the `90m/6h/10h` rows' indices in the derived `src`/`tgt` Hugging Face datasets. Every curation operation that reorders or filters cells therefore has pairing consequences:

| Curation decision | Pairing consequence if skipped |
|---|---|
| Ordered categorical time keys | Time-step dict lookup (`tgt_dataset_t{t}`) has no canonical keys |
| Cell type harmonization | Weighted sampling groups fragments into near-duplicate strata |
| Timepoint completeness filtering | `dataset_length = min(src_len, tgt_len)` silently drops real cells |
| Raw counts restoration | `tgt_size_factor_t{t}` sums log-normalized values, corrupting the count decoder |
| Pinned Ensembl mapping | Token vocabulary mismatch between cohorts breaks joint training |

Sources: [preprocessing_curation.ipynb](docs/examples/preprocessing_curation.ipynb#L2271-L2356), [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L80-L89), [datamodule.py](perturbgen/Dataloaders/datamodule.py#L331-L398)

## Where to Go Next

- To see how curated, paired cells are converted into the token sequences consumed by `src_dataset`/`tgt_datasets`, continue to [Geneformer-Style Gene Tokenization](9-geneformer-style-gene-tokenization).
- For how the paired `tgt_counts_t{t}` tensors supervise the generative objective, see [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training).
- For the analogous bronze→silver harmonization applied to the *pretraining* cohort (a batch-oriented script pipeline, distinct from this notebook workflow), see [Pretraining Cohort Harmonization Pipeline](15-pretraining-cohort-harmonization-pipeline).
- For the on-disk format of the tokenized outputs of this workflow, see [Tokenized Dataset Layout](16-tokenized-dataset-layout).

# Pretraining Cohort Harmonization Pipeline



This page documents the standalone data-engineering pipeline that lives under `pretraining_cohort/` in the repository root. Its purpose is to convert a heterogeneous collection of raw, per-study `.h5ad` datasets (the **bronze tier**) into a vocabulary-harmonized, quality-controlled **silver tier**, then derive cohort-wide per-gene median expression statistics, and finally produce Geneformer-format tokenized datasets ready for large-scale pretraining. Unlike the model code in `perturbgen/`, these scripts are cohort-scoped infrastructure: they are parameterized by one YAML config (stage 1) or by hardcoded NFS paths edited per cohort (stages 2–3). This page covers the architecture, per-stage mechanics, execution walkthrough, and the artifacts the pipeline emits; it does not cover how the model consumes those artifacts.

## Pipeline Architecture at a Glance

The directory layout encodes the pipeline topology directly: each subdirectory is one stage, and each stage consumes the previous stage's output convention. Stage 1 writes one subdirectory per input dataset under a shared output root; stages 2 and 3 then recursively discover those files with `os.walk`. To read the following diagram: solid arrows are data flow between tiers, dashed arrows are reference assets (mapping pickles, dictionaries) that feed a stage without being transformed by it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph S1["Stage 1 · preprocessing/"]
        B["Bronze .h5ad<br/>(raw per-study exports)"] --> H["harmonize_bronze_to_silver.py"]
        CFG["config_am74.yaml"] -.-> H
        M["vocab pickles:<br/>dev stage · tissue · disease"] -.-> H
        H --> S["Silver {stem}_qc.h5ad<br/>(harmonized + QC-filtered)"]
    end
    subgraph S2["Stage 2 · median_calculation/"]
        S --> M1["median_calculation_1.py<br/>CP10K + per-gene TDigest"]
        M1 --> D["{stem}.gene_median_digest_dict.pickle"]
        D --> M2["aggregate_medians.py<br/>sketch merge (reduce)"]
        M2 --> A["total_gene_median_dict.pickle<br/>detected_gene_median_dict.pickle"]
    end
    subgraph S3["Stage 3 · tokenization/"]
        S --> T["tokenization.py<br/>Geneformer TranscriptomeTokenizer"]
        A -.-> T
        V["token dict ·<br/>Ensembl mapping"] -.-> T
        T --> O["Tokenized cohort shards"]
    end
```

The three stages are deliberately decoupled on disk: there is no orchestrator script that runs all three, and each stage is idempotent over its inputs. This makes the pipeline resumable — a failed dataset can be re-harmonized without recomputing medians for the rest of the cohort.

Sources: [harmonize_bronze_to_silver.py](pretraining_cohort/preprocessing/harmonize_bronze_to_silver.py#L206-L212), [median_calculation_1.py](pretraining_cohort/median_calculation/median_calculation_1.py#L10-L14), [aggregate_medians.py](pretraining_cohort/median_calculation/aggregate_medians.py#L53-L55), [tokenization.py](pretraining_cohort/tokenization/tokenization.py#L23-L42)

## Stage 1: Bronze → Silver Harmonization

### Configuration Contract

Stage 1 is the only config-driven stage. `harmonize_bronze_to_silver.py` declares a required `--config_file` CLI argument, loads it with `yaml.safe_load`, and reads every behavioral knob from that mapping. The shipped example, `config_am74.yaml`, defines the full contract: input/output roots, three vocabulary-mapping pickles, an optional exclusion switch, and a nested `gene_filtering` block.

| Config key | Type | Role |
|---|---|---|
