- **Run the notebooks that consume these assets** — see [Tutorial Notebooks Walkthrough](4-tutorial-notebooks-walkthrough)
- **Warm-start training from a checkpoint yourself** — see [CLI Command Reference](22-cli-command-reference)

# ZINB and Negative Binomial Losses



This page explains how Perturbgen models single-cell RNA-seq count data probabilistically. The repository ships two mathematically central functions — `nb` (Negative Binomial log-likelihood) and `zinb` (Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial log-likelihood) — plus the model heads and trainer wiring that produce their inputs (`mu`, `theta`, `pi`). Because raw scRNA-seq counts are overdispersed and dominated by dropouts (excess zeros), Gaussian losses on normalized values are a poor fit; the NB family models counts directly. Here we cover the distributions, their numerical-stability implementation, and how `CountHead`/`CountDecoder`/`CountDecoderTrainer` consume them.

## The Distribution Losses: Origins and Location

The core likelihood functions live in two identical copies: `perturbgen/src/losses.py` and `scmaskgit/src/losses.py`. Both were transplanted verbatim from **scvi-tools** (code version 0.8.1, attributed to Romain Lopez, Adam Gayoso, and Galen Xing), as documented in the function docstrings. Alongside them sit two plain MSE helpers, `mse` and `mse_loss`, completing the loss utility set.

Sources: [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L49-L58), [losses.py](scmaskgit/src/losses.py#L51-L58)

An important architectural subtlety: the trainers do **not** import `nb`/`zinb` from these local modules for training. Both `perturbgen/Model/trainer.py` and `scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py` instead import the distribution classes `NegativeBinomial` and `ZeroInflatedNegativeBinomial` directly from `scvi.distributions`, while pulling only `mse_loss` from the local `losses.py`. The local `nb`/`zinb` functions are therefore the standalone, dependency-light reference implementation of the exact same math — useful for tests, notebooks, and reasoning about the likelihood without instantiating scvi distribution objects.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L23-L28), [trainer.py](scmaskgit/Model/trainer.py#L24-L29)

> [!TIP]
> Despite docstrings saying "Computes negative binomial loss", both functions return the **log-likelihood** (values to be maximized), not a loss to be minimized. Negation and reduction are delegated to the caller — in the training path, scvi's distribution objects handle this via their `loss` API.

## Mathematical Foundation

The Negative Binomial distribution parameterizes each gene's count with two positive quantities: the mean `mu` and the **inverse dispersion** `theta`. Its variance is `mu + mu²/theta`, so small `theta` means heavy overdispersion — exactly the gene-to-gene variability seen in UMI counts. The log-likelihood evaluated by `nb(x, mu, theta, eps)` decomposes into three terms, each implemented as one pure-tensor expression (L81-87):

```text
res = θ·(log(θ+ε) − log(θ+μ+ε))            # dispersion normalization
    + x·(log(μ+ε) − log(θ+μ+ε))            # mean/count interaction
    + lgamma(x+θ) − lgamma(θ) − lgamma(x+1) # Gamma-function normalization
```

A key preprocessing step handles broadcasting: if `theta` arrives as a 1-D tensor of shape `[n_genes]` — i.e., one dispersion shared across all cells — it is reshaped to `[1, n_genes]` so it broadcasts against cell-batched `mu` and `x`. The `eps=1e-8` constant guards every logarithm against `log(0)` when counts or parameters approach zero.

Sources: [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L77-L89), [losses.py](scmaskgit/src/losses.py#L77-L87)

The ZINB distribution adds a dropout mixture component: with probability `π` an observation is a *structural zero* (dropout event), otherwise it is drawn from the NB component. Since `π` is passed as **logits** (unbounded real values, per the docstring), the implementation never materializes a raw probability — it works entirely in log-space using the identity `log σ(x) = −softplus(−x)`.

Sources: [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L107-L116), [losses.py](scmaskgit/src/losses.py#L113-L116)

## Inside the `zinb` Implementation: the Two-Case Split

The zero-inflation requires evaluating a different formula depending on whether the observed count is zero. The implementation computes both branches unconditionally, then selects with multiplicative indicator masks — a fully vectorized, branch-free strategy that keeps the computation GPU-friendly:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["x, mu, theta, pi (logits)"] --> B["Broadcast theta: 1-D → [1, n_genes]"]
    B --> C["softplus_pi = softplus(−pi)<br/>log_theta_eps = log(theta+eps)<br/>log_theta_mu_eps = log(theta+mu+eps)<br/>pi_theta_log = −pi + θ·(log_theta_eps − log_theta_mu_eps)"]
    C --> D["case_zero = softplus(pi_theta_log) − softplus_pi<br/>(log P(x=0))"]
    C --> E["case_non_zero = −softplus_pi + pi_theta_log<br/>+ x·(log(mu+eps) − log_theta_mu_eps)<br/>+ lgamma terms<br/>(log P(x>0) via NB)"]
    D --> F["mask (x &lt; eps)"]
    E --> G["mask (x &gt; eps)"]
    F --> H["res = mul_case_zero + mul_case_non_zero<br/>= ZINB log-likelihood tensor"]
    G --> H
```

The clever part is `case_zero = softplus(pi_theta_log) − softplus_pi`. This equals `log(π + (1−π)·NB(0))` in log-space: the `softplus` of the combined log-ratio naturally adds the NB-mass-at-zero contribution to the dropout logit without ever computing an explicit `log(exp(a) + exp(b))` that would overflow. Likewise `case_non_zero` folds `log(1−π)` (as `−softplus_pi`) into the NB density for strictly positive counts. For count data the masks `(x < eps)` and `(x > eps)` are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

Sources: [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L130-L149), [losses.py](scmaskgit/src/losses.py#L131-L148)

## From Embeddings to Distribution Parameters: `CountHead`

The likelihood functions need `mu`, `theta`, and `pi` as inputs — those come from the count-prediction architecture. `CountHead` is the final MLP that maps decoder embeddings to distribution parameters, configured by a single `loss_mode` switch with options `'mse'`, `'zinb'`, `'nb'` (default `'zinb'`). Before the parameter heads, the MLP output is L2-normalized along the feature dimension, which stabilizes the scale of downstream activations.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1429-L1471), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1501-L1510)

The heads differ per loss mode:

| `loss_mode` | Head(s) created | Forward outputs | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'mse'` | `relu_output`: Linear → ReLU | `count_lognorm` | Regress log-normalized counts point-wise |
| `'zinb'` | `softmax_output`: Linear → Softmax(dim=-1)* and `linear_output`: plain Linear | `count_mean`, `count_dropout` | NB mean (proportional profile) + dropout logits π |
| `'nb'` | `softmax_output`: Linear → Softmax(dim=-1)* | `count_mean` | NB mean only; no zero-inflation term |

\* When `use_size_factor=False`, the activation switches from Softmax to **Softplus** so the mean is predicted as an absolute rate rather than a fraction of a library.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1474-L1493), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1511-L1525)

Size factors — the library-size scaling that converts the Softmax output into a gene-specific mean — follow a two-flag contract: if `use_size_factor=True` and `use_observed_size_factor=False`, the head *learns* a size factor via `exp(Linear(d_model, 1))`; if `use_observed_size_factor=True`, `size_factor` is emitted as `None` and supplied externally from observed counts. This mirrors classic scVI practice where `mu = softmax(h) · library_size`.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1494-L1499), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1518-L1523)

Notably, `CountHead` produces **no theta output**. Dispersion is deliberately kept out of the network forward pass and handled at the trainer level (next section) — the network models the *mean structure* conditioned on embeddings, while dispersion is a condition-indexed global parameter.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1513-L1517)

## Class and Module Interaction Diagram

The count-decoding stack is a three-layer composition, designed for the two-stage training regime (see [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training)) where the generative transformer is frozen first and the count head is trained on top of its embeddings:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Trainer["CountDecoderTrainer (LightningModule)"]
        TH["theta: nn.Parameter<br/>shape [n_genes, n_conditions_combined]<br/>created only if loss_mode ∈ {nb, zinb}"]
    end
    subgraph CD["CountDecoder"]
        PM["pretrained_model: PerturbGen<br/>(frozen masked-generative transformer)"]
        CH["count_decoder: CountHead<br/>loss_mode ∈ {mse, zinb, nb}"]
    end
    Batch["batch tensors"] --> PM
    PM -->|"mean_embedding<br/>per time step t"| CH
    CH -->|"count_mean (μ)"| NBZ["scvi.distributions<br/>NegativeBinomial /<br/>ZeroInflatedNegativeBinomial"]
    CH -->|"count_dropout (π logits)"| NBZ
    CH -->|"size_factor (library)"| NBZ
    TH -->|"θ (dispersion)"| NBZ
    NBZ -->|"negative log-likelihood"| Loss["Training loss"]
```

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1527-L1636), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L602-L723), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L23)

Two parallel entry points feed this stack. `CountDecoder.forward` runs the frozen pretrained model in `not_masked=True` mode over ground-truth target token dictionaries, then applies `CountHead` to the `mean_embedding` of each predicted time step, emitting `count_output_t{t}`. `CountDecoder.generate_counts` performs the same head application on **iteratively generated** embeddings from the MaskGIT-style decoder — this is how in-silico perturbation predictions get count-space outputs.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1620-L1636), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1638-L1667)

## Dispersion (theta) Wiring in the Trainer

`CountDecoderTrainer` materializes theta only under the probabilistic modes. The gating condition requires `loss_mode in ['nb', 'zinb']` **and** both `conditions` and `conditions_combined` to be provided; otherwise `self.theta = None`. When active, theta is a raw `nn.Parameter` initialized with `torch.randn` and shaped `[n_genes, n_conditions_combined]` — meaning the model learns a **separate inverse-dispersion value for every gene in every perturbation condition**, capturing the fact that different perturbations induce different levels of count noise per gene.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L739-L751)

> [!TIP]
> theta lives on the trainer, not on `CountHead`, and is indexed by combined condition — so gradient updates to dispersion come only from batches that carry the condition bookkeeping. If you instantiate `CountDecoderTrainer` for pure MSE fine-tuning, confirm `self.theta is None`; the NB/ZINB likelihood is undefined without it.

The trainer also exposes `use_size_factor` and `use_observed_size_factor` as constructor arguments, which it forwards verbatim into `CountDecoder` → `CountHead`, selecting the Softmax-vs-Softplus mean parameterization and the predicted-vs-observed library size strategy described above.

Sources: [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L650-L651), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L706-L723)

## Choosing Between MSE, NB, and ZINB

The three loss modes form a modeling spectrum with distinct statistical assumptions and head configurations:

| Aspect | MSE (`'mse'`) | NB (`'nb'`) | ZINB (`'zinb'`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Output space | Log-normalized counts | Raw counts (mean μ) | Raw counts (μ + dropout π) |
| Zero handling | Treats zeros as values | Poisson-like zeros only | Explicit structural zeros via dropout |
| Overdispersion | None (implicit Gaussian) | Gene×condition θ | Gene×condition θ |
| Distribution parameters learned | Mean only | μ, θ | μ, θ, π |
| Extra heads | ReLU head | Softmax/Softplus head | Softmax/Softplus + linear head |
| Best suited for | Normalized embeddings, quick baselines | Overdispersed UMI counts | UMI counts with heavy dropout (typical scRNA-seq) |
| | | | |

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1446-L1460), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1474-L1525), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L611-L612)

The pros/cons trade-off is worth making explicit. **NB** buys you a principled count likelihood with a single dispersion mechanism, at the cost of underestimating dropout-driven zeros. **ZINB** matches the generative process of droplet-based single-cell data most faithfully — the mixture handles amplicon/dropout zeros separately from biological zeros — but requires one more head, one more parameter tensor per element, and can over-parameterize when true dropouts are rare. **MSE** is the cheapest and most stable to optimize, but its gradients are dominated by high-count genes and it cannot express count uncertainty — which downstream evaluation metrics (see [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport)) may rely on.

Sources: [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L91-L150), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1440-L1461)

## Numerical Stability Summary

All three numerical hazards that typically plague discrete likelihoods are neutralized in this codebase. First, every `log()` call is wrapped with `eps=1e-8` (`log(θ+ε)`, `log(μ+ε)`, `log(θ+μ+ε)`) so zero counts and vanishing parameters never produce `-inf`. Second, the ZINB dropout probability is kept in logit space throughout — `softplus` identities replace naive `log(sigmoid(·))` and `log(1−π)` computations, eliminating overflow at extreme logits. Third, Gamma normalizers use `torch.lgamma` (log-space directly) rather than `torch.gamma` followed by a log, which would underflow for large `x + θ`. These choices are inherited intact from scvi-tools and are the reason the same expressions serve both the local reference functions and the production `scvi.distributions` path.

Sources: [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L77-L89), [losses.py](perturbgen/src/losses.py#L130-L149)

## Practical Checklist for Extending the Loss Stack

When adding a new likelihood or modifying the count head, four touchpoints must stay consistent: (1) `CountHead.__init__` — register parameter heads under the new `loss_mode` branch; (2) `CountHead.forward` — emit the matching keys in `count_outputs` (e.g., `count_mean`, `count_dropout`, `size_factor`); (3) `CountDecoderTrainer.__init__` — extend the `loss_mode in ['nb', 'zinb']` gate if the new likelihood needs trainer-held parameters like theta; and (4) the import at the trainer top if you switch between the local `losses.py` functions and `scvi.distributions`. Because `CountDecoder` iterates generically over `pred_tps`, new outputs automatically flow to every predicted time step without further plumbing.

Sources: [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1462-L1525), [trainer.py](perturbgen/Model/trainer.py#L739-L751), [transformer.py](perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L1630-L1636)

## Where to Go Next

This page sits at the intersection of the model-design and evaluation chapters. To see how the masked generative stage feeds embeddings into the count stage, read [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training). For how the predicted counts are scored at evaluation time — where the distributional view really pays off — continue to [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport). To position this count-modeling choice against GEO-based and VAE-based alternatives, see [Comparison with Alternative Perturbation Models](25-comparison-with-alternative-perturbation-models).

# Comparison with Alternative Perturbation Models



This page positions PerturbGen against the broader family of in-silico perturbation models — VAE-based response predictors (scGen, CPA), graph-based combinatorial models (GEARS), and token-based foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT) — by mapping each design decision in the PerturbGen codebase onto that landscape. Everything claimed about PerturbGen below is verified directly against the repository; claims about alternative tools summarize their published designs and are marked as such. This page is deliberately conceptual: for hands-on usage, start with [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes).

## The Differentiating Claim: Static Response vs. Dynamic Trajectories

The repository's own positioning is explicit in its introduction: most recent approaches "can predict single-cell perturbation responses in silico, [but] cannot predict responses across dynamic cell trajectories" ([README.md](/README.md#L8-L9)). This single sentence defines the axis along which PerturbGen differentiates itself, and the axis is architecturally real, not just narrative. It is implemented as a **conditional sequence-to-sequence design**: a source (observed) token sequence is encoded, and target sequences at *multiple future time steps* (`pred_tps`) are decoded, with optional context time points (`context_tps`) that the decoder attends to ([perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L80-L124)). Most VAE-family baselines operate on a single control→stimulated transition, which structurally cannot express "cell state at hour *t* under perturbation."

Time enters the model as a first-class signal rather than a covariate: the `PositionalEncoding` class offers sinusoidal time+position modes (`time_pos_sin`, `comb_sin`) that are *functions of the target time step*, and the code notes that learnt time encodings "cannot be used for time interpolation and extrapolation" while sinusoidal ones can ([perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L50-L114)). This is what allows PerturbGen to predict at unseen intermediate times — the property the tutorial demonstrates by perturbing at 6 h and predicting at 10 h ([README.md](/README.md#L96-L97)).

## Design-Space Comparison

The table below contrasts the main published model families on the dimensions that matter architecturally. The PerturbGen column is verified against this codebase; the other columns summarize each method's published design.

| Dimension | scGen (VAE) | CPA | GEARS | **PerturbGen** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Data representation | Log-normalized continuous vectors | Log-normalized continuous vectors | Log-normalized gene-wise deltas | **Discrete Geneformer-style rank tokens** ([9-geneformer-style-gene-tokenization]) |
| Perturbation operator | Latent vector arithmetic (Δ stimulation) | Learned additive covariate embeddings | Message passing on a gene-gene graph | **Token-level edits: `mask` / `pad` / `delete` / `overexpress`** ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L57-L64)) |
| Time / dynamics | One pre/post transition | Static conditions | Static conditions | **Multi-timepoint trajectories with time-aware positional encoding** ([perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L87-L114)) |
| Decoding | One-shot VAE decoder | One-shot decoder | One-shot regression head | **Parallel masked iterative decoding (MaskGIT, ~18 iterations)** ([perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L36-L37)) |
| Likelihood / loss | Gaussian (MSE) on normalized data | Gaussian + adversarial | MSE on deltas | **ZINB / NB count likelihood, borrowed from scvi-tools** ([perturbgen/src/losses.py](/perturbgen/src/losses.py#L49-L89)) |
| Stochasticity | Latent sampling | Mostly deterministic | Deterministic | **Stochastic token sampling + `n_samples` count draws averaged** ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L510-L512)) |
| Evaluation style | Per-gene R²/correlation | Differential-expression overlap | Per-gene delta correlation | **Distribution-level: MMD, Wasserstein, cosine of embeddings** ([perturbgen/src/mmd.py](/perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L60-L67)) |

PerturbGen is best understood not as a member of one family but as a **synthesis**: it inherits the tokenization philosophy of token-based foundation models, the count likelihood of the scvi-tools lineage, the decoding machinery of masked generative image models, and the evaluation philosophy of distribution-matching methods — and adds the trajectory dimension as its own contribution.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph F["Published model families"]
        VA["VAE family (scGen, CPA, scVI)"]
        GF["Token foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT)"]
        MG["Masked generative models (MaskGIT, vision)"]
        DM["Distribution matching (CellOT-style OT, MMD)"]
    end
    subgraph P["PerturbGen synthesis"]
        TK["Geneformer-style rank tokens"]
        MD["Parallel masked iterative decoding"]
        TP["Time-aware positional encoding"]
        CD["Count decoder with ZINB/NB"]
        EV["MMD / Wasserstein / OT evaluation"]
    end
    GF -->|"tokenization borrowed"| TK
    MG -->|"MaskGIT-style decoding"| MD
    VA -->|"NB/ZINB from scvi-tools"| CD
    DM -->|"evaluation metrics"| EV
    MD --- TP
    TK --- MD
```

## Perturbation Operator Semantics: Token Edits vs. Latent Arithmetic

The sharpest contrast with the VAE family is *where the perturbation happens*. scGen-style models encode cells into a continuous latent space and apply vector arithmetic; PerturbGen applies the edit **directly to the token sequence** and lets the trained encoder–decoder–count-decoder pipeline propagate it. The implementation is compact and entirely verifiable: `perturb_sequence()` replaces tokens with the `<mask>` token (knockout) or the pad token, or removes them and left-shifts (`delete`), or removes and re-prepends them at the sequence head to inflate their rank abundance (`overexpress`) ([perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L269-L303), with the replacement-token selection at lines 313–322).

Two further axes make the operator more expressive than the latent-arithmetic baseline. First, the edit can be applied to the **source** sequence (so the perturbation propagates through the model into all predicted future states) or to the **target** sequences at selected time points (`pert_tps`), enforced by an explicit validation error ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L506-L575)). Second, knockout is additionally enforced during *generative* decoding by setting the perturbed genes' logits to −∞, so the model can never re-select the knocked-out gene while filling the masked sequence ([perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L235-L237)) — a guarantee that latent arithmetic cannot offer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph L["VAE-family operator (scGen / CPA)"]
        A1["Observed cells"] --> A2["Encode to latent z"]
        A2 --> A3["z plus delta vector"]
        A3 --> A4["One-shot decode"]
    end
    subgraph T["PerturbGen token operator"]
        B1["Observed tokenized cell"] --> B2{"perturbation mode"}
        B2 -->|mask| B3["Replace with mask token"]
        B2 -->|pad| B4["Replace with pad token"]
        B2 -->|delete| B5["Remove and left-shift"]
        B2 -->|overexpress| B6["Remove and re-prepend at head"]
        B3 --> B7["Conditional encoder-decoder"]
        B4 --> B7
        B5 --> B7
        B6 --> B7
        B7 --> B8["Count decoder predicts counts"]
    end
```

> [!TIP]
> The `overexpress` operator exploits the Geneformer tokenization itself: expression magnitude is encoded by token rank, so duplicating a gene's token at the sequence head raises its rank-encoded abundance — the perturbation acts on the representation's *native* magnitude encoding, not on raw counts.

## Generation Paradigm: Parallel Masked Iterative Decoding

Autoregressive token models (scGPT-style) generate genes sequentially, one token per forward pass; VAEs decode everything in a single pass. PerturbGen follows the **MaskGIT** paradigm, which is a deliberate middle ground: all masked positions are predicted in parallel each iteration, then re-masked by confidence, for a fixed budget of ~18 iterations — a number the code explicitly annotates as the MaskGIT optimum ([perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L36-L37)). Confidence comes from `1 − p(chosen token)`, tokens with high confidence are frozen first (`can_remask_prev_masked=False` freezes them), temperature is linearly annealed, and candidates are Gumbel-sampled after top-*k* filtering ([perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/transformer.py#L246-L263)).

Crucially for practitioners, perturbation inference in the released workflow does **not** use this generative loop: `perturb()` runs `validation_mode="inference"`, which decodes the *observed* target cells with the edit applied — the same mode as the released LPS and HSPC configs ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L514-L518)). The `temperature`/`iterations` arguments are retained only for backward compatibility and warn if changed ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L558-L563)). This is a pragmatic contrast with autoregressive baselines: perturbed responses are grounded in real observed cells rather than sampled from scratch, trading generative diversity for per-cell fidelity.

## Representation and Likelihood: Discrete Tokens with Count-Aware Losses

Both scGen and CPA model log-normalized, roughly Gaussian expression with MSE-style objectives; GEARS regresses gene-wise deltas. PerturbGen instead trains its count decoder with **zero-inflated negative binomial** likelihoods by default (`loss_mode="zinb"` in the API defaults, [perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L172-L176)), with the NB/ZINB functions explicitly ported from scvi-tools ([perturbgen/src/losses.py](/perturbgen/src/losses.py#L49-L89)). This gives it the overdispersion- and dropout-aware count modeling that the VAE lineage pioneered, while the discrete token front-end comes from the Geneformer lineage — the two lineages rarely meet in a single architecture. A compatibility hook confirms the contrast is deliberate: setting `loss_mode="mse"` in an eval config switches target data to `normalize_total` + `log1p`, i.e., the exact continuous regime VAE baselines operate in ([perturbgen/Perturb/val.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/val.py#L128-L132)).

The full stack is a two-stage design — a MaskGIT-style masking model, then a count decoder trained on top ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L15-L17)) — so the discrete generative model produces token identities and a separate likelihood head produces interpretable counts. See [scMASKGIT Masked Generative Encoder](6-scmaskgit-masked-generative-encoder), [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training), and [ZINB and Negative Binomial Losses](24-zinb-and-negative-binomial-losses).

## Evaluation Paradigm: Distribution-Level Metrics

VAE-family and GEARS papers evaluate primarily with per-gene correlations and differential-expression overlap. PerturbGen's perturbation harness instead records **distribution- and embedding-level** statistics per run: `wasserstein_distance`, `delta_probs`/`delta_gene_probs`, embedding cosine similarities (CLS, gene-mean, background), plus true/perturbed/predicted counts ([perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L200-L225)). The MMD implementation supports linear, polynomial, and multi-bandwidth RBF kernels ([perturbgen/src/mmd.py](/perturbgen/src/mmd.py#L14-L67)), and optimal transport lives alongside as a first-class metric module (`src/optimal_transport.py`). The rationale mirrors CellOT-style evaluation: when the model predicts *distributions of cell states* rather than point estimates, per-gene correlation alone under-measures fidelity — a fuller treatment is in [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport).

> [!TIP]
> Because `perturb()` decodes observed cells in inference mode, each perturbed cell is paired with a real unperturbed counterpart — which is exactly why embedding cosine similarity and delta-probability metrics are computable at single-cell granularity, something pure generative baselines cannot report without held-out pairs.

## Practical Selection Guidance

| Your situation | Better fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| One control/stimulated snapshot, no time series | scGen / CPA | Minimal data, well-understood latent arithmetic |
| Unseen *combinatorial* perturbations, static setting | GEARS | Graph priors generalize across combinations |
| Intermediate/unobserved time points along a trajectory | **PerturbGen** | Sinusoidal time encoding supports interpolation/extrapolation ([perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py](/perturbgen/Modules/transformer.py#L63-L67)) |
| Count-level, overdispersed predictions with uncertainty | **PerturbGen** | ZINB count decoder + `n_samples` draws ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L494-L512)) |
| Population-level response distributions | **PerturbGen** | MMD/Wasserstein/OT metrics built into the harness ([perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py](/perturbgen/Perturb/trainer.py#L200-L225)) |
| Pretrained encoder transfer across cohorts | **PerturbGen** | Frozen `pretraining_cohort` encoder loaded by default ([README.md](/README.md#L106-L113)) |

Two operational caveats follow from the comparison. A source knockout requires the gene to actually be expressed in the source state, or every cell is filtered out ([perturbgen/model.py](/perturbgen/model.py#L539-L541)) — unlike latent addition, which silently accepts any gene. And the perturbation operator is defined only for genes in the tokenized vocabulary (mapped via the `mapping_dict`), matching the foundation-model constraint of Geneformer-style tokenization. For benchmarking PerturbGen against such baselines yourself, the repository's harness is the starting point — see [Test and Benchmark Suite](26-test-and-benchmark-suite).

## Summary

PerturbGen occupies a distinctive point in the perturbation-modeling design space: **Geneformer-style discrete tokenization** (from foundation models), **MaskGIT-style parallel masked decoding** (from image generative models), **time-aware positional encoding** (its own contribution for dynamics), **scvi-tools-style count likelihoods** (from the VAE lineage), and **distribution-level evaluation** (from the OT/MMD lineage). Its perturbation operator — `mask`/`pad`/`delete`/`overexpress` applied to source or target token sequences — is structurally more constrained and more interpretable than latent arithmetic, while remaining expressive enough to propagate edits across predicted trajectories. To go deeper into the machinery compared here, continue to [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview), [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes), and [Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding).


# Test and Benchmark Suite



Perturbgen ships a compact but deliberately structured quality infrastructure: five functional test modules that validate correctness end-to-end, and four standalone microbenchmarks that quantify performance-critical refactors. Unlike conventional CI-driven suites, this suite is built for **HPC-cluster execution and refactor verification** — tests exercise real PyTorch Lightning training loops on synthetic data, while benchmarks use CUDA event timing to isolate the cost of specific optimizations (fused optimizers, `torch.compile`, context caching, projection skipping). This page explains the suite's architecture, the fixture strategies that keep GPU-backed tests fast, and how to run each component.

## Suite Architecture: A Two-Tier Design

The suite separates **correctness verification** from **performance measurement** into two distinct file families with different execution models. Functional tests (`test_*.py`) assert behavioral invariants — deterministic generation, checkpoint reproducibility, config validation — and run under either `unittest` discovery or `pytest`. Benchmarks (`benchmark_*.py`) are standalone scripts that print timing reports rather than asserting pass/fail, and are executed directly with `python`. This split mirrors the actual development workflow: tests guard against regressions, benchmarks quantify whether a refactor delivered its intended speedup.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Tier1["Tier 1 — Correctness (test_*.py)"]
        direction TB
        T1["test_api_perturb.py<br/>unittest · CPU-only · mocked"]
        T2["test_generation_efficiency.py<br/>pytest · golden refs · GPU-optional"]
        T3["test_cellgen_training.py<br/>unittest · full pipeline · shared ckpts"]
        T4["test_perturbation.py<br/>script-style · inference"]
    end

    subgraph Tier2["Tier 2 — Performance (benchmark_*.py)"]
        direction TB
        B1["benchmark_generation_efficiency.py<br/>cache ablation"]
        B2["benchmark_skip_context_logits.py<br/>monkey-patched A/B"]
        B3["benchmark_fused_adam.py<br/>optimizer step"]
        B4["benchmark_training_compile.py<br/>torch.compile"]
    end

    U["utils.py<br/>dummy_dataset + dummy_cell_gene_matrix"]
    RUN["run_test.sh<br/>LSF job → unittest discover"]

    U --> T3
    U --> T4
    RUN --> T1
    RUN --> T2
    RUN --> T3
    RUN --> T4
    T3 -. "speedup validated by" .-> B1
    T2 -.-> B1
    T2 -.-> B4

    style Tier1 fill:#e8f4e8
    style Tier2 fill:#e8e8f4
```

The dependency arrows matter: `utils.py` fixtures feed only the Lightning-based tests, while the efficiency benchmarks exist specifically to validate the caching and compilation features that `test_generation_efficiency.py` guards for *correctness*. Together they form paired correctness/performance contracts per optimization.

Sources: [tests/utils.py](perturbgen/tests/utils.py#L1-L74), [run_test.sh](perturbgen/run_test.sh#L20-L24), [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L1-L12)

## Inventory of the Suite

The suite comprises ten files with clearly partitioned responsibilities. The table below is the authoritative map for deciding where a new test or measurement belongs.

| File | Framework | Scope | Hardware | Key Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `utils.py` | — | Shared fixtures | CPU | Synthetic HF `Dataset` + Poisson count matrices |
| `test_api_perturb.py` | `unittest` | `PerturbGen.perturb()` config assembly | CPU only | `mock.patch` + temp dirs |
| `test_cellgen_training.py` | `unittest` | Masking → embedding → count decoder → generation | GPU-conditional | Shared checkpoint fixtures in `setUpClass` |
| `test_generation_efficiency.py` | `pytest` | `generate()` determinism, golden IDs, `torch.compile` | GPU-optional | Golden reference tensors, cache resets |
| `test_perturbation.py` | script | `PerturberTrainer` end-to-end inference | GPU-conditional | `trainer.test()` with 1 batch |
| `benchmark_generation_efficiency.py` | standalone | `generate()` wall-clock | CPU + GPU | `--baseline` arg, cache ablation |
| `benchmark_skip_context_logits.py` | standalone | Skip LM-head in context path | GPU | Monkey-patched `call_decoder` A/B |
| `benchmark_fused_adam.py` | standalone | Fused vs. non-fused Adam | GPU | CUDA event timing on `.step()` |
| `benchmark_training_compile.py` | standalone | `torch.compile` training step | GPU | Warmup + median of reps |

Sources: [test_api_perturb.py](perturbgen/tests/test_api_perturb.py#L1-L5), [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L1-L45), [benchmark_training_compile.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_training_compile.py#L1-L9)

## Synthetic Data Fixtures: The Foundation of GPU-Free Realism

All Lightning-backed tests avoid real datasets entirely. `utils.py` provides two fixture factories that mimic the tokenized data layout the models consume. **`dummy_dataset()`** builds a Hugging Face `Dataset` with random gene token IDs sampled from `range(2, vocab_size)` (reserving indices 0–3 for special tokens), forces the last 10 positions to `0` (the `<pad>` token, simulating masked positions), and attaches `cell_type`, `length`, and `cell_pairing_index` columns. When called with `total_time_steps`, it returns a dict of per-timepoint datasets keyed `tgt_dataset_t1`, `tgt_dataset_t2`, ... — matching the multi-timepoint pairing schema.

**`dummy_cell_gene_matrix()`** complements this with raw count matrices drawn from a Poisson distribution (λ=10), squeezed to `(num_cells, 1, num_genes)` and keyed `tgt_h5ad_t1`, ... when multi-step. The pairing between token IDs and counts mirrors what `PerturbGenDataModule` expects in production, so tests exercise the real dataflow path without any file I/O. This is why tests can run a full train-epoch in seconds: the fixture shapes (100 samples, vocab 100–101, seq len 50, batch 4) are deliberately tiny.

Sources: [tests/utils.py](perturbgen/tests/utils.py#L7-L55), [tests/utils.py](perturbgen/tests/utils.py#L57-L74)

## Functional Tests in Depth

### API-Level Config Tests: Fast, Mocked, Deterministic

`test_api_perturb.py` is the only true unit-test module: it needs no GPU, no data, and no model weights. It verifies the contract that `PerturbGen.perturb()` builds a valid YAML config for `Perturb/val.py`. The fixture `_make_tokenized_dir()` creates an empty directory tree with exactly the filenames the tokenized-dataset layout validator checks for (`dataset_10_hvg_src/src.dataset`, `token_id_to_genename_10_hvg.pkl`, etc.), satisfying path validation without real data. The `_run()` helper then **mocks `perturbgen.Perturb.val.main`** with a function that reads back the generated YAML — capturing what would have been executed.

Five test cases pin the config contract: `extra_config` user keys must merge into the generated config (`test_extra_config_is_merged`); defaults appear when no override is given (`validation_mode='inference'`, `num_workers=4`); relative gene-file paths are absolutized; protected keys like `trainer.n_samples` or `trainer.num_heads` raise `ValueError('cannot set')`; and malformed sections raise `ValueError`/`TypeError`. This module demonstrates the suite's layered philosophy — test the *cheapest observable surface* first before escalating to GPU-backed integration.

Sources: [test_api_perturb.py](perturbgen/tests/test_api_perturb.py#L13-L25), [test_api_perturb.py](perturbgen/tests/test_api_perturb.py#L42-L61), [test_api_perturb.py](perturbgen/tests/test_api_perturb.py#L63-L100)

### End-to-End Pipeline Tests with Checkpoint Fixtures

`test_cellgen_training.py` is the suite's heavyweight: it runs the complete two-stage pipeline (see [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training)) on synthetic data. Its defining innovation is the **shared checkpoint fixture hierarchy**, which eliminates redundant training across test classes:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph ClassHierarchy["Class Hierarchy (shared state flows down)"]
        MIX["TestConfigMixin<br/>init_shared_state():<br/>seed 42, dummy data, configs"]
        FIX["MaskCheckpointFixture<br/>setUpClass(): train masking<br/>model 1 epoch → new_mask.ckpt"]
        CD["TestCountDecoder<br/>setUpClass(): train count decoder<br/>1 epoch → new_count.ckpt"]
        GEN["TestGeneration<br/>reuses BOTH checkpoints<br/>→ trainer.test() generation"]
    end

    MIX --> FIX
    FIX --> CD
    CD --> GEN

    subgraph Standalone["Standalone Classes"]
        TM["TestMasking<br/>forward-pass shape check"]
        TE["TestEmbedding<br/>h5ad embedding export"]
        TC["TestCheckpointConsistency<br/>ref vs new weight compare"]
    end

    MIX -.-> TM
    FIX -.-> TE
    TC -.->|"reads res/*.ckpt"| FIX

    style FIX fill:#fff4e0
    style CD fill:#fff4e0
```

The `MaskCheckpointFixture.setUpClass` (lines 198–246) implements memoization via class-level attributes `_shared_ckpt_path` / `_shared_tmpdir`: the *first* class to trigger it trains a `PerturbGenTrainer` for exactly one epoch with `limit_train_batches=1`, checkpoints it, and copies the result to `tests/res/new_mask.ckpt`. Every subsequent inheriting class (embedding export, count decoder) loads that checkpoint instead of retraining. `TestCountDecoder` applies the identical pattern one level deeper, producing `new_count.ckpt`. This converts what would be ~4 full training runs into exactly 2.

Individual assertions target the invariants that matter scientifically: `TestMasking.test_forward_pass` checks `dec_embedding` has shape `(batch, max_seq_length, d_model)`; `TestEmbedding.test_cell_embeddings_only` verifies that `return_embeddings=True` with `return_gene_embs=False` still writes exactly one `*inference_embs*.h5ad` containing `cls_embeddings` in `obsm` and *no* gene embeddings in `varm` — a regression guard against a previously observed `None`-iteration bug (documented in the inline comment at line 297–298).

Sources: [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L49-L191), [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L198-L246), [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L272-L322), [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L325-L367)

### Checkpoint Reproducibility Testing

The final class, `TestCheckpointConsistency`, implements a **reference-checkpoint comparison** pattern: it loads `tests/res/reference_mask.ckpt` and `reference_count.ckpt` (previously recorded baselines) and compares every tensor against the newly produced `new_mask.ckpt` / `new_count.ckpt` using `torch.allclose(atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-4)`. The `compare_weights()` helper collects mismatches with their max absolute diff, and the test deliberately accumulates *all* failures before calling `self.fail()` once — so a single run reports every divergent checkpoint pair rather than aborting at the first. This is the suite's defense against nondeterministic training drift, complementing the seed pinning (`pl.seed_everything(42)`, `cudnn.deterministic=True`) established in `init_shared_state`.

Sources: [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L452-L484), [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L486-L532)

### Generation Regression Tests: Determinism and Golden References

`test_generation_efficiency.py` guards the generation-optimization refactor in `Modules/transformer.py` (relevant background: [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes)). Its docstring enumerates the four guarded properties: deterministic token IDs under fixed seeds, stability of the no-context path, non-`None` `mean_embedding` in training forward, and cache-invariant generation. The module is organized into six pytest classes, each addressing one invariant:

| Class | Invariant Guarded | Technique |
|---|---|---|
| `TestGenerateDeterminism` | Same seed → identical token IDs | Run `generate()` twice, reset `_enc_cache_key`/`_ctx_cache_key` between runs, `torch.equal` |
| `TestGoldenReference` | Output matches refactor-era snapshot | Hard-coded `REFERENCE_IDS_T3` tensor compared bit-exact |
| `TestTrainingForward` | `not_masked=True` path intact post-cleanup | Shape + non-`None` assertions on `mean_embedding` |
| `TestContextCacheCorrectness` | Cache hits don't alter output; multi-`pred_tps` isolation | Cache reset + re-run comparison; `sequence_length` param |
| `TestCountDecoderGenerate` | `generate_counts()` end-to-end | Shape check on `count_output_t3['count_mean']` |
| `TestCompiledModel` | `torch.compile` equivalence | `torch.equal` on token IDs; `allclose(atol=1e-4)` on logits; CUDA-only |

The **golden reference pattern** deserves explanation. `REFERENCE_IDS_T3` is a 2×30 tensor of token IDs recorded from the unmodified codebase with seeds (model=42, run=7) and `iterations=4`. If a future change alters generation semantics — even by one token — the test fails with an explicit expected-vs-got diff. The code also includes a self-recording escape hatch: when the reference is `None`, the test prints the tensor to copy back in and skips, formalizing the snapshot-update workflow in a single file.

> [!TIP]
> The cache-reset idiom `model._enc_cache_key = None; model._ctx_cache_key = None` before each timing or determinism run is essential — without it, the second `generate()` call would hit the encoder/context caches and measure cache lookup rather than full computation. Both the tests and all four benchmarks replicate this idiom.

Sources: [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L1-L37), [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L109-L175), [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L183-L250), [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L292-L345)

### Perturbation Inference Test

`test_perturbation.py` validates `PerturberTrainer` (the perturbation-mode trainer) using the shared dummy fixtures and a realistic production configuration: `d_model=768`, `perturbation_mode='overexpress'`, `perturbation_sequence='tgt'`, `context_mode=True`, `temperature=1.5`, 19 MaskGIT iterations, and `pos_encoding_mode='time_pos_sin'` (see [Time-Aware Positional Encoding](8-time-aware-positional-encoding)). Rather than asserting individual tensors, it delegates to Lightning's `trainer.test()` with `limit_test_batches=1` — a single inference batch through the full test step, including perturbed-sequence construction and metric computation. This is a smoke test in structure but an integration test in coverage, and like the training tests it adapts precision to hardware (`16` on GPU, `32` on CPU).

Sources: [test_perturbation.py](perturbgen/tests/test_perturbation.py#L27-L62), [test_perturbation.py](perturbgen/tests/test_perturbation.py#L70-L100), [test_perturbation.py](perturbgen/tests/test_perturbation.py#L124-L138)

## Execution Model

The canonical entry point is `run_test.sh`, an LSF (`BSUB`) batch job header targeting a CPU-interactive queue with 10 GB RAM. After loading CUDA 12.1 and activating the `cytomeister` environment, it runs:

```bash
python -m unittest discover /.../perturbgen/tests/
```

Note the discovery implications: `unittest discover` collects `unittest.TestCase` subclasses (`test_api_perturb.py`, `test_cellgen_training.py`), and because pytest is a superset runner, the same directory also works under `pytest` for the function-style classes in `test_generation_efficiency.py`. Module-level code executes at *collection* time in both frameworks — which is why `test_cellgen_training.py`'s hard path assertions (lines 37–40) fail fast at import if the Lustre-mounted encoder or mapping dictionaries are absent. Two alternative invocation forms appear in comments: single-module discovery and direct pytest per file.

Sources: [run_test.sh](perturbgen/run_test.sh#L1-L25), [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L25-L44)

## The Benchmark Layer: Measuring What Refactors Deliver

### Common Measurement Methodology

All four benchmarks share a rigorous timing protocol that intermediate developers should replicate in their own measurements. The pattern is: **N warmup iterations** (to trigger CUDA kernel compilation and allocator warm-up) followed by **N timed repetitions**, each bracketed by `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before and after, measured with `torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)` pairs, and summarized by the **median** rather than the mean — median is robust to the occasional garbage-collection pause or clock-spike that would otherwise inflate averages. Every benchmark resets `_enc_cache_key`/`_ctx_cache_key` before each repetition so that cache effects are measured deliberately, not accidentally.

Sources: [benchmark_fused_adam.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_fused_adam.py#L61-L93), [benchmark_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py#L65-L111), [benchmark_training_compile.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_training_compile.py#L69-L100)

### The Four Benchmarks Compared

| Benchmark | Question Answered | Dimensions | A/B Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| `benchmark_generation_efficiency.py` | How fast is `generate()` overall, and what does the context cache save? | CPU config: batch 4, seq 200, vocab 300, 18 iters | Runs WITH and WITHOUT cache by patching `forward` to clear `_ctx_cache_key` after every call; `--baseline <s>` flag computes speedup vs. a recorded pre-refactor number |
| `benchmark_skip_context_logits.py` | What does skipping the `decoder_fc` LM-head projection in `generate_context` save? | GPU: vocab 25000, d_model 768, 6 layers, batch {4,16,32} | Monkey-patches `call_decoder` to force `compute_logits=True` (BEFORE) vs. native `False` (AFTER); also verifies training-step timing is untouched |
| `benchmark_fused_adam.py` | Does fused Adam accelerate the optimizer step? | GPU: vocab 25000, d_model 768, 2 layers (fits MIG slice) | Two full models, `Adam(fused=False/True)`, timed on complete forward+backward+step; graceful fallback if fused is unsupported |
| `benchmark_training_compile.py` | Does `torch.compile` speed up training steps? | GPU: vocab 25000, d_model 768, seq 128, batch 32, 6 layers | Two model builds with `compile_model=False/True`, identical step function, per-step median |

Sources: [benchmark_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py#L147-L172), [benchmark_skip_context_logits.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_skip_context_logits.py#L1-L14), [benchmark_fused_adam.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_fused_adam.py#L1-L8), [benchmark_training_compile.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_training_compile.py#L1-L9)

### The Cache-Ablation Technique

The most methodologically interesting is the **context-cache ablation** in `benchmark_generation_efficiency.py`. To isolate what the context cache contributes, the benchmark cannot simply "turn it off" via a flag — instead it wraps `model.forward` with a patch that clears `_ctx_cache_key` after every call, guaranteeing the cache never hits during the measured run. The report then prints the derived call-count arithmetic: with `context_tps=[1,2]` and 18 iterations, the cache saves `len(context_tps) × (iterations − 1) = 34` decoder passes per `generate()` call. The no-context config (`context_tps=None`) runs as an experimental control where the cache should show *zero* effect — a built-in sanity check on the measurement itself.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph MeasuredRun["Measured Run WITH cache"]
        G1["generate() iter 1..18"] --> C1["ctx cache HIT<br/>1x context compute"]
    end
    subgraph AblatedRun["Ablated Run (cache defeated)"]
        P["patched forward:<br/>clear _ctx_cache_key<br/>after every call"] --> G2["generate() iter 1..18"] --> C2["ctx recomputed<br/>each iter"]
    end
    C1 --> S["speedup = median_ablated / median_cached"]
    C2 --> S

    style C1 fill:#e8f4e8
    style C2 fill:#f4e8e8
```

Sources: [benchmark_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py#L53-L86), [benchmark_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py#L147-L168), [benchmark_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py#L175-L204)

### Monkey-Patch A/B for Projection Skipping

`benchmark_skip_context_logits.py` targets a different waste pattern: `generate_context` builds context embeddings by running the decoder, but only consumes `dec_embedding` — the `d_model → vocab` projection (`decoder_fc`) was previously computed and discarded. The BEFORE state is reconstructed *without modifying source code*: the benchmark monkey-patches `model.call_decoder` to force `kwargs['compute_logits'] = True`, times it, restores the original, and times the native AFTER path. Batching over {4, 16, 32} reveals how the projection waste scales, and the closing `bench_training()` section confirms the training loop never calls `generate_context`, so the optimization carries zero training-side risk. The final summary table prints per-batch BEFORE/AFTER/speedup rows.

> [!TIP]
> The monkey-patch pattern (swap a bound method, measure, restore) is the suite's standard for benchmarking hypothetical code states — it lets you quantify a proposed optimization *before* committing it, and the same pattern is reusable for any `compute_logits`-style gated computation.

Sources: [benchmark_skip_context_logits.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_skip_context_logits.py#L1-L14), [benchmark_skip_context_logits.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_skip_context_logits.py#L79-L135), [benchmark_skip_context_logits.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_skip_context_logits.py#L138-L171)

## Development Workflow: Tests and Benchmarks as Paired Contracts

The suite encodes a repeatable refactor workflow, visible in the `benchmark_generation_efficiency.py` usage docstring:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. Record baseline<br/>python benchmark_generation_efficiency.py<br/>→ note median seconds"] --> B["2. Implement optimization<br/>(caching, compile, projection skip)"]
    B --> C["3. Verify correctness<br/>pytest test_generation_efficiency.py<br/>determinism + golden refs + compile equivalence"]
    C --> D{"Tests pass?"}
    D -->|No| B
    D -->|Yes| E["4. Quantify gain<br/>python benchmark_generation_efficiency.py<br/>--baseline <recorded>"]
    E --> F["5. Lock invariants<br/>refresh golden IDs only if<br/>semantics intentionally changed"]
```

Step 3's equivalence tests are the linchpin: `TestCompiledModel` asserts compiled and uncompiled models produce *identical* token IDs and `allclose` logits, meaning `torch.compile` must be semantically transparent — any speedup it delivers is "free." This correctness-before-performance ordering is the suite's core discipline, and the same contract applies to DeepSpeed-scale training discussed in [Distributed Training with DDP and DeepSpeed](19-distributed-training-with-ddp-and-deepspeed).

Sources: [benchmark_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_generation_efficiency.py#L7-L13), [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L288-L345)

## Practical Caveats

Three operational realities affect anyone running this suite. **First, hardcoded infrastructure paths**: `test_cellgen_training.py` and `test_perturbation.py` assert the existence of Lustre-mounted encoder checkpoints and token-mapping pickles (e.g., `/lustre/scratch126/cellgen/.../foundation_107m/checkpoints/...`) at import time, and `test_perturbation.py` force-changes the working directory to a cluster root — the suite as committed assumes execution on the originating HPC environment and needs path substitution elsewhere. **Second, mixed frameworks and conventions**: `test_generation_efficiency.py` is pytest-native, `test_cellgen_training.py` is unittest-native with pytest-compatible shared fixtures, and `test_perturbation.py` is cell-delimited script style (`# %%`) — `unittest discover` will execute the last only as a flat script. **Third, hardware gating**: benchmarks exit immediately without CUDA, compiled-model tests `pytest.skip` gracefully, but the two full-pipeline test files will import-fail on missing cluster artifacts before any skip logic engages.

Sources: [test_cellgen_training.py](perturbgen/tests/test_cellgen_training.py#L25-L44), [test_perturbation.py](perturbgen/tests/test_perturbation.py#L22-L24), [benchmark_fused_adam.py](perturbgen/tests/benchmark_fused_adam.py#L106-L111), [test_generation_efficiency.py](perturbgen/tests/test_generation_efficiency.py#L293-L296)

## Where to Go Next

To understand what the tests are actually verifying, read the architecture pages first: the generation loop guarded by the golden references is detailed in [In Silico Perturbation Modes](10-in-silico-perturbation-modes), and the two-stage checkpoint fixture mirrors [Two-Stage Masking and Count Decoder Training](7-two-stage-masking-and-count-decoder-training). The metrics computed inside `trainer.test()` (MMD, EMD, optimal transport) are explained in [Evaluation Metrics: MMD, EMD, Optimal Transport](13-evaluation-metrics-mmd-emd-optimal-transport), while the config keys asserted by `test_api_perturb.py` map directly onto [Configuration System and Path Management](17-configuration-system-and-path-management). For the training infrastructure the benchmarks measure, continue to [Distributed Training with DDP and DeepSpeed](19-distributed-training-with-ddp-and-deepspeed) and [Experiment Tracking with Weights and Biases](20-experiment-tracking-with-weights-and-biases).
